c700u10-jun24-03-q:
This question was more demanding. It was worth ten marks and focused on a longer section of the text. It was a two-part question and, although its main aim was to test analysis of how writers use language to achieve effects, it allowed credit to be given for understanding of the character of Alice’s aunt. The issue of ‘how’ the writer created impressions of the aunt was often a matter of selecting the relevant evidence but the successful answers required some inference and analysis. The aunt perhaps seemed kind and well-meaning in offering to take Alice and bring her up in the town, but she was also assertive and forceful, turning up at the farm to argue her case. She told her brother in no uncertain terms that he could not bring up a girl properly. She had strong views and was not afraid to express them bluntly, insisting that a girl needs ‘other women’ in her life. She was combative and when Jack ‘fought back’ rather aggressively and insisted on his rights as a father, the aunt was not intimidated. She stood up to him and just changed her argument.

She used emotional pressure on her brother, insisting that he would ruin Alice’s life by keeping her ‘cooped up’ on the farm and denying her the opportunity to make friends or learn how to run a home. Her priorities perhaps seemed rather conventional or old-fashioned, but she did seem to be concerned for Alice’s well-being. However, she knew Alice would not choose to leave the farm and, knowing when she was beaten, she gave up arguing and muttered ‘dire warnings’ about girls who lack a ‘proper education’. She was secretly disappointed when Jack managed well and she complimented her brother on his parenting only once, and grudgingly at that. However, she did acknowledge that Alice had turned out rather well and that bringing her up cannot have been easy. Most candidates saw her as a strong and rather abrasive character, but she was also well- intentioned in her way. It was not too difficult to engage with the character of the aunt and the better answers were methodical and detailed, using the text purposefully to support a good range of impressions. Some candidates noticed the author’s use of dialogue and action and the omniscient author employing ‘showing’ as well as ‘telling’. The successful answers showed a good grasp of the character and the text and had some substance as well as insight. Less successful responses tended to be thin and unfocused, offering limited impressions and focusing on the aunt’s thoughts, actions and beliefs. Some merely ‘told the story’.

She was allowed to go to parties and stay in town with friends, but she was always back on time. c700u10-jun24-05-q: This question invited evaluation of the character of Jack Cogdon across the whole passage. The teacher described him as a lonely and pathetic farmer, depending on his daughter to cook and keep house and the candidates were asked to respond to that view. The key to success was to take a coherent stance and to use the textual detail to develop a persuasive and valid argument. As usual, a methodical approach seemed to work best here. At the beginning of the story the author made it clear that Jack fought to keep Alice and he did offer to let her choose whether to stay with him on the farm. He expected her to work on the farm and in the house, but the author explicitly stated that he was ‘kind in his way’ and loved his daughter. Alice was not presented as a domestic servant. Jack managed well as a parent and even his sister had to pay him a grudging compliment. He seemed to be a conscientious father and also quite tolerant. However, the issue of Alice’s future was not discussed, and he seemed to assume that nothing would change and that she would stay on the farm. Their life on the farm seemed to have settled into a routine with which they were both content. She did not complain. Jack was alone, and possibly lonely, and he was ‘taken aback’ when Alice raised the subject of what she was going to do after school. He smiled but ‘weakly’. A day he had dreaded had arrived and he was clearly uncomfortable as Alice pressed on with the conversation. The possibility of ‘losing’ his daughter to the big city was unsettling for him and he concentrated on eating his food, avoiding her gaze when she mentioned art school and Melbourne. He did say ‘why not?’ and admitted it was her life but the prospect of losing Alice left him silent and unsettled and anxious, although he tried to act normally. Alice understood what her father was feeling and what was at stake. If she left the farm Jack could never retire. He would work until he was no longer able to work and then he would have to sell the farm and move into one of ‘those houses’ filled with retired farmers. Jack desperately wanted a successor to leave the farm to and he hoped that Alice would marry a farmer’s son. When he spoke to Mr Paget, both men were laughing and smiling but he seemed attracted to the idea of marrying Alice to his friend’s son. In some ways the narrative supported the teacher’s view, and it was possible to argue that there was some truth in her claim that Jack was selfish and controlling. However, those who ‘strongly agreed’ with the teacher’s view had a difficult case to argue and most did so only by ignoring much of the text. It was possible to make the case against Jack, but it was not easy. Those candidates who felt that the teacher’s judgement was rather harsh and unfair were usually on safer ground. The most successful answers grasped that the situation was complex, and that Jack was conflicted. He clearly would have preferred it if Alice had married the farmer’s son and taken over the farm. It would have been very convenient for him and the farm, but he was not a tyrant and there was no real evidence that he was going to force Alice to sacrifice herself. Those who tried to agree and disagree with the teacher often got into a muddle and failed to establish a clear direction for their answer.
c700u10-jun24-11-q:
This section followed the familiar pattern and there was a choice of four titles which offered opportunities to write imaginatively or from personal experience. All four titles attracted significant numbers of candidates. There was some evidence of ‘prepared’ stories being used as batches of candidates produced identical responses. This is not in the spirit of the examination and can be counter-productive in preventing candidates from showing what they can really do. Handwriting was also an issue and there were more problems than usual with legibility. There are solutions available, and it would be beneficial if they were used where appropriate.

Comments on individual questions/sections

(a) This title allowed a range of narrative perspectives and, although most wrote from the perspective of a pupil, some described events through the eyes of a teacher. Less successful responses sprawled across months or even years, but the better ones captured the feeling of being new and facing a school for the first time. There were a minority of implausible melodramas, but most had a sense of authenticity.

(b) This was clearly a first-person narrative, but it was quite open and offered a wide range of opportunities. Some candidates struggled to match their stories to the title but most described exploits in sport or in helping others. (c) This title invited a focus on a specific incident involving the telling of a lie. The lies were rarely too serious but most candidates who attempted this title did not seem to hesitate when falsehood was required. (d) This was an open title which involved the notion of choice but really left the candidates to decide which direction they wished to take it. Characteristics of Successful Responses • In Q01 the successful responses are clear in presentation and concise and focused in content • A successful response to a question asking for ‘impressions’ of a character should move beyond quotation from the text to explore the significance of the evidence and to suggest what it shows. • Successful writing responses are well-judged in length and are neither too brief nor too long. • Successful writing displays technical control, particularly with tenses and sentence construction.

Areas for Improvement • The ‘attempt rate’ for question 05 is relatively low and time management is an issue. It is sensible to leave enough time for the narrative but not at the expense of 05. • Reading responses need to be focused and as concise as is reasonable. Candidates need to select relevant material from the specified section of text and use it effectively. • In Q05 there is a need to establish a coherent line of argument and use the text to support it. Answers which ‘agree and disagree’ usually drift in to muddle or contradiction. A sensible overview of the text is required here. • Technical control of spelling, sentences and punctuation is a familiar area of weakness in writing. Basic errors are often numerous, and this aspect of writing has a significant weighting. Candidates should leave themselves enough time to proofread their creative writing.

7 For example, Mary was Clive’s ex-wife and she had not seen Clive for years. She was inevitably older and greyer, but she was still an undeniably attractive woman. She was tall and dressed stylishly and tastefully. She also dressed expensively. She seemed friendly as she smiled warmly when talking to an old aunt.

c700u10-jun25-02-q:
This question assessed AO2 and was only worth five marks and only covered a short paragraph of the text. As usual, the challenge to the candidates was to be thorough but concise. The question asked for impressions of Clive and this inevitably involved direct reference to the text but also some inference and explanation. The better candidates achieved a pragmatic blend of inference and evidence while remaining aware of time.

This was the candidates’ first opportunity to engage with the character of Clive, and it was fair to say that whatever the reader had made of him in the opening paragraph, he now emerged as selfish and cruel. He forgot that he had left her and only saw now that he had hurt her. He had left her because she had begun to look old and most candidates saw that he was self-absorbed and apparently oblivious to the effect of the passage of time on him. Some argued, quite rightly, that he seemed to find younger women irresistible (Colette was twenty four and French) but he was shallow and fickle. He could barely remember Colette and his relationships did not last very long. There had been ‘a string of successors’ and he seemed to need constant change and ‘the thrill of a new interest’. Clive was described as enjoying the excitement of a ‘secret meeting’ and he seemed to relish the thrill of adulterous affairs. He seemed to have no grasp of the concept of fidelity. He was also obviously vain as he liked the ‘flattery’ of a new face turned to his.

Less successful answers offered limited impressions and relied simply on quoting ‘facts’ from the text without drawing out a relevant comment. The best answers got the measure of Clive and supported their impressions with well-chosen reference to the text.
c700u10-jun25-03-q:
The first two questions were based on short sections of text and offered a relatively straightforward opportunity to score well, which most candidates grasped. However, question 03 was on a longer section of text and required exploration of how the writer showed Clive’s thoughts and feelings about growing older. That said, credit could be given for accurately identifying his thoughts and feelings and supporting those observations by appropriate reference to the text. The answer to ‘how does a writer...’ is usually a matter of content and language and those who tracked the lines of the text methodically did well.

Close attention to language and what it showed or suggested was the best way into this question and the very first words of this section stated that Clive was ‘terrified of ageing’, showing his abnormal fear of growing older. It was a long-term concern and his fear of ageing had begun in his twenties when he realised that there were people younger than him. He was consumed by ‘dismay’ and ‘self-pity’, suggesting not only his consternation but also that he felt sorry for himself. His fear of getting older affected him physically as he felt ‘nausea’. Clive’s thirtieth birthday had ‘smashed’ into him and the writer clearly used the strong verb to convey Clive’s distress. The powerful simile ‘like a rock in a tranquil sea’ reinforced his horror.

8 He looked in the mirror more often and watched the faces of his contemporaries to compare how he was doing. His behaviour showed his fear and perhaps also his need for reassurance.

Mary’s calm and rational response to the passage of time made him feel resentful and misunderstood. The writer got inside character to show his extreme emotions, describing his feelings as ‘fits of terror’ and ‘cold fear’. When he reached fifty nine his feelings were shown in the choice of language. It was ‘an awful fact’ which ‘reared up’ at him and left him ‘reeling. He felt depressed and the writer mentioned Clive’s ‘dark moments’.

However, Clive thought ageing could be resisted through activity. He thought that travel and socialising with younger people could solve his problem. He avoided friends when they began to look ‘a touch decrepit’ and, of course, he had married a younger woman.

The basic point that Clive was afraid of ageing was not difficult to grasp but the better answers engaged with the text in detail and showed understanding and coherence. The very best answers understood the writer’s technique, particularly the use of language for effect.
c700u10-jun25-04-q:
This was a two-part question which also assessed AO2 and required the candidates to identify impressions of the character of Mary and also explore ‘how’ the writer created those impressions. The question covered a longer section of the text but, again, the best approach was to track the text and take ‘what’ and ‘how’ together, using the details in the text to draw out the impressions of Mary.

For example, the first impression in these lines was that, contrary to Clive’s expectations, she was completely oblivious to his presence. He expected her to be thinking about him and scouring the room for him, but the writer dismissed that fanciful notion with the unequivocal statement ‘She did not’. It was true that the writer used a short sentence here, but the better candidates had something to say about why that was effective and mentioned that it was blunt and emphatic. The simplicity of the statement was crushing, and it was worth noting that the writer used a single short sentence for effect. The vague assertion that the writer ‘used short sentences’ was not enough on its own and was imprecise.

Mary also seemed pleasant and considerate as she was described talking patiently with the aunt and laughing in a way that made Clive jealous. The writer used Clive’s knowledge of Mary over the years since their separation and his perspective painted a picture of an independent woman who lived alone, had never remarried and had built a career in hospital administration. When Clive made his move, Mary was polite but showed no enthusiasm for him. She responded in a ‘flat tone’ showing no emotion, least of all surprise. Clive noticed how attractive she looked, and her good taste in jewellery, but she was unmoved by his ‘look’ which was intended to ‘unsettle’ her and, unlike Clive, she seemed calm and composed. She merely asked about ‘poor Susan’ and her flu. Some thought she was sympathetic but others read it as sarcastic. She gave terse, factual responses to his attempts to impress by engaging her in conversation. The writer used Clive’s perspective to present Mary as ‘confident’ and ‘high-powered’. Mary had ‘authority’ and was ‘a woman of her time’. When Clive gazed at her with ‘unashamed admiration’ she was ‘restless’. She looked over his shoulder and sipped her drink. Clive interpreted her behaviour as positive and convinced himself that it was time for a ‘direct approach’. Mary hesitated when he asked her to meet and, although Clive did not see it, the better candidates saw that she was uncomfortable with his advances and probably searching for a way out.

9 The best answers understood that Mary was presented as the opposite of what Clive expected and built their responses on a series of clear and detailed impressions which showed insight.
c700u10-jun25-05-q:
The last question in this section, as always, required critical evaluation of the text as a whole and the wording of the question invited a personal response to the character of Clive Harper. However, while all candidates are entitled to their opinions, there is not an infinity of sensible responses to any text. For example, it was possible to feel some sympathy for Clive at times, but most successful candidates argued only too clearly that he was selfish and vain and richly deserved his humiliation at the end of the story. Those who tried to argue a ‘balanced’ position made life very difficult for themselves and those who disagreed unequivocally with the statement in the question found themselves in deep trouble.

A methodical approach worked best here, and the initial presentation of Clive showed him as cruel and selfish in his treatment of Mary. He had deserted her when he became aware that she ‘had begun to look old’ but his memory seemed rather selective as he ‘quite forgot that he had left her’. He moved from one relationship to another, not caring or remembering much about the women in his life. He was presented as self-obsessed and addicted to the thrill of the chase. He delighted in flattery as it boosted his vanity. There was little to say in defence of Clive in this part of the narrative.

Most candidates regarded his fears about ageing as an extension of his vanity and he could easily be seen as childish, self-pitying and irrational, particularly when contrasted with Mary’s calm and logical response to the passage of time. However, it was possible to argue that his fears were genuine and even to sympathise with him to some extent. That said, sympathy for Clive was in rather short supply, particularly when his fears were so clearly self-regarding. He was not one to feel the tragedy of the human condition. He only felt the tragedy of his own condition. The best answers noted that there were moments of possible sympathy but usually rejected them.

Clive felt a ‘tingle of pleasure’ when he thought of how Mary would react to seeing him and his vanity was as excruciating as his self-regard when he thought himself ‘lucky’ that his wife was unwell and unable to attend the wedding. The best answers spotted that Clive had the audacity to think that he could have an affair with Mary without it affecting his marriage. He believed that Mary would just melt into his arms and the relationship could be ‘tactfully concealed’. He was convinced that the ‘groundwork’ had been done and that Mary would be unable to resist him. He was too vain and full of himself to grasp her lack of enthusiasm and he convinced himself that all was needed to rekindle their relationship was ‘a direct approach’. His letter seemed calculated and transparently manipulative and his first inkling that things were not going as planned was when Mary was nowhere to be seen in the restaurant. Her letter of rejection was uncompromising and crushing in its tone and content. The references to his appearance were cutting and he was humiliated. His inflated ego was unceremoniously punctured and most candidates argued that it was richly deserved. Some found a touch of sympathy for a sad, self-deluded and ageing man but most felt he had only himself to blame and that a form of justice was done. Some candidates tried to argue that Clive was genuine in his declared feelings for Mary but the perceptive noted that he was not interested in making ‘amends’ but in pursuing an affair.

The best answers established a coherent line of argument and pursued it with detail and often with a lot of energy and commitment.
c700u10-jun25-11-q:
This section followed a familiar pattern and there was the usual choice of four titles which allowed the candidates to write imaginatively or from personal experience. All four titles attracted significant numbers of candidates.

Comments on individual questions/sections

(a) Write about a time when you took part in a race.

This title gave the candidates plenty of scope to write positively about an event which involved a celebration. Some responses perhaps focused too much on the events leading to the celebration but that was not really a problem. Family celebrations were an obvious choice but sporting triumphs were also legitimate options.

(b) The Celebration.

This title also offered a range of possible directions, and the race could be interpreted in a variety of ways. A sporting contest was the obvious choice for many candidates but there was some range of approach. This title was worded to invite personal experience, but some embellishment of the truth was entirely acceptable in the interest of entertainment.

(c) Write a story which begins: That phone call changed my life.

The popularity of this title was probably a reflection of the importance of the phone in modern life. The introduction suggested that the phone call was life-changing but there was no clear direction of travel in the opening and the content could be positive or negative.

(d) Write a story which ends: …and I felt rather pleased with myself.

This option also encouraged the candidates to write from personal experience and the narrative had to be structured to lead to a positive conclusion. Endings can be difficult but this seemed straightforward, and most candidates managed to sustain a clear sense of direction. Inevitably perhaps, there were some ‘crash landings’ but most managed to construct a coherent narrative.

Characteristics of Successful Responses

• Successful responses to reading questions have some substance and textual detail but stay focused on the question. • Successful responses to reading questions have fluency and cohesion (as opposed to a selection of disjointed comments and quotations). • Successful writing is plausible (and legible) but it can be imaginative. • Successful writing communicates clearly and makes it possible for the reader to follow the narrative.

Areas for Improvement

In the reading section: • Use the key words of the question to structure a response. (For example, a question which ask for ‘thoughts and feelings’ should have a lot of sentences beginning he/she thinks, or he/she feels) • In Question 05, take some time to think about and establish the direction of the argument and remember to use the whole text. Do not assume that a ‘balanced’ view is always the best option. • Answers which show quality in content and organisation are valued more than those which are lengthy but unfocused.

11 In the writing section: • Pay attention to the structure as well as the content of narrative writing. Spending 5-10 minutes planning the narrative is time well spent. • Be very careful with tenses (simple past tense is the safest option). • Take care with spelling, grammar and punctuation. Decent stories are often undermined by too many technical errors.

The structure of this specification requires one question worth five marks to identify explicit ideas and information and the marks were available for a straightforward selection of relevant points. The question asked for a list of what was learned about one of the main characters, Brian Faulkner, and the candidates could simply locate facts or make inferences.

There were enough surface facts available to allow the candidates to gain full marks here. For example, he teamed up with a man he met in a pub to import cheap leather jackets from Spain. He ordered Maureen to move to Luton and promised to find a flat. He did not find a flat and the ‘earner’ fell through. He made trips to Spain but then moved on to another scheme involving carpet sales. He did not supply his wife with the money for the rent, according to Maureen. However, it was also possible to make some inferences about Brian. For example, the evidence suggested he was an opportunist and not the most reliable or responsible husband and father.

Some of the responses were unselective, imprecise or unfocused and the weaker answers revealed some basic misreading of the text such as Brian teamed up with a man from Spain. However, it was possible to handle this question concisely and efficiently.
c700u10-nov17-02-q:
This question was only worth five marks and, although it invited some understanding of the effect of the writer’s choice of language, the emphasis was also on the evidence used to show the relationship between Lucy and Brian. Given the modest weighting of this question, and the pressure of time in an examination, we have to be realistic about how much range and depth we can reasonably expect and the sensible candidates dealt with this question with minimum fuss. It also helped that the question only focused on a few lines of the text.

The writer informed us that Lucy was only ‘acquainted’ with her father for a few years so the relationship was brief and, like the link to Luton, it was ‘meaningless’. Some candidates did pick up and explain the significance of the use of the word ‘acquaintance’. Brian was described as ‘amiable’, suggesting he was a pleasant, friendly enough character in his way, and the writer pointed out that he took Lucy to the funfair and bought her candyfloss. However, very few candidates understood ‘amiable’ and consequently very few indeed grasped the subtlety in the relationship. Lucy’s memory of him was described as ‘appropriately shabby’ and, although Brian was a ‘jaunty figure’ who apparently wanted to make up for his weaknesses and failings, the writer described him as selfish. Brian was presented as well-intentioned in some ways but too feckless and selfish to be a good father and the relationship with Lucy was short-lived and shallow. Quite a few candidates got that the relationship was ‘weak’ or ‘short-lived’ but very few saw the complexities.
c700u10-nov17-03-q:
This question was challenging and required the candidates to see how the writer showed the differences between Lucy and her mother, Maureen. Understanding of the two characters was clearly essential to a good response but the better answers kept the focus on the writer and how she used contrasts in the personalities of the two women.

It made sense to begin with the character of Maureen, not least because this gave the answer a point of reference. The writer described Maureen as ‘constant’ and only changing over the years in ‘slow motion’ from a harassed and loving figure in her youth to ‘good humoured, opinionated and forever a great deal younger than her daughter’ as an older woman. The writer then told us directly that Lucy was ‘not like her mother’. Lucy was described as not ‘easy going’ or ‘trusting’ and the writer used verbs such as ‘stared, probed and queried’ to show the challenging, questioning, rather edgy nature of Lucy.

The writer used a specific anecdote to illustrate the difference between the characters. When Lucy was four, she ‘demanded’ to know where the sun goes at night and Maureen was reassuringly comforting and her language, and perhaps her thoughts, were childish. However, the writer showed Lucy’s disapproval, describing her ‘knotted mouth’ as she listened to her mother’s explanation. Lucy’s temper erupted as she ‘burst out’ her reply and the anecdote showed her rational, rather literal nature. She had no patience with Maureen’s well-intentioned but fanciful version of the real world.

Lucy was described by the writer in various adjectives such as combative, competent and enterprising. She was also said to be curious, hardworking and unwilling to admit defeat but the writer explicitly told us that these qualities did not come from her upbringing with Maureen, who was judged to be ‘unable or unwilling’ to confront serious questions about the universe. She was described as ‘unlikely to turn out to be inspirational’. The writer showed Lucy as assertive, intelligent and questioning whereas Maureen seemed passive, limited and resigned to life.

The writer’s language choices were important in showing the differences between Maureen and Lucy and, although she did use examples of the characters in action, there was more ‘tell’ than ‘show’ here.
c700u10-nov17-04-q:
This question allowed the candidates to gain credit for giving their impressions of the characters of Brian and Maureen and the relationship between them but it also invited analysis of how the writer created these impressions. The best responses took the two questions together and gave their impressions linked to supporting evidence and analysis of the writer’s method.

Most candidates got the impression that Maureen was a sympathetic, pitiable figure and they supported that idea with the evidence that she had two small children, another on the way and a husband who was ‘gently easing himself out’ of their relationship. It was clear to most candidates that Maureen was blind to what was happening to their relationship, some arguing that she was foolish and others seeing her as cruelly deceived. Brian was away often and was vague and evasive about what he did, claiming that work was ‘his problem’ and therefore none of her business. Maureen seemed desperate for contact with Brian, crying ‘reverse the charges’ when he bothered to telephone home. She remained loyal to him, convinced that he is busy with work and even feeling sorry for him as he was ‘rushed off his feet, poor dear’. Some argued she lived in hope as contact became less and less frequent but she displayed the postcards he sent. She did not complain and contemplated the postcards ‘without comment’. However, some found her exasperating in her naivety and willingness to be a downtrodden victim.

3 Some got the impression that Maureen was dogged or determined and just got on with life as she was left to cope with solicitors and social security. She was passive in accepting routine humiliation and resigning herself to the situation by accepting ‘that’s life’. Some noticed that, despite being mistreated by her husband and by various officials, she was not bitter and remained accepting of her situation.

It would have been difficult to argue convincingly that Brian was anything other than devious and selfish. His excuses for his absence really only convinced Maureen and the presents he brought for the children did not impress anyone. The presents and ‘nights of love’ he gave Maureen seemed empty and selfish and the hugs and waves diminished to phone calls on which he would hang up. Gradually his absences became longer and more significant and contact was reduced to ‘infrequent’ phone calls and ‘erratic’ postcards. Brian was not an attractive character and he had few redeeming features.

The relationship seemed one-sided and Maureen’s feelings for him were exploited and betrayed. The writer used the interaction of the characters but also captured the tone and thoughts of Maureen, even though it was third-person narrative.

There was a wealth of textual material to use in answering this question and some candidates constructed convincing responses. The weaker answers tended to be thin but very few missed the nature of the relationship between the characters.
c700u10-nov17-05-q:
The concept of evaluation is not easy for most candidates and the better answers were organised as a personal response to the character of Maureen with some comment on how successfully she was presented by the writer.

In the final section of the passage, after a lifetime of being disappointed and downtrodden, Maureen was resigned to her situation as a victim of ‘absent husbands’ and ‘arrogant officials’. The passage as a whole had led readers to be angry and indignant on her behalf and the writer successfully encouraged them to feel admiration and sympathy for her. She had been subjected to endless humiliation and betrayal and reacted to it all ‘without bitterness’. The writer used Lucy’s reaction to her mother’s treatment to guide the reader and she was not simply presented as weak and downtrodden, although many candidates did emphasise that aspect of her personality. Lucy understood that Maureen has been ‘burdened’ by poverty and children but she also understood that her mother had admirable qualities. Maureen was ‘resilient’, ‘resourceful’ and ‘doggedly protective’ and those words were not a description of someone who was just weak and pitiable. Lucy saw that Maureen had behaved like ‘any creature of whatever species’ and had done what was necessary to survive and to allow her children to survive. Her ‘survival tactic’ was to ‘keep her head down and weather the storms of life’, accepting life and grinning and bearing it. Maureen did not question life but she survived by resigning herself to it. Lucy also admitted that she has probably gained her ‘sharp wits’ from the circumstances of her childhood. Maureen’s ‘rough time’ had had a positive effect on Lucy.

Lucy ‘adored’ her mother but she was also ‘maddened’ by her and, as a teenager, she found Maureen’s view of life ‘exasperating, inconsistent and plain wrong’. Lucy was infuriated by Maureen’s naive faith in astrology and her willingness to spend money on it and, when Maureen explains, Lucy just sighed as if she knew it was hopeless to argue with her mother. Maureen emerged as a complex character rather than simply a victim and the better answers saw at least some of that complexity. Most candidates at least had something sensible to say about the character.
c700u10-nov17-11-q:
(a) The Competition.

This title was popular and, unsurprisingly, often focused on a sporting competition or a personal rivalry. There were some rather unconvincing or implausible approaches to this title but overwhelmingly they were coherent. The less successful responses tended to be brief accounts of ‘what happened’ but some did attempt to explore feelings and emotions and develop the narrative.

(b) Write about an occasion when you were embarrassed by your family.

The responses to this title invariably tackled the idea of embarrassment but some did not read the title carefully and did not see that the family were intended to be the source of embarrassment. It was not a fatal weakness but it did lead to some structural problems. Some responses were not very convincing but the better answers had a feel of authenticity and there was a real opportunity here to develop ideas and reflect on them. Some answers were refreshingly honest and sometimes amusing.

(c) Write a story which ends: … and Sam felt so proud.

Some candidates had difficulty constructing a narrative which moved seamlessly to its given conclusion and, to be fair, it is not easy to achieve a smooth ‘landing’. Some narratives were uncertain in structure and limited in content but a number of them did manage to put together a reasonably coherent and relevant response to the title. Reflecting the age of the entry, there were some moments of pride resulting from successful driving tests.

(d) Write a story which begins: My career on stage was short but it was certainly memorable.

The implication of this title should have been clear and the suggestion that a stage debut ended in a disaster which would not be repeated was picked up by most, though not all, candidates. Some could not resist a theatrical or musical triumph, leading to a successful career covering several decades. However, most were coherent and relevant and this was the option that usually provided the most entertainment for the reader. Some interpreted the notion of ‘the stage’ rather loosely but this was not a serious issue as most focused quite clearly on a performance of one sort or another.

Technical errors are a persistent cause for concern and many candidates continue to struggle with basic accuracy in written expression. I am sorry to say that problems in spelling, punctuation and sentence construction are still very much in evidence as is ability to control tenses. Candidates would be well-advised to spend five minutes or so proof-reading their narrative writing at the end of the exam to try to improve their technical accuracy.

5 EDUQAS ENGLISH LANGUAGE

GCSE

November 2017
c700u10-nov18-01-q:
This question, worth five marks, focused on the opening paragraph of the passage and required the candidates to identify explicit and implicit ideas and information. The question asked for a list of what was learned about the Hamiltons in the specified lines and the candidates could simply locate facts or make inferences. The marks were available for a straightforward and clear selection of relevant points.

The opening paragraph provided the Hamilton family background and informed the reader that Samuel and Liza were both from the north of Ireland. The Hamiltons were a farming family and were described as ‘neither rich nor poor’. They had deep roots on their farm, having lived there in the same house for hundreds of years. They were also described as ‘intelligent and well-educated people’ and, typically of people in Ireland, they were related to the great and the small. Of course, they were, or at least claimed to be, descended from the ancient kings.

A lot of the candidates located the relevant material with minimum fuss but a significant number did not line it up very well and the focus of their answers was uncertain. They often focused too narrowly on Samuel himself rather than ‘the Hamiltons’.

It is also worth remembering that bullet points should be coherent in themselves and not relying on the examiner’s knowledge of the passage.
c700u10-nov18-02-q:
The candidates had plenty of opportunities to gain credit in this question and the wording was such that they could focus on the characters as individuals or as a couple in a married relationship. The best responses did some of both approaches.

2 There was a lot to say about Sam Hamilton and he was presented as a man of moral principle. He was described as ‘totally honest’ and the use of ‘totally’ emphasised his integrity. The impression was also created of a man who was attractive in both appearance and personality. He had ‘good looks and charm’. Sam was a man of energy and invention and he had practical skills as a blacksmith and carpenter. However, he had no business acumen. He had no talent for making money, but he was ‘a man of love’ who may have secretly loved another girl. The text suggested that he may have left Ireland because he was heartbroken by this relationship or perhaps because it was ‘too successful’. I did not see any responses which picked up the implication of that comment.

Liza was described as ‘tiny’ and ‘hard and humourless’. The reader was also told that she was a woman who did not show her feelings. Although there were fewer details about Liza, it was clear that as a couple they were very different and perhaps ill-suited. Many candidates had got the impression that they were an odd match.

There was a temptation for some to spend too long on this question but it is better to have too much to say than too little in an examination. That said, the candidates needed to bear in mind that the question was only worth five marks.
c700u10-nov18-03-q:
This question was in two parts but it allowed credit to be given for understanding of the character of Sam Hamilton as well as for understanding how the writer had shown his character. Too many candidates make the issue of ‘how does the writer’ too complicated and get lost in unconvincing assertions about the effects of sentence structure, punctuation and ‘short syntax’ (sic). The best way to tackle this type of question is to link comments to evidence and to embed any relevant terminology in an exploration of the text. It is not sensible to start with the effects of literary devices and, as I have said many times in earlier reports, trying to find devices should not be the focus of candidates' responses. The text and what happens in that text should be the centre of the reader’s attention.

The writer presented the character of Sam Hamilton in a positive and almost reverential way, stressing his many and varied skills and qualities. The initial focus was on Sam in his working life and the writer showed Sam’s practical skills by saying that he built his own house and used his ‘clever hands’ to invent a machine to bore for water. He was presented as a hardworking man who worked for others as a blacksmith and thresher. He clearly struggled to make a living from his own barren land and he was not one of the ‘lucky’ men. He came across as patient, uncomplaining and accepting of his lot in life.

Sam was also presented as a raconteur, a sociable man, who could entertain his customers and who earned a reputation as ‘a comic genius’ among his neighbours, who lacked his gift as a natural story teller. However, he had no head for business and was too understanding to press for payment for his services. He was a soft touch when it came to money, although some candidates tended to overstate Sam’s altruism and generosity by claiming that he worked willingly for free or had no interest in making money.

The writer showed a very different side of Sam’s character by telling the reader that he delivered his own children and knew what to do if things went wrong. He also delivered local children, and animals too, suggesting his range of skills and the sensitive side of his personality. The writer stressed that his hands were ‘so good’ and ‘so gentle’ that people came from miles around for his help with a birth. He was shown to be caring and could soothe a frightened child with his ‘sweet’ voice and ‘the tenderness of his soul’. He was even shown to have a moral influence on those around him as the men did not curse in the blacksmith shop, instinctively feeling that it was not the place for such language.

3 The writer’s language consistently emphasised Sam’s skill, patience and virtue and the tone indicated respect, affection and admiration. Even Sam’s failings in business matters were presented as a virtue and evidence of his kindness and sensitivity to others.

There was plenty to explore in this part of the question and not many failed to see that Sam Hamilton was presented as a wholly admirable character.
c700u10-nov18-04-q:
This question turned the focus to the other major character in the passage and the candidates were asked to analyse the rather withering presentation of Liza Hamilton.

This was a relatively short passage of text but it was packed with detail about the character and significant credit was given to those who showed a grasp of the character and used the text effectively to support their comments.

The writer immediately employed the contrast with Sam in this section of the text and ironically referred to Liza as ‘a different kettle of Irish’. She was presented as a formidable and rather intimidating woman. The passage had established earlier that she was physically small, and ‘disapproving’ when it came to whisky, and here the immediate focus was on the description of her head, which was described as ‘small and round’. However, this apparently straightforward descriptive detail was followed by the sharply critical and unflattering comment that her head held ‘small, fixed convictions’. In contrast with the warm and generous Sam, Liza was immediately nailed as narrow-minded, a woman of unbending and fixed opinions who was ‘set on her course’ and would not change for ‘the angels of God’. Liza was a woman of firm moral principles but that was not presented favourably as her morality was harsh and hostile to pleasure. The writer claimed that she ‘beat the brains out of nearly everything that was pleasant to do’ and the violence of the language was clearly intended to influence the reader’s perception of the character.

Liza was described as a ‘good, plain cook’ but the word ‘plain’ suggested rather grudging appreciation of her culinary skills. She was house-proud but the parenthetic suggestion that it was always ‘her house’ and the use of the adverb ‘fiercely’ did not suggest that her cleanliness was a particularly endearing quality.

She was certainly presented as strong and resilient and even childbirth did not ‘hold her back very much’. However, her ‘finely developed’ sense of sin focused on idleness and card playing and her disapproval extended to dancing, singing and even laughter. Her antagonism to anything that was fun or might have encouraged having a good time placed her clearly in a familiar tradition of puritanical self-righteousness. She was a killjoy and she took it upon herself to protect Samuel from sin, whether he wanted to be protected or not. He was described as ‘wide open to the devil’ because he was ‘a laughing man’ and the writer’s sarcasm was evident in the wry comment that ‘this was a shame’.

The writer suggested that her severe appearance matched and reflected her personality and the savage presentation continued with the suggestion that she had ‘no spark’ of humour. Even her occasional ‘sharp blade’ of wit suggested that it was cutting and perhaps hurtful. Perhaps the most damning detail of all was the fact that she frightened her own grandchildren, including the writer/narrator, because she had no weaknesses. She seemed inhuman in her strength and this was a good example of where the choice of content clearly was being used to influence the reader.

4 The writer acknowledged her courage as she ‘suffered bravely and uncomplainingly’ but also suggested that even this was a feature or consequence of her stern religion.

The writer used carefully-chosen detail and some very significant language choices to present Liza’s character and the verbs and adjectives were particularly effective in influencing the reader. The tone was sharply ironic and any praise or appreciation was limited and grudging.

Overall, this question was not handled as well as Question 0.3 and a lot of candidates did not really get the measure of Liza. Some went too far in condemning her as ‘evil’ and ‘the devil’ while others completely misread the character and argued that her ‘convictions’ suggested a criminal past and accused her of gambling and other vices.
c700u10-nov18-05-q:
This type of question requires the ability to range across a whole text and establish an overview of the text and a coherent stance. It is the ability to construct and support a convincing argument that is required here.

It would have been very difficult to argue convincingly that life was easy for the immigrants and most candidates were at least able to identify some examples of hardship in the lives of the early settlers in California.

For example, the writer made it clear farming was very tough. Sam Hamilton was full of energy and invention but he struggled to make much money. Some candidates argued, quite convincingly, that Sam could have been more successful and his business failings were self- inflicted. However, the good land was all taken by the time the Hamiltons arrived in California. Those people may have had an easier time of it, but latecomers such as Sam and Liza were forced by circumstance to scrape a living on the ‘barren hills’. The description of the area above the Salinas valley illustrated that life was hard. The land Sam Hamilton and others like him tried to farm was described by the writer as ‘harsh’ and ‘dry’. The topsoil was described as ‘a thin crust’ where even grass struggled to grow. The cattle were thin because they ran around searching for water and the abundance of land made no real difference. Without water, even ten thousand acres were worthless.

The passage also conveyed a clear sense of the self-reliance needed by these isolated ranchers. People had to be practical and determined and possess a variety of skills. Sam had to build his own house and barn and earn a living by working with his ‘clever’ hands and physical strength. There were usually no doctors to deliver the children who arrived as ‘regularly as the years’ and were perhaps a mixed blessing for people struggling to get by. One candidate pointed out the danger to women of childbirth in such a situation.

There was also a sense of the narrow horizons and isolation in this life. Sam Hamilton became the local fountain of knowledge about the world outside the confines of the valley. It was perhaps self-inflicted in the case of the Hamiltons but there was little sense of these people having fun in their lives. They seemed to live to work and their pleasures were simple.

There was no doubt that these people had a tough life but some candidates also grasped that they were not really presented by the writer as victims. Life was certainly hard but there was a sense of tenacity and resilience in these people and the reader was more likely to admire them than pity them. The writer painted a picture of friendship and togetherness as the men gathered at the forge to talk and drink whisky while Sam repaired their tools. As well as friendship, there was mutual assistance as Sam delivered children and animals alike.

5 Some candidates focused too exclusively on the Hamiltons in this question but it was true that Steinbeck used the experience of Sam and Liza to illustrate the wider experience of immigrants to California in the nineteenth century.
c700u10-nov18-11-q:
As usual, there were four options in this section and the candidates were instructed to produce a narrative of about 450-600 words. Most candidates try their best to produce a narrative which has some detail and substance but some are too brief and thin to develop convincingly and often they provide limited evidence on which to base a fair assessment. There is nothing to be gained from writing endlessly and aimlessly but the examiners do need enough evidence to inform their judgement.

Narrative writing in the context of an examination is really the art of the miniaturist but there is time and space to develop setting and characterisation.

(a) Write a story which begins: I can clearly remember that family gathering.

This type of question, which provides an opening for a narrative, is intended to be helpful and to give the candidates a starting point and a sense of direction for their writing. However, there is often an awkward transition from the given opening to the rest of the narrative and there are frequent problems with structure and chronology which could be avoided if the candidates just took a few moments to plan their writing.

This specific opening allowed the candidates to focus on one of a variety of family occasions and reminisce about events which could have been amusing or dramatic.

There were some lively responses but a lot were largely uneventful or drifted into action which had little to do with the idea of a family gathering.

(b) The Race.

This type of title is relatively open to interpretation but the expectation was clearly that some kind of race would feature significantly in the narrative. Some ‘races’ were quite imaginative in approach but some were merely fanciful and unconvincing.

There were some obvious approaches here and the writer usually appeared as a competitor. Ironically, those who could not resist the chance to win an Olympic gold medal were often less successful than those who won the egg and spoon race in primary school. The latter usually had authenticity and charm and allowed some development of character and exploration of feelings. Convincing details and observation are engaging.

(c) Write about a time when you felt let down by a friend.

This was a narrative based on personal experience and it had a clear and specific focus. I suspect that few people have been fortunate enough to have never experienced a sense of being let down by someone who was, or seemed to be, a friend. The advantage of this type of narrative is that it should have the coherence and authenticity of real experience. Some of the narratives were uneasily constructed but most were relevant.

6 (d) Write a story which ends: …and I realised that some things are more important than money.

Constructing a narrative which is tailored to a given conclusion can be difficult and it requires careful planning and clear thinking if a ‘crash landing’ is to be avoided. Those who chose this option had mixed fortunes and a lot of them struggled for overall coherence and direction.

Many candidates struggled with basic accuracy in written expression. I regret to say that problems in spelling, punctuation and sentence construction are still very much in evidence and, as I have mentioned in previous reports, the ability to control tenses is a real issue for some. Too often it is the lack of technical control and accuracy which undermines the writing as a whole. There is no easy solution to this issue but, if possible, candidates should try to spend a few minutes checking for errors in their narrative writing at the end of the exam.

GCSE

November 2018
c700u10-nov19-01-q:
The opening question was worth five marks, as usual, and focused on a relatively short section of the text. The first ten lines of the story included the flashback to the lunch twenty years earlier but the question simply asked for a range of ‘things’ (facts or inferences) that the reader learned about the narrator in those lines.

For example, he had seen the woman at a play (not in a play) and had sat beside her at the interval. He had not seen her for twenty years and he hardly recognised her. The reader also learned that he had been manipulated into taking her out to lunch at a clearly expensive hotel.

At the time of their first meeting, the narrator was living in a tiny flat in London and he was earning very little money. He had written a book, which the woman claimed to have read, but he was a struggling author.

The candidates could use explicit or implicit information and most tackled this question economically and quite successfully. However, they did need to be careful with chronology and some were too imprecise at times. For example, the narrator did not ask the woman out to lunch and there was absolutely no suggestion that he was romantically attached to her.
c700u10-nov19-02-q:
This question was only worth five marks and the best answers were not too long but showed clear understanding of the narrator’s thoughts and feelings with at least some focus on how the writer had shown those thoughts and feelings. The best way to approach this question was to track the narrator’s thoughts and feelings and use appropriate textual support. The text followed a series of thoughts and feelings and it was sensible for the candidates to do the same, providing appropriate evidence from the text. Too many lost focus on the narrator’s thoughts and feelings when they attempted this question.

The narrator’s initial response was anxiety as the Grand was ‘so expensive’ he had never even thought of going there. However, he also felt trapped by her flattery and his lack of experience in saying no to a woman. He reassured himself that he could manage if he cut out coffee for a few weeks.

When he met her, he was surprised and disappointed by her appearance. She was ‘not as young’ as he expected and was ‘imposing’ rather than ‘attractive’. His observation that she had more teeth than necessary was particularly cutting.

The menu ‘startled’ him because it was ‘a good deal’ higher than he had expected but he was reassured by what the woman said about not eating lunch and he was relieved enough to speak ‘generously’.

The writer used verbs and adverbs precisely to show the narrator grappling with his hopes and fears.
c700u10-nov19-03-q:
This question focused on a much longer section of text and allowed the candidates to express their thoughts and feelings about the woman by tracking the impressions created by the writer. The question was set up to encourage engagement with the character of the woman, but it also included some focus on the writer and the better answers avoided unsupported assertions.

At first, she claimed to eat nothing or very little for lunch, suggesting that in her opinion people generally eat too much. The initial impression was created of a woman of moderate appetites and this was reinforced by her almost reluctant concession that she might manage ‘a little fish perhaps’.

However, she then ordered lobster and the writer used the narrator’s reaction to show how extravagant her tastes were. He ‘gulped’ and asked the waiter ‘apprehensively’ if they had lobster. Asking for smoked salmon added insult to injury, contradicting her words and exposing her hypocrisy as she said one thing but did the opposite. The narrator’s heart ‘sank’ and she then had the nerve to lecture him about eating too much, particularly meat.

She repeated her tactic in relation to drink, flashing a smile as she claimed that she only drank champagne on doctor’s orders. The narrator ordered champagne for her but he went ‘pale’ and ordered water for himself. She was oblivious to him and his reactions and the impression created was of an insensitive, self-obsessed hypocrite.

She was quick to take the narrator ‘seriously to task’ about his ‘heavy lunch’ but her hypocrisy was reinforced when she forced herself to have the expensive asparagus, despite her insistence that she only ate one thing for lunch. She was shameless in lecturing the narrator about his self-indulgence and opinions differed as to whether she was totally lacking in self-awareness or, more likely perhaps, a manipulative hypocrite who knew exactly what she was doing in exploiting this naïve young man. Most agreed that she was a horrible, unpleasant character and completely rude and selfish.

The writer used action and dialogue as well as the reactions of the narrator to show what she was like and the ironic discrepancy between her words and actions was used very effectively.

The key point in all of this was her hypocrisy but some candidates did comment on a decent range of impressions.
c700u10-nov19-04-q:
This was a familiar type of question and again the best way to tackle it was to track the text methodically, looking for the narrator’s thoughts and feelings and integrating textual support and any comments on authorial method into the response. The wording of the question allowed credit to be given for understanding of the writer’s thoughts and feelings, and those who also provided appropriate evidence to support and illustrate their points did well.

The narrator was gripped by ‘panic’ as he feared not only that he would have nothing to see him through the rest of the month but also that he would not even have enough money to pay the bill. He thought about how ‘embarrassing’ it would be if he could not pay the bill and he could not face having to borrow money from his guest. He then considered leaving his watch as surety.

When the asparagus arrived, the writer used the narrator’s perspective as he watched in horrified fascination as she ‘thrust’ them down her throat in ‘large mouthfuls’. He was ‘past caring’ when she added an ice cream to the offer of coffee. The writer used the verb ‘devoured’ to describe the way the woman ate the ice cream and the adverb ‘faintly’ suggested disbelief, or perhaps despair, as she insisted that one should always still feel a little hungry after a meal. The narrator was clearly terrified that she might indeed still be hungry and the arrival of the peaches was described as ‘a terrible thing’. When he thought ‘God alone knew what they would cost’ it showed his utter despair and anxiety. He felt embarrassed at leaving an ‘inadequate’ tip and was convinced that the woman would see him as mean as well as a glutton. Some candidates, quite rightly, saw him as ashamed of himself. As he left the restaurant he felt miserable, thinking that he had ‘not a penny’ in his pocket and the rest of the month before him. He left his guest with another lecture ringing in his ears. However, the story was not quite finished and the narrative returned to the ‘present’, twenty years after the lunch. Despite his disingenuous claim that he was ‘not a spiteful man’, the narrator seemed very pleased to have his revenge as he ‘merely’ pointed out that the woman weighed twenty-one stone.

Some candidates commented on the writer’s use of the narrator and the dialogue but a methodical focus on thoughts and feelings and supporting detail (language and action) proved most effective. Relevant subject terminology should be used to enhance a point made. Searching for technical devices without commenting on the impact of these devices was not a helpful approach.
c700u10-nov19-05-q:
This question required the candidates to range across the whole text and evaluate the story as a whole and in particular the ending. Candidates can find the evaluation question challenging and there is always a danger of candidates relying on simple and/or unsupported assertion and opinion for no very obvious reason. Some candidates simply resorted to telling the story or providing character sketches with no focus on the question. This narrative had most of the virtues of the good short story and it was difficult to argue convincingly that it was not successful in most respects. However, there were several ways of approaching the question and some candidates did make valid criticisms. The examiners were instructed to follow the candidates in any coherent line of argument.

Good answers tried to engage explicitly with the craft of the short story but some progress could be made through a personal response to the content of the story and the characters. As always in this type of question, the key was to take a coherent stance. Opinion is free and the candidates are completely entitled to their views but it was probably easier and safer to argue that the writer had indeed written an enjoyable story with a satisfying ending. Those who tried to argue the opposite view were usually struggling to justify their views and find supporting evidence.

It was possible to comment on various technical features of the story which made it ‘enjoyable’, or at least entertaining and interesting. For example, the structure of the story was tight and, although it employed flashback, the focus was on a single incident. The use of flashback showed some careful plotting in the story as it was mentioned at the beginning that the narrator hardly recognised the woman but it was not until the end that it was revealed why she was difficult to recognise. The plot was set up neatly and the chronology was complex but it was clear and used effectively, particularly in relation to the twist at the end of the story.

Some commented on the clever use of narrator and how his perspective and reactions contributed to the enjoyment of the story. Like most successful short stories, this story had few characters but they were clearly drawn and the characterisation was economical and sharp. The dialogue was funny and there was humour and irony throughout the story.

However, most answers approached this question by exploring the detail of the situation in the restaurant and the interplay between the characters. There was always potential for humour in the situation of the rather impoverished young man feeling obliged to behave in a generous and gentlemanly way in a very expensive restaurant and most candidates sympathised with his predicament and were able to pick out specific instances of his discomfort. The writer’s language choices and use of dialogue showed the emotions of the narrator and how he was struggling with the situation very effectively.

It would have been surprising if the woman had attracted much sympathy but she was one of those characters readers love to hate. Her selfishness and hypocrisy were so clear and there were plenty of examples of both. Some candidates realised that this ‘pantomime villain’ contributed massively to the impact of the story.

The ending focused on the narrator’s ‘revenge’ and most felt that there was an entirely appropriate and poetic justice in the fact that the woman had suffered the consequences of her gluttony. A few felt that the ending was cruel but the woman did not attract widespread sympathy.

Overall, the responses to this question could have been better and some candidates really struggled with the idea of a critical evaluation of a text.
c700u10-nov19-11-q:
The Rebel.

This title allowed any narrative which pitted an individual against authority. It was possible to be very imaginative here and some candidates attempted epic tales of rebellion. Some were perhaps too ambitious in scope and some relied too obviously on inspiration from well-known television programmes. Others went for personal experience which was usually set at home or in school.

Some of the responses struggled with structure and seemed rather awkward and uneasy in relation to the title. However, there were some commendable attempts.

(b) Write about a time when you lost your temper.

This was a straightforward, first-person narrative and the title offered a clear structure, encouraging a focus on a single incident which culminated in the narrator losing his or her temper. This was probably the most successful option as it was usually rooted in clear and relevant personal experience.

(c) The New Pet.

There were opportunities in this title for some humour and, although most responses were probably loosely based on real experience, some embellishment in the interest of entertainment was perfectly possible.

Most responses were straightforward accounts of the acquisition of a new pet for a birthday or Christmas present but there were some more imaginative efforts.

(d) Write a story which ends: … and it showed Alex that we always have a choice.

This type of question does pose a structural challenge to many candidates and certainly requires planning and organisation. This could be a first or third- person narrative but the sequence of events should have led neatly and seamlessly to the concluding sentence. Sadly, that was not always the case and most struggled to bring their narrative to a convincing resolution.

Overall, most candidates do manage to construct a reasonably coherent narrative but many are seriously undermined by technical shortcomings and limited, or misused, vocabulary. The technical aspects of written expression are specifically weighted at 40% of the total available for writing and any preparation candidates can do to improve the accuracy of their work is time well spent.

Summary of key points

In the reading section:

• Candidates should think carefully about approaching the question appropriately and maintaining focus.

• Candidates should usually track the text (this is almost always the best way to approach reading questions).

• Candidates should link comments to supporting evidence.

• Candidates should think particularly carefully about the focus of their answers to evaluation questions.

In the writing section:

• Candidates should think carefully about which title they choose.

• Candidates need to plan and organise their work before they start writing.

• Candidates should take care with technical accuracy, particularly tenses and sentence construction.
