November 2019
c700u10-nov20-01-q:
The first question addressed the requirement to identify explicit ideas and information and five marks were available for a straightforward selection of relevant points. The question asked for a list of what was learned about the main character, who was also the narrator of the story, and there were lots of details available in the opening lines. A neat, concise list of details (facts or inferences) sufficed here.

For example, the first sentence of the passage made it clear that her only companion was a horse which lived in a field at the end of her garden and it was easy enough to infer that she was lonely. The narrator admitted that she was not used to horses and she fed them with chapatis. She was ‘born and bred in England’ but she was of Asian origin. She was from London but she lived in the country near Swindon. She was married and she was proud of her husband. She had limited contact with her neighbours which she thought was because she had no children rather than because of prejudice. She did not wear a sari. She talked to the horse about EastEnders and what she was cooking, and she confided in the horse that she thought she was going mad. There were other possible answers but there were plenty of details here and most candidates took advantage of this opportunity to score full marks. Most candidates had no difficulty in finding relevant points or sensible inferences.

However, some lacked precision. For example, some claimed that the narrator owned the horse, which was not true. The only other point to make here is that some candidates need to be more careful about their choice of pronouns. Using ‘he’ or they’ or ‘I’ was neither sensible nor helpful.
c700u10-nov20-02-q:
This question switched the focus to the narrator’s husband. Of course, in a question only worth five marks, the sensible responses were quite concise, offering some impressions with a well-chosen range of language choice and supporting evidence. No more was required here.

For example, Ranjit was perhaps rather set in his ways or even intimidating as he ‘didn’t like disturbance’ so the narrator did not confide in him and kept her problems to herself. He also seemed mature and capable of ‘deeper thoughts’ than his wife as he was older and had grey in his hair. He was considerate and generous in his way and the narrator admitted he was ‘kind’ and bought her a range of the latest gadgets. His only religion was technology and he ‘worshipped’ the silicon chip. He regarded the microwave as a modern miracle. He had plenty of qualities as he didn’t drink, he kept himself fit and he never lost his temper. He was generous with money and he was hardworking and apparently conscientious as he worked late and had been promoted to a marketing manager.

Some candidates were perceptive enough to pick up the sense of him as not unkind but old-fashioned with a rather traditional view of marriage and the roles of men and women in a relationship. The best answers did not take Ranjit entirely at face value and questioned some of his behaviour such as treating his wife almost as a kitchen maid, despite the stream of ‘practical’ gifts.

There were a lot of impressions here and most of the inferences were not too difficult. The opening two questions were a real opportunity to score well and a lot of candidates made the most of it.
c700u10-nov20-03-q:
This question focused on a longer section of the text and most candidates saw that the writer used language and content to build a picture of a sad, lonely woman who was struggling to cope with life.

The section of text began with the minor incident in the shop which left her in tears and feeling foolish. Her emotional fragility and vulnerability were also emphasised when she was affected by the disappearance of the horse and even felt that she had told it too many of her secrets. She clearly felt isolated and lonely as she admitted that she should have got out more. However, the thought of getting on a bus made her heart ‘thump’, emphasising her anxiety. She had ‘panic attacks’ when she went to Swindon and in supermarkets she would break into a sweat. Even ‘little things’ made her ‘sad’ and her insecurity was demonstrated as she ‘fumbled’ for her purse and keys and convinced herself that she had forgotten things. The string of questions she asked herself all showed feelings of self-doubt and insecurity. Thinking that she was the centre of everyone’s attention showed her paranoia. She worried excessively about catching the bus and, in her confusion and panic, she was flustered and her stomach ‘churned’. At the end of the section she revealed that she kept all of her anxieties to herself, feeling that her husband was too busy to be troubled by her problems.

The writer used internal monologue to reveal the thoughts and feelings of the narrator and the language and content indicated her insecurity and isolation. The deliberate accumulation of details created the picture and most candidates made at least some progress by selecting relevant textual details.

The best answers were thorough and kept a focus on the question. Of course, the responses covered the full range of ability but overall this question was attempted quite well.
c700u10-nov20-04-q:
It made sense to approach this question methodically and track through the specified section of text. The structure was significant here and it was difficult to see how the narrative developed from ‘normality’ into rather dramatic events without a step-by- step analysis.

At first the narrator did something ‘out of character’ and ordered a taxi so that she could take a trip to a famous beauty spot. In a way the writer laid a false trail here and the reader possibly thought that the narrative was moving in a positive direction, showing the narrator trying to cope with her problems.

However, the narrator’s familiar anxieties appeared again as she worried about the cost of this long trip by taxi. The taxi driver encouraged her to appreciate the view, but she was feeling sick as she was too far from home and her kitchen. By this point she was experiencing familiar panic ‘swelling’ inside her. All of this was tense and dramatic enough in its way, but the writer had laid a false trail as the real drama was about to unfold.

The real moment of drama was when she spotted her husband’s car in the car park. In a flashback she described the initial moment of recognition (it was a white Ford like her husband’s car) and her failure to make the precise connection between the car and her husband. When the driver asked her something she did not hear as her attention was focused on the car and presumably her imagination was running wild. When she told herself there was only one head in the car it was fairly clear that she trying to convince herself that there was an innocent explanation for his presence in this spot. She tried to tell herself that she was ‘mistaken’ and wanted to go home, presumably to escape from this potentially shattering situation. All of this built drama and tension but eventually she was forced to accept the evidence of her own eyes. She still tried to convince herself that they were ‘just looking at the view’ and that that was a reasonable explanation for why their heads were so close together. Some candidates noticed that the writer used the first-person narration to capture the sense of seeing but not wanting to believe in this section of the narrative.

When she was close to her husband’s car, she saw what they were doing and the details were left to the reader’s imagination. However, there was no real doubt about what was happening. The narrator wanted to go home immediately and when she got there she packed two suitcases. The marriage ended decisively and, although she admitted that it hurt, there was no going back. As far as she was concerned, everything was ‘clear’. She went back to London and moved in with her sister, sticking to the fiction that it was country life which had driven her to drastic action. There was no confrontation, no attempt to seek an explanation. Her departure from her marriage was as decisive as it was dramatic.

Some candidates saw that the narrator seemed to have recovered her identity and independence. She insisted she was ‘not mad at all’. In attempting to deal with her own problems, the narrator discovered her husband’s infidelity and the marriage immediately fell apart.

The better answers tracked the development of the narrative in detail and made an attempt at least to analyse what was tense and dramatic about the text.

However, a significant number of candidates found it difficult to line up the answer effectively and resorted to narrative, often failing to separate the dramatic from the mundane. The other problem was that a number of candidates did not understand, or even mention, what happened in the car park. Those answers which got no further than the narrator’s arrival at the beauty spot were severely limited in coverage, and quality.
c700u10-nov20-05-q:
The best approach to this question was for candidates to track their response to the character, working out exactly what they thought about him at various points in the narrative. The writer dropped hints about Ranjit throughout the text, and many of them could be interpreted in different ways, but the key to this question was to establish a coherent stance based on the details in the text.

For example, most saw him as a decent enough character at first and were surprised when it was revealed that he was betraying his long-suffering wife. Others were less forgiving from the beginning.

At first he seemed ambitious and keen to make his way in the world and the narrator admitted that she was ‘proud of him then.’ The admiration for his diligence was clear but the alert readers picked up the implications of the word ‘then’ which suggested that things would change. He seemed oblivious, or indifferent, to his wife’s problems and absorbed by work, and technology. However, the narrator pointed out his redeeming qualities and she deferred to him, accepting her role as the dutiful housewife.

Although this was open to a rather different interpretation later in the narrative, Ranjit seemed to work ‘so hard’ in a responsible job. He was often late and his frequent overnight absences initially seemed to be work-related and merely evidence of how conscientious he was. At this point in the narrative, the alert reader could have made some valid criticisms of his behaviour and attitudes, not least his failure to notice his wife’s anxieties. However, the fact that she was making excuses for him perhaps encouraged most readers to see him as just a hardworking man who was set in his ways and rather old-fashioned in his ideas about marriage.

When he was discovered in the car park and the truth was revealed, it was difficult to mount any defence of him. He had deceived and betrayed his wife and most readers suggested that his despicable infidelity did change their view of him. The narrator packed her bags without giving him any opportunity to explain or defend himself but there was little sympathy for him. He had perhaps never been the ideal husband but by this point in the narrative he attracted unequivocal condemnation. Some suggested that this had come as a surprise, but others claimed that the ominous signs had been there from the outset. The character certainly provoked a response.

It is worth stressing that it is vital to establish a coherent line of argument and support it with textual evidence. Some had coherence but little reference to the text while others had the detail but limited coherence. Those who managed both did well.
c700u10-nov20-11-q:
As usual, the extended writing offered a choice of four titles and an opportunity to write imaginatively or from personal experience.

The better responses maintained a coherent perspective, using either first or third person, and the content was relevant, though not necessarily predictable, showing a sense of direction and structure. They used detail, dialogue and characterisation appropriately to keep the reader engaged and interested.

Less successful narratives were often implausible or lacking substance.

(a) Write about a time when you were pushed to the limit.

This title was popular and offered plenty of scope for physical or emotional challenges. It was a first-person narrative and the better responses had a ring of authenticity as the candidates drew on personal experience.

(b) The day that changed everything.

This title often prompted writing from personal experience ranging from examination results to the loss of a relative or friend. Some of the narratives were a little awkward in structure but most focused on a significant day either for the writer or the wider world.

(c) Write a story that begins: I had volunteered to help with the primary school trip.

Although the responses to this title were mostly imaginative in the sense that the writer had never actually volunteered to help with a primary school trip, the candidates who chose it were writing about an event most of them had experienced as children and therefore they had plenty of material to work with.

The less successful responses tended to be either rather uneventful, focusing mostly on what was for lunch, or rather implausible. The better answers maintained a coherent perspective and contained convincing detail and characters.

(d) Write a story that ends: ... and the teacher never found out.

Writing towards a given ending can be difficult but this title worked well enough and there were few responses that lacked a clear structure. Predictably, the responses to this option focused on pranks, or sometimes more serious or illegal behaviour. The better answers were engaging and sometimes alarmingly authentic.

Summary of key points

In the reading section:

• Candidates should take care with their approach to lists in Question 01, using bullet points and the appropriate pronouns.

• Candidates should ‘line up’ the question and the answer to ensure that they are using the text to answer the question (using the words of the question is often helpful).

• All questions require candidates to ‘use’ the text but never simply to tell the story.

• In evaluation questions, a well-argued and well-supported personal response is the key.

In the writing section:

• Candidates should aim to write a brief plan before starting their narrative

• Candidates should develop their ideas so that their writing has some substance and detail. (There is no need for excessive length but a narrative needs development).

• Most candidates need to be consistent with tenses and take more care with technical accuracy.

• Narrative writing needs shape and direction and candidates should think about the structure of their work before they start writing.

November 2020
c700u10-nov21-01-q:
The opening question tested the candidates’ ability to identify implicit and explicit information and ideas and it was not intended to put barriers in their way. There were some possible inferences but mostly the relevant information was factual, and five marks were available for a clearly presented selection of relevant details about Mma Ramotswe.

For example, the writer made it clear that she had raised money by inheriting and selling her father’s cattle. All the animals went to her. She was an only child and she had used the money to set up her detective agency. She loved her father more than any other man and she appreciated what he had done for her. Her agency made a slow start but her services as a detective were, surprisingly, in considerable demand. She usually came up with some information for her clients, suggesting she was good at her job, and she did not charge a fee if she did not succeed, which suggested she was fair and honest in her dealings with clients.

As usual, a concise list of bullet points is sufficient here but it is worth pointing out that bullet points should make sense to the examiner. There is a danger that the candidates take too much for granted and use bullet points which lack internal coherence. Most scored well here but some needed to read the selected area of text more carefully. For example, it was not true that Mma Ramotswe did not charge a fee for her services. That was only the case when she failed to deliver.
c700u10-nov21-02-q:
This question, which assesses AO2, changed the focus to Mma Ramotswe’s client, Happy Bapetsi, and asked for impressions of her character based on reference to the language in the text. In practice, the sensible responses were quite concise, offering some impressions with a well-chosen range of language choice and supporting evidence. No more can reasonably be required in a question worth only five marks and, although there was plenty of material for the candidates to use here, there was not so much that they were potentially overwhelmed by it or tempted into wasting time with answers which were unnecessarily lengthy.

For example, the first impression created in the text was that Happy Bapetsi was anxious or timid as Mma Ramotswe gave her some tea, which she always did if clients were “nervous”. However, Happy seemed “intelligent” to Mma Ramotswe and the fact that she was good at arithmetic seemed to confirm this impression. There were few lines on her face, suggesting to Mma Ramotswe that Happy Bapetsi had had few worries in her life. The fact that she did well at school suggested she was hardworking and conscientious and “promotion after promotion” at work reinforced this impression and perhaps suggested that she was successful and capable in her chosen career. However, she was also aware of sexist attitudes at work which limited her progress up the career ladder. Nevertheless, she appreciated that she had a decent job, good pay and a nice house. She seemed to accept her situation. The fact that there was no mention of a husband or partner suggested to some that she was single, a career woman, and that was fair enough. Some candidates suggested that she was an independent woman. Most of the inferences were not too difficult and the opening two questions were a real opportunity to access marks.
c700u10-nov21-03-q:
This question also assesses AO2 and is worth ten marks. The question focused on a slightly longer section of the text. It was a two-part question and, although its aim was to test analysis of how the writer used language to achieve effects, it allowed some credit to be given for understanding the thoughts and feelings of two of the main characters in the story. In this section the significant part of Happy Bapetsi’s story was revealed and it explained why she was looking for help from a private detective.

One approach was to tackle each character separately, but it was easier to track the text methodically and engage with the dialogue between the two women. Their interaction was the key to understanding their thoughts and feelings as the narrative progressed. Broadly, the writer showed the reader what the characters were thinking and feeling but he also told the reader what they were thinking and feeling. Language choice was often key.

At first in these lines Mma Ramotswe seemed to feel genuinely pleased that Happy had had a successful and happy life. She smiled and complimented her on ‘doing well’. Happy took the compliment and admitted she was very happy but her use of the past tense suggested that her feelings had changed and she was not happy at all. She bluntly stated the reason for her change of circumstances as the arrival of her father.

This revelation clearly shocked Mma Ramotswe as she “drew in her breath” and her thought that Happy was having boyfriend trouble was replaced by “a different matter altogether”. Mma Ramotswe seemed to feel apprehensive at this point as the narrative had taken an unexpected turn.

Happy described the arrival of her ‘father’ with no obvious enthusiasm and says she “almost fainted” when he turned up. A potentially joyful reunion had resulted only in misery for Happy. When she paused in her story she was perhaps doing it deliberately for effect, waiting for the full implications to sink in, but also perhaps she was finding it difficult to go on because she was so unhappy. She obviously felt resentment at having to do all the work for her self-invited guest and Mma Ramotswe clearly felt that was a typical situation as she expressed her opinion that “many men are like that.”

Happy claimed that she was “tired” of running after her so-called father and said she suspected that he was not really her father at all. She thought he was an “impostor” who was looking for a retirement home. At this point, Mma Ramotswe stares in disbelief and the writer’s use of the word “astonishment” conveyed the impact on her.

Happy’s questions and her plea for help are said in a tone of “desperation” but Mma Ramotswe felt determined to help this woman as she does not hesitate. Her acceptance of the task was emphatic as she repeated “I’ll find out” in no uncertain terms.

In general, Mma Ramotswe reacts in a series of thoughts and feelings to Happy Bapetsi’s story, ranging from shock to astonishment to determination. Happy herself felt unhappy and exploited and desperate. The overview was not too difficult and the writer used the dialogue and interaction as well as significant language choices.
c700u10-nov21-04-q:
This question (which again assesses AO2) involved a long section of text and explicitly addressed the issue of how the writer showed Mma Ramotswe to be both clever and effective through plot, language and structure. Given that she succeeded completely in unmasking and removing the impostor from Happy Bapetsi’s home, it would have been difficult to argue against the premise of the question and the sensible responses tracked the details of Mma Ramotswe’s plan as it unfolded, identifying how what she said and did achieved her aims. She formulated a clever plan and she executed it quickly and very effectively.

For example, she borrowed a uniform to give authenticity to her disguise as a nurse and she increased the speed of her van as she approached the house to make it look as if she was in a hurry and was responding to a genuine emergency. She also ran up to the house to reinforce the impression of urgency and create a sense of alarm.

When she reached the house, she pretended to be out of breath and she was convincing as she told the tale of Happy’s life-threatening “accident” and her need for an operation. She was not fooled by his emotional reaction to her news and saw through his outburst of grief and concern, judging it to be “an act”. The next stage of her plan was to claim that Happy needed a lot of blood and, when he suggested paying for it, she cleverly responded by insisting that it could only be supplied by a family member.

There was a battle of wits and he made excuses such as pointing out that he was an old man. However, his reluctance had confirmed Mma Ramotswe’s suspicions and already almost proved that he was a fraud.

She then pushed him into a corner by claiming that the hospital needed so much blood that it would be dangerous for the donor and she said bluntly, “You could die”. The success of her plan was shown clearly as his mouth fell open and she suggested that a real father would make this sacrifice for his daughter.

The collapse of his resistance came quickly at the end as she tugged him towards the van and confronted him with her arms folded in a pose that brooked no argument. She threatened him with the law and she acted and spoke “firmly”, giving him just five minutes to get his things. Her tone was forceful and she spoke with authority throughout the confrontation. Her plan was a complete success.

The better answers tracked the development of the narrative in detail and made an attempt at least to identify what was clever and effective in Mma Ramotswe’s plan. However, some candidates found it difficult to line up the answer effectively and resorted to simple narrative. Some candidates made a decent selection of relevant material but really struggled to explain why any of it was either clever or effective. There were also examples of candidates answering a different question as they discussed how the text was tense and dramatic.
c700u10-nov21-05-q:
This question was evaluative, inviting a critical response to the text as a whole, and the specific focus of the question was the way men were presented in the passage. The wording of the question suggested that men were not presented in a good light in this story and generally it was difficult to argue with that proposition as most of the men were not attractive characters with the notable exception of Mma Ramotswe’s father who made only a brief appearance at the beginning of the story. However, as always, the key to this question was to establish a coherent stance based on the details in the text.

Those who worked on the text methodically began with Mma Ramotswe’s father. He passed an inheritance to her and wanted her to have her own business. He obviously cared for his only daughter and she appreciated that he had worked and saved to give her a good life. The fact that Mma Ramotswe loved him beyond all other men confirmed the unequivocally positive presentation of her father as a caring, responsible and generous man.

Some candidates paused to consider and include the behaviour of Happy Bapetsi’s colleagues at the bank. The presentation of these men was much less positive and they were criticised as envious of a woman’s ability, causing Happy’s career to stall as she reached a ceiling because of this envy. It was also suggested that the men were worried because Happy would make them look stupid.

Mma Ramotswe also expressed some unflattering opinions about men in general, assuming that it had to be a man’s “bad behaviour” that ruined Happy’s happiness. When Happy described her fake daddy as lazy and selfish, Mma Ramotse suggested that “many men are like that”.

However, the male character who attracted the most attention was Happy’s father. Her ‘real’ father had gone away to work, according to her mother. It was possible to argue that this was well-intentioned. However, the apparent lack of communication and the fact that Happy’s mother did not mind his absence because she never really liked him anyway implied that this was not a positive move and it seemed to most that he had simply abandoned his family and responsibilities.

The best answers had coherence and good coverage, but a number of candidates answered a different question and got distracted by the issue of whether the presentation of men was fair or accurate. It is important to read the question carefully.
c700u10-nov21-11-q:
The choice of four titles offered an opportunity to write imaginatively or from personal experience.

As always, the better responses maintained a coherent perspective, using either first or third person, and the content showed a sense of direction and structure. They used detail, dialogue and characterisation appropriately to keep the reader engaged and interested. Responses do not have to be predictable, but they should be relevant and engage the reader’s interest. Less successful narratives are often implausible or lacking substance.

(a) The fresh start almost always involved moving to a new school or college. Some of the responses were unconvincing but most were coherent enough, often contrasting the restrictions of school with the freedom of college.

(b) This was a popular choice and offered a good opportunity to write from personal experience. Some were unconvincingly melodramatic, but most described the trials and tribulations of looking after small children without becoming implausible. Life as a babysitter rarely goes smoothly it would seem.

(c) There were some rather awkward transitions from this opening, but it was another popular choice. Cheating in examinations or relationships were the obvious paths to take and there were some good responses to this option. It helps the candidates when the title offers a clear structure and direction, as it did here.

(d) Constructing a narrative to fit a given conclusion can be difficult. However, this title offered a clear ‘target’ for the writing and most managed to put together a story which involved selfishness of one sort or another. Some responses misfired but most were relevant and reached the conclusion appropriately.

Summary of key points

In the reading section:

• Candidates need to work methodically through the text, particularly in questions worth ten marks.

• Candidates need to provide some substance and detail in questions worth ten marks. Some answers are too brief and offer very limited coverage of the text.

• Candidates need to line up the question (for example in Q.03) and answer the question that is actually there (for example in Q.05).

In the writing section:

• Candidates need to think about using relevant detail to give their work substance and authenticity.

• Candidates need to take care with tenses. This has been mentioned in previous reports but the failure to control tenses is a widespread problem and it seriously undermines a lot of writing.

• Candidates need to take care to communicate clearly and accurately.

c700u10-nov22-01-q:
The opening question is never intended to put barriers in the way of the candidates and there were lots of details about Lily in the first few lines of this passage. All that was required was a degree of care with content and presentation. Clarity and precision are the key qualities in this type of response. For example, she was called Frears, and she was the narrator’s mother-in-law, or Ewan’s mother. She was a successful painter in her day, and she had been a beautiful girl. She had had several relationships and she had been married twice. She could be stubborn and she kept her name and her independence. It was claimed that lots of people loved her but, according to her son, she only loved her cats. According to the narrator, Lily was a free spirit but Ewan thought she was not a good mother.

This type of question tests location of implicit and explicit information and there were more than enough explicit details to enable the candidates to gain full marks relatively easily. Most candidates took the opportunity to score well and many gained full marks with minimum fuss. However, some did get into a muddle and failed to sort out the difference between Lily and the narrator. Some were just careless and/or imprecise and lost marks unnecessarily.
c700u10-nov22-02-q:
This question involved a very short section of text and maintained the focus on impressions of Lily, who was seen through the eyes and experience of the narrator. According to the narrator, Lily was an attractive woman and she described her as ‘lovely’. In this context, ‘lovely’ did not mean kind or caring. She was also a striking woman who could turn heads in the street. She was clearly extrovert and self- confident and wore flamboyant and colourful clothes. A significant number of candidates misread this part of the text and claimed that Lily wore dull clothes. She was described as ‘a living legend’ at the art school and this was open to some interpretation. Most suggested that she was well-known or respected. She was certainly untidy or messy, living in a ‘cluttered flat’ but she was sociable and talkative, entertaining the narrator for hours with her conversation. Overall, the reader was given the impression of a bohemian ‘character’, an individual with a rather unconventional style.

The better answers were concise but clear, seeing the essential features of the character. The question was only worth five marks and it was possible to deal with it quickly and efficiently. Most candidates made some progress but not very many were thorough enough to gain full marks.
c700u10-nov22-03-q:
This question required the candidates to see the general contrast between Lily and the narrator’s parents and also the way the writer used very specific details to show the differences between them.

In general, the narrator’s parents were presented as traditional, conventional grandparents whereas Lily was presented as informal and unconventional to say the least. The narrator’s parents seemed organised and responsible whereas Lily was exactly the opposite.

In detail, the narrator’s parents lived in a ‘tidy and comfortable’ house while Lily lived in an untidy flat. The narrator’s parents had ‘safe’ lawns where the children could play but at Lily’s rather dangerous flat they sucked paintbrushes and tripped over cat litter trays. The narrator’s parents had a fridge which was always ‘crammed’ whereas Lily’s fridge contained only gin and cat food. The narrator’s parents always provided a ‘proper’ Sunday lunch, contrasting with Lily who ‘had never cooked a proper meal in her life’. Sherry was not allowed for children at the home of the narrator’s parents but Lily, predictably enough, allowed them to have a sip of sherry. The narrator’s mother was ‘Granny’ (no first names) but Lily did allow them to use her first name and they called her Lily.

This question gave the candidates every opportunity to score well but very few explicitly addressed the second part of the question and looked at how the writer showed the differences. In fact, it was quite straightforward as the writer used a series of pointed and explicit contrasts to highlight the differences.
c700u10-nov22-04-q:
This question focused on a longer section of the story but the better answers approached the incident methodically and tracked the text. The weaker answers were often brief and lacking substance or unselective, failing to sort out the dramatic from the mundane.

Some candidates showed awareness of the structure of the story and saw the context of this incident was a visit to the Ladies’ Lake where the rules meant that the narrator went swimming alone and left her children in the care of Lily.

She remembered noticing that the children were quiet and that was perhaps the first hint that something was wrong but the incident began with little sense of imminent danger. When the narrator returned from her swim, Lily was engaged in drawing the sleeping Cassandra and all seemed tranquil and quiet. However, when the narrator asked, quite calmly, about Alex’s whereabouts, all she got was silence and then a casual ‘he was here a minute ago.’ This was probably the first real suggestion that something could be wrong and the narrator’s voice had ‘sharpness’ in it when she asked again about Alex and questioned if he really had been gone for just a minute. The drama and excitement then began to develop quickly.

The meadow was full of long grass where a child could be concealed but when the narrator called him all she got was more ‘silence’. At this point in the story the writer’s language was deliberately chosen to build the excitement and drama. The exclamation when she shouted Alex’s name indicated her rising panic and she ‘barked’ commands at Lily while ‘frantically’ trying to unbuckle Cassandra. She admitted that her hands would not work and verbs such as ‘fumbles’, ‘wrenches’ and ‘grabs’ were all further evidence of her panic. The narrator ‘bundled’ Cassandra under her arm and ‘plunged’ into the long grass. The better candidates saw the urgency in her movements and the fact that she no longer trusted her child with Lily. She tried to run, even though it was difficult, and she stumbled over hidden potholes. She used the word ‘sinister’ to describe the meadow and she began to torment herself with accusations of why she left her ‘most precious possession’ with a ‘self- absorbed old lady’. The writer described the narrator as having eyes blurred with tears and condemning the weeds as ‘wicked’. The fact that she ‘screeched’ at people, hating them and herself, showed the fear and hysteria which had consumed her. She thought of Lily as ‘a stupid old woman’ and related the incident to the reader’s experience. A missing child is perhaps every parent’s nightmare and the narrator vividly captured the terrible emotions felt in that situation as time stops and frightening pictures crowd your head. Eventually, she found Alex back where they had started and looking like a ‘lost boy’ with a red face. Alex was ‘matter of fact’ about the incident but he slept for fourteen hours, showing the traumatic impact on him.

There was a lot to explore here and the candidates who engaged fully with the text and the question were not short of material. The whole incident was presented from the perspective of the narrator/mother and the drama and excitement were largely conveyed through her increasing and understandable panic and hysteria.
c700u10-nov22-05-q:
The first four questions in this section were relatively straightforward but, as is usually the case, the final question was the most challenging. It tested the ability of the candidates to show an overview of the whole story and construct a coherent argument. This proved very difficult for some candidates and many of them failed even to mention lines 69-86.

The final section of the story moved on eight years to a time when Lily was dead and Alex had no memory of the events surrounding the ‘beautiful drawing’ of Cassandra in their lounge. When he asked about the drawing, the narrator wanted him to know the real Lily. She wanted to put the record straight and the question focused on the extent to which these revelations changed the reader’s view of Lily.

In the early part of the story, the narrator described Lily as a very successful artist and teacher who was extrovert (and perhaps irresponsible and selfish) but much admired. However, she now exploded some of the mythology surrounding her mother-in-law.

At the end of the story the narrator told Alex that Lily was not a ‘famous’ painter but just an artistic woman who had people in her life who loved her and admired her. She was not ‘a living legend’ at the art school but had actually been kept on out of kindness. Her flamboyant appearance meant people sometimes giggled at her in the street. All of this certainly altered the reader’s perception of Lily and the narrator explained that her admiration for Lily had been based on resentment of her own parents and it had hurt her husband because it was ‘undeserved’ and ‘untrue’. However, the narrator still talked about Lily being a ‘striking beauty’ and she also maintained that she was an ‘original’ who was ‘completely herself’. The narrator insisted that she loved and admired Lily, not least because she had time for her when no-one else did. This contradicted the earlier impression of Lily being totally self- absorbed and self-centred.

Some candidates successfully picked a way through the contradictions in the character of Lily whilst other candidates made some progress by simply identifying the ways in which the narrator changed the reader’s view of Lily. The better answers saw that in some ways the perception of Lily did not change. However, some candidates were struggling to construct a coherent or relevant response, and many were very brief. Unfortunately, a number of candidates did not respond to this question at all suggesting time management was a problem for some candidates in this November series.
c700u10-nov22-11-q:
This title usually involved moving school or house and the responses were often quite convincing in content and tried to convey how it felt to experience a new beginning. Some were improbable in development but those who chose this option generally had something relevant to write about.

(b) This was quite a popular choice but not always a successful one. Some candidates found the transition from the given opening rather awkward while others did not really produce a creative piece of writing and their responses tended to be discursive rather than narrative. Some of the stories of attacks by dogs seemed rather alarming but the most effective narratives in terms of content and structure tended to be those where the writer was won over by a pet dog and eventually found the animal irresistible.

(c) There were various interpretations of this title, ranging from driving tests to tests of endurance or sporting prowess. However, the most obvious, and popular, approach was to describe taking an examination. This approach had the not inconsiderable advantage of providing real experience on which the candidates could base their writing. Most were only too familiar with the nerves and stress of being tested in examinations and they could draw on convincing detail to give some substance to their writing.

(d) This title pushed the candidates towards personal experience, and I suspect few of them have not experienced some sort of sporting event which took place in bad weather. Some of the responses were rather implausible, and others strained the definition of ‘an event’, but most described cross-country runs, football matches or other sporting events. Surprisingly, examiners reported seeing few accounts of musical events such as Glastonbury.

In general, it is perhaps worth repeating some observations from a report of some years ago which read as follows: ‘Most candidates do manage to construct a reasonably coherent narrative, but many are seriously undermined by technical shortcomings and limited, or misused, vocabulary. The technical aspects of written expression are specifically weighted at 40% of the total available marks for writing and too many candidates lose marks because of the lack of accuracy in their work.’ Sadly, those words remain true and problems with technical accuracy, including inconsistency with tenses, still prevail.

Summary of key points

In the reading section: • Candidates need to be careful and precise in answering questions such as 1. • When dealing with longer sections of text, candidates need to be selective and focused on the requirements of the question. • Candidates should think particularly carefully about the focus of their answers to evaluation questions (5). It is vital that they read the question carefully and think about a coherent line of approach and argument.

In the writing section: • Candidates need to think about their writing and make sure that it has some substance and detail. There is no need to write endlessly but the target is 450 words. • Candidates need to be consistent with tenses. Simple past tense is usually the safest. • Most candidates write well when they write from personal experience, and some can write original narratives which are imaginative and convincing but it isn’t always easy to do this. Candidates should practise writing imaginatively and from personal experience to help them make an informed decision about which title to choose in the exam. • Technical accuracy is important and should not be neglected. Building in time for proofreading is essential.

This question tested the ability to identify explicit and implicit information and ideas and the relevant points were all to be found in the opening paragraph of the passage. The instruction to ‘List five things’ was not always followed as clearly as it might have been. However, examiners are not looking to put obstacles in the way of the candidates and most candidates did produce a list of bullet points. There was plenty of material about Adam in the opening paragraph but not so much that it could tempt the candidates into unnecessarily lengthy answers.

For example, the reader learned that Adam spent five years in the army. Some said he was a soldier, which was an entirely accurate alternative. He spent his time in the army doing routine tasks such as polishing and drilling and the time passed quickly. He rarely communicated with his brother (or he rarely wrote letters home). The reader also learned that he left the army in 1890 in San Francisco and he did write to say that he was coming home. He then ‘disappeared’ for three years.

6 This type of question is not intended to be too challenging but it is a test of understanding. Some candidates were careless or imprecise in handling this question (a surprising number got the date he left the army wrong) but it should have offered a straightforward way into the passage, and the character of Adam Trask.
c700u10-nov23-02-q:
Questions 02, 03 and 04 all assess assessment objective 2 (AO2). This five-mark question asked for impressions of Adam Trask and this inevitably involved direct reference to the text but also some inference. The more successful candidates achieved a pragmatic blend of inference and evidence while remaining aware of the pressure of time in a question only worth five marks. In practice, this question was looking for a range of impressions supported by some textual evidence. The answers had to come from the information contained in the second paragraph of the passage.

The fact that Adam spent his first winter out of the army in the warmth of San Francisco perhaps showed his commonsense but also that he was in no rush to go home, or anywhere else for that matter. Some argued, not unreasonably, that he did not like the cold of winter. He ended the winter with no money, but he did not seem to care about money or material possessions and he set out to walk a formidable distance home, enjoying the freedom of the road. He showed resourcefulness in hitching risky rides on freight trains and he learned to beg for food but not money, which perhaps indicated some pride and self-respect. He was a shrewd judge of a house as a source of charity and he also learned how to avoid arrest by travelling alone and making sure he was clean and shaven. He gave the impression of being a loner (though not necessarily lonely) and he became ‘expert’ at hiding his personality and staying invisible. He did not attract attention to himself. Some candidates noticed that he was afraid of the police and prisoners, but he seemed to enjoy the freedom of his life on the road.

Merely locating details from the text was not really enough on its own but a reasonable selection of impressions and textual references was enough to gain full marks in this question.
c700u10-nov23-03-q:
This question was worth 10 marks and covered a significantly longer section of text. The issue of ‘how’ a writer creates drama and tension involves understanding and referring to the content and the question instructed the candidates to look at what happened in this section of the text as well as language and structure. A focus on what happened and in what order was a perfectly sensible way to approach this question. It is also worth mentioning that it is very difficult to engage with the idea of structure without a methodical approach.

Events took a dramatic turn as this section began with Adam being arrested and sentenced to six months on a road gang for being homeless. Most candidates reacted to the dramatic injustice when Adam was immediately arrested again after his release as the authorities seemed to be playing a version of ‘cat and mouse’ with him. The writer described the harsh conditions and punishments he endured and his strategy of surviving by making himself invisible and apparently passive. It was not absolutely clear at this stage what Adam was planning but it was not difficult to argue that this part was dramatic as the reader waited to see how things would develop.

7 Then came the escape which was well-planned and meticulously executed. There was a lot of detail the candidates could use as evidence here as the tension mounted, not least in the dogs searching for him. Adam’s cautious tactics added to the tension as he showed ‘iron control’ in not allowing himself to rush his escape. For example, he stayed hidden on the edge of town until well after midnight and he eventually entered the town ‘like a shadow’. He broke into a store and took some clothes. This was a risky but necessary move and he covered his tracks and concealed the robbery as well as he could. He stayed hidden by day and stole food by night, although he took nothing that would be missed. All of this took place against the backdrop of what Adam, and the reader, knew would be a relentless search for him. There was an unspoken but very ominous sense of the consequences of capture and this was emphasised by Adam’s extreme caution.

When he reached the station with escape tantalisingly close, he was tense and took a deep breath. The station manager talking to his friend seemed to threaten Adam’s plan at the last moment and there was a tense wait of twenty minutes. However, he showed nerves of steel as he took a deep breath to calm himself then walked past the ticket office and sneaked onto a train ‘unobserved’.

A lot of the tension and drama here lay in the obvious question of whether he would escape, and how. The chase was inherently dramatic and tense.

The better answers did more than simply ‘tell the story’ but those candidates who stuck methodically to the sequence of events and at least attempted to address the issues of tension and drama usually coped well enough. Less successful responses lacked substance and detail, and some placed too much emphasis on spotting techniques without developing clear points.
c700u10-nov23-04-q:
There were only two characters in this passage and the relationship between them occupied a significant section of the text. A series of impressions securely rooted in the text did the job in this question and the more successful candidates worked through the passage systematically, linking impressions to textual evidence.

It was important to work methodically and follow the narrative as the relationship between the brothers deteriorated after a promising start into anger and recrimination. At first Charles seemed pleased to see Adam and he made a real effort. He came out of the barn ‘quickly’ and ‘hurried’ to shake hands. He had been looking forward to Adam’s return for three years and his actions showed he was eager to see him again. However, some candidates did notice that the writer used the dialogue to suggest some awkwardness in the relationship. Their conversation did not develop very far, although at this point it could be argued that this was just a consequence of their long separation or a natural reticence. They were men of few words. Some candidates also argued that the handshake was rather formal.

However, Charles had also gone to some trouble to make Adam feel welcome, and perhaps impress him. He had painted the house and barn and employed a woman to clean the house. He was driven into living in a shed while the house was cleaned but he was so anxious to keep everything clean in the house that he continued to live in the shed until Adam arrived. Some answers perhaps overstated the ‘love’ between the brothers but there was plenty of evidence to suggest that they were pleased to see each other.

8 For several months Adam conformed to the routine established by his brother but they began to get on each other’s nerves and the writer observed that they saw too much of each other and not enough of anyone else. Living in such close proximity began to increase the pressure on the relationship, particularly as Charles was so inflexible in his ways. For example, he rose at four thirty every morning and never varied. This provided a flashpoint as Adam found the rigid routine hard to take and the brothers started to quarrel. They clearly had different priorities and they clashed over Charles’ work ethic. Adam questioned the need to work so relentlessly just to buy more land and do more work. Charles ‘snapped’ at him in reply and his temper flared. He argued ‘angrily’ and when Adam suggested he could leave Charles made no attempt to make him change his mind. Adam knew the quarrel was ‘silly’ but he could not help himself and provocatively pointed out that the farm belonged to him as much as it did to Charles. The final words on the subject went to Charles as he challenged Adam to do some work.

The brothers then argued about Charles’ irritating habit of not wiping his butter knife and it leads to Adam being told to leave. He departed, claiming that he would ‘rather live in a pigsty.’ The relationship, which had begun so well, ended in bitterness and childish temper. They were just too different to get along. Some candidates understood that Charles was dedicated to the farm but Adam was a free spirit.

The overview of the relationship was quite straightforward but the better responses engaged with the text in detail.
c700u10-nov23-05-q:
As usual, the final question in this section required critical evaluation of the text as a whole and specifically a personal response to the presentation of Adam and Charles Trask. Time is often an issue with this question as candidates, quite rightly, are anxious to leave enough time for their writing. However, the main problem for many candidates is establishing a coherent stance from which they can argue a convincing case. The obvious response here, and certainly the most convincing, was to argue that both brothers had their qualities and, as individuals, were presented ‘positively’ to some extent.

In the first part of the passage the focus was on Adam, who took three years to get home after he left the army. He became a vagrant, a beggar and a thief but he was also presented as resourceful and shrewd and the writer presented the events from his perspective. He tended to be seen just as a free spirit who attracted sympathy as a victim of brutality and injustice. He did steal but he did not really hurt anyone and the writer showed him only taking what he needed such as clothes and food. He did not beg for money, or steal it, and the character of Adam seemed to engage the readers, at least at first. The readers wanted him to escape and complete his journey home.

Similarly, there was a lot to admire in the initial presentation of the character of Charles. He seemed keen to welcome his brother home and he made an effort to paint and clean the house. He was a dedicated and respected farmer, working hard and running the farm well.

However, both had their flaws and weaknesses and when they were living together on the farm they seemed to bring out the worst in each other. They were different in values and temperament and they saw ‘too much of each other and not enough of anyone else.’

9 For example, Adam did not seem to make much of an effort to adapt to life on the farm and he was argumentative over ‘silly’ things. He could not resist provoking his brother and eventually he left the farm in a mood of anger, claiming he would rather live in a pigsty.

Charles was not a sociable man and, although he was respected for his work ethic, he avoided the local villagers. He followed rigid and uncompromising routine on the farm and he came across as a dour character who was set in his ways. Both brothers showed they had a temper and were prepared to argue.

The better answers engaged with the detail of the text and pursued a coherent argument. The weaker answers tended to be thin or struggling to respond convincingly to the presentation of the characters.
c700u10-nov23-11-q:
(a) The Holiday Job.

It was possible to write imaginatively here but it was more likely that the responses were based on real experience of a holiday job. Many candidates clearly had had actual experience of holiday work in a variety of roles. The more successful responses showed some self-awareness and humour. However, some responses followed rather unconvincing notions of a holiday job.

(b) Write about a time when you took a young relative out for the day.

Although there was plenty of scope here to embellish the truth, most

responses seemed to be based on real events and visits to tourist attractions.

(c) The Rivals.

This title was ‘open’ and invited a narrative which included some sort of competition or rivalry. There was often a clearly personal element in these responses but it was perfectly acceptable to write imaginatively.

(d) Write a story which begins: There are days when things just go right.

The opening of a narrative is often helpful as it provides a way into the writing and a sense of direction. This example clearly offered the opportunity to write about the perfect day but the ‘things’ that went right were very much open to individual choice. Good things take many forms and it was possible to write about financial gain or sporting achievement or a range of other possibilities. However, a surprising number of responses involved a day when things went wrong.

Characteristics of successful responses

• In the reading section, candidates who tracked through the stated lines were able to accumulate relevant textual details and, in most cases, explore these. • In the 10-mark questions that assess AO2, answers that selected a range of evidence to comment on and analyse were more successful in gaining marks in the higher bands. • In question 05, those candidates who immediately established a clear point of view were more successful in maintaining a coherent stance in their response. • In the writing section, successful responses used characterisation and dialogue to engage the reader and purposefully structure their responses.

Key Areas for Improvement

• In the reading section candidates need to allocate time sensibly and stick to the timing plan. Missing out a question, especially a 10-mark question will inevitably affect the candidate’s overall result. • In question 05 candidates need a coherent argument and they should support their opinions by using the text. • In narrative writing the responses should have direction and substance. A brief plan can help with this. • Technical errors and uncertainty with tenses are still too frequent.

c700u10-nov24-01-q:
The opening question followed a familiar and predictable pattern, and the focus was on what the reader learned about a person. It tested the ability to identify explicit and implicit information and ideas and the relevant points were all to be found in the short opening paragraph of the passage. Weaker answers were clumsy in approach or phrasing.

Lack of clarity and precision make it very difficult to reward candidates who do not present their answers clearly and coherently. That said, there were plenty of valid points available here. Some reorganisation of the text was possible but most of the relevant material was on the surface.

For example, Tom Ramsay had been a problem to his family for twenty years. He had started life ‘decently’. Some candidates showed their understanding by replacing ‘decently’ with words such as predictably or respectably but that was not essential. Tom followed a predictable path as he went into business and he married and had two children. He seemed to be destined for a ‘useful and successful life’ but he suddenly decided to give up work and family. He wanted to enjoy himself and he spent two years happily travelling around Europe.

Those candidates who separated the facts about Tom Ramsay into five clear bullet or numbered points scored full marks with minimum fuss. Only a small minority of candidates missed out on five marks here.
c700u10-nov24-02-q: This question had a clear focus on how the writer showed George Ramsay’s unhappiness in a short section of the text. In general, the writer used action, description, dialogue and tone but most answers, quite rightly, concentrated on the details in the text rather than abstract techniques. Some candidates suggested that the fact George was eating alone indicated his unhappiness. This was not an unreasonable suggestion but the writer’s description of his ‘expression of deep gloom’ was totally clear. He was described as ‘staring into space’ which suggested he was at least preoccupied or distracted by things on his mind. The writer also described George looking as though he had ‘the whole world sat on his shoulders’. He told the writer/narrator that he was ‘not in great spirits’ and he sighed at the suggestion that it was Tom again. The adverb ‘miserably’ emphasised his unhappiness. The best answers picked out the relevant details and produced an answer which was concise and coherent. Weaker answers relied exclusively on quotation without any supporting comment.
c700u10-nov24-03-q:
This question was worth ten marks and focused on a slightly longer section of the text. It was a two-part question and, although its main aim was to test analysis of how writers use language to achieve effects, it allowed credit to be given for understanding of the character of Tom Ramsay. The issue of ‘how’ the writer created impressions of the aunt was often a matter of selecting the relevant evidence but the good answers required some inference and a clear range of impressions. The key was to get the measure of the character.

Tracking the text closely and combining impressions with evidence was the most effective approach and it was clear that Tom’s behaviour ‘profoundly’ shocked his respectable family. He had ‘a very good time’ and when he ran out of money he simply borrowed. The evidence suggested that he was a playboy, dedicated to his own pleasure and a spendthrift. He was a charmer and it was difficult to refuse him a loan. He was irresponsible and self-indulgent, claiming that spending money on necessities was ‘boring’ and enjoying spending on luxuries. He found self-indulgent spending ‘amusing’. Tom relied on his brother to fund his extravagant lifestyle and lied to him, making false promises to mend his ways but then using the money to buy expensive luxuries such as jewellery and cars. Tom was presented as totally unscrupulous and selfish. He had no conscience about blackmailing George, or exploiting his brother’s sensitivity to the family reputation. He was seen, quite rightly, as manipulative and no fool as he did not waste his charm on George but targeted his weak spot.

Some candidates were not attracted by Tom’s unconventionality, but others were more seduced by the presentation of him, seeing him as a likeable rogue rather than a scoundrel.
c700u10-nov24-04-q:
This question asked the candidates to identify the differences between Tom and George Ramsay and how those differences were shown by the writer. Less successful answers tended to be thin or to produce a jumble of comment and evidence but the better answers had some organisation and clarity of purpose. The writer used a series of general and specific contrasts in lifestyle, behaviour and attitudes to show the differences and the authorial voice was also important in shaping the reader’s perception of the two brothers.

The best approach was to link the characters of Tom and George in a series of specific contrasts. For example, Tom was described as having been ‘selfish, thoughtless and wild’, showing no care for the family’s reputation, but George was thoroughly respectable. He was ‘terribly upset’ at the thought of Tom going to prison and he cared about the family name. Unlike Tom, he perhaps cared about his brother too.

In these lines Tom was also shown to be cunning and unscrupulous. He played an elaborate hoax on his brother, tricking and exploiting George into paying a large amount of money which he then spent in Monte Carlo with his partner in crime. In sharp contrast to his brother, George was described as ‘honest’.

Tom was presented as extravagant and self-indulgent in a series of details such as his taste for gambling, expensive restaurants, pretty girls and stylish clothes. Tom looked like a movie star. He looked younger than his age and was presented as handsome and glamorous. George was thrifty and hardworking, and he looked much older than he was.

Tom was described as ‘perfectly worthless’ but a ‘most amusing companion’. Time spent with Tom was enjoyable and he had ‘high spirits’ and ‘charm’, which made him irresistible. Tom was popular and well-known. He may have been an incorrigible wastrel but ‘you could not help liking him.’ Unlike Tom. George was a committed family man. He was a faithful husband and a good father to his daughters. In contrast to the spendthrift Tom, George was careful with his money. He had saved and planned his retirement, unlike Tom who simply squandered his money.

Some argued that Tom was glamorous and exciting whereas George was dull and boring, planning to spend a quiet retirement gardening and playing golf. A few noticed that where Tom was charming and amusing, George was jealous and vindictive, wanting Tom to get his just desserts and taking pleasure in the prospect of his brother ‘ending in the gutter’.

Too many responses relied on what were really two completely separate character studies, but this was actually an opportunity to score well.
c700u10-nov24-05-q:
As is usually the case, the final question was the most challenging and for one reason or another, the completion rate was lower than for the rest of the paper. It tested the ability of the candidates to focus on a specific section of the text but also show an overview of the whole story and construct a coherent argument. This proved very difficult for most candidates and some of them failed even to mention lines 59- 75.

The early part of the passage revealed that George had many virtues and was indeed ‘hardworking, decent and respectable.’ He was also clearly a victim, exploited and cheated shamelessly by his brother. Some candidates mentioned that George was resentful and expressed his desire for revenge as he imagined the satisfaction of living comfortably while his brother suffered in old age. His desire for revenge was perhaps unattractive and Tom’s high spirits made him appealing, but most candidates seemed to feel that George was both a decent man and a victim who had every right to feel aggrieved.

In the final section of the passage the story returned to the narrator/writer meeting George in the restaurant and immediately assuming that Tom was the reason for him being upset and hardly able to speak. The narrator sympathised with George and agreed with everything he said when he contrasted himself with his brother. George was clearly very angry and described his brother as a ‘worthless rogue’ who would be living on the streets if there were any justice in the world.

It was then revealed that there was indeed no justice in the world as Tom had inherited a fortune from a wife ‘old enough to be his mother’. George’s rage was evident as he slammed his fist on the table and denounced the unfairness of life. The narrator reacted with a ‘shout of laughter’ which was almost uncontrollable. He found the situation ‘hysterical’ and the narrator’s response was important in shaping the reader’s response. George never forgave the narrator and seemed mean-spirited and churlish, but Tom continued to dine with the narrator.

The blanket assertion that ‘I agree’ or ‘I disagree’ did not work very well here. There were three elements in the quotation in the question and they needed to be addressed individually. For example, most responses agreed that George was a decent man and a victim, but opinion was divided on whether to sympathise with him.
c700u10-nov24-11-q:
The choice of four titles offered an opportunity to write imaginatively or from personal experience.

(a) Write a story that begins: It was going to be a special day out with the family.

It was possible to take this title at face value and describe a special day out with the family. However, it was also possible to use the hint in the wording and describe a day where things did not go to plan. Some answers went off in a completely unexpected direction, but most were relevant and had some coherence.

(b) Write about an occasion when you went to a live performance such as a concert, theatre visit or sporting event.

This option encouraged the candidates to draw on their own experience of going to a live performance. The less successful responses had limited reader-awareness and tended to concentrate just on a simple string of events but the better answers captured the atmosphere and texture of the event. It was clear in most responses that the anticipation of the event was often the most memorable aspect.

(c) The Rescue.

This title was very open and gave the candidates a lot of scope to write from personal experience or from the imagination. Some ‘rescues’ were rather tenuous but most were coherent.

(d) Write a story that ends: Mum just looked at me, and I knew that if I did it again I was in big trouble.

Endings are not always easy to structure, and the conclusion can seem rushed or rather forced, an uncomfortable fit with the rest of the story. This option was relatively straightforward, but there were some awkwardly structured responses.

Characteristics of Successful Responses

In the reading section: • In 05 the successful responses are clear in argument and direction. They are coherent and based on a clear personal response to the text • A successful response to a question asking for ‘impressions’ of a character get beyond quotation from the text to explore the significance of the evidence and to suggest what it shows. In the writing section: • Successful writing can be imaginative but is plausible at least on its own terms. • Successful writing displays a measure of technical control, particularly with tenses and sentence construction.

Areas for Improvement

• The ‘attempt rate’ for question 05 is still relatively low and time management is an issue. • Reading responses need to be focused on the actual question. The questions follow a pattern but are not totally predictable. • Candidates need to select relevant material from the specified section of text and use it sensibly. • Quotations work best when they embedded into comments. A methodical tracking of the text usually works well but too many responses are not organised effectively. • Technical control of spelling, sentences and punctuation is a familiar area of weakness in writing. Basic errors are often numerous, and this often undermines narrative writing.

The first question, on the text by Mark Binelli, required the candidates to identify explicit information and there were three marks available for the location and selection of the appropriate details. This was a straightforward 'search and find' task but candidates’ responses indicated the real importance of reading the question carefully. The first part of the question asked for one example of how the worst prisoners were punished in the past. This presented few problems to most candidates and there were a number of possible points that they could select from, all mentioned in the opening paragraph. Working in silence in chain gangs, being physically isolated from others on Alcatraz Island were two of the possible responses but Binelli also discussed corporal punishment as well as solitary confinement as methods of punishment. However, some candidates failed to read the question carefully enough and wrote about the current punishment regime in Florence Prison.

The second part of the question asked candidates to note the number of prisoners on roll at the time of the article and again, most had no difficulty in finding the correct number: 439, although some gave the number of beds in the prison rather than how many prisoners were housed there. The final part of the question asked for one example of the privileges that could be earned in the prison for good behaviour and few failed to select one of those mentioned: mirrors, radio, televisions that would be allowed in a cell, additional 'outside' time from the cell and the possibility of transfer back to a less-secure prison. As an opening question, the intention was to allow candidates to settle into the text and when carefully read, this provided a useful foundation for the following question.
c700u20-jun17-12-q:
This question required candidates to now tackle the whole of the Binelli text, inviting them to explore how the article showed that prisoners lived in conditions he described as 'harsh'. This type of question assesses AO2 and the two bullet points asked candidates to explore what he told his readers about the conditions in which prisoners were contained, along with the way language, tone and structure were used to emphasise these conditions.

8 Additionally, many candidates recognised that in exploring 'how', Binelli had made use of the views of others, for example, the warden of Florence, who offered his view of the conditions.

Although the demands made on candidates in this type of question have increased, many candidates who tracked the text methodically found they had plenty of material upon which to base their answer. Many began with Binelli’s own view that the prison is 'known for its harsh conditions' which then led on to some specific details of the conditions that prisoners were kept in. Most saw that keeping prisoners in a cell on their own for 23 hours a day would be regarded as harsh, especially as the cell itself was 'incredibly small'. The whole of the fourth and the following three paragraphs offered very specific details of the tough conditions prisoners found themselves in and some candidates took the opportunity to note Binelli’s use of adjectives that emphasised the harshness of their incarceration, or the list-like approach to giving information which showed how many restrictions prisoners faced.

Some candidates focused their attention on the sense of physical isolation the prisoners faced, using details such as the cell doors that prevented prisoners seeing others, the limitations of the 'tiny' windows, the way parts of the prison were designed to prevent prisoners knowing where they were or the absolute lack of contact with other prisoners for the first three years. These were all rightly seen as examples of the harsh regime; as further evidence, some then used these details to explain how these conditions led to some struggling with mental problems.

There was plenty of information in the article upon which to base an answer and decent reward could be gained just by exploring this. However, by looking at Binelli’s use of language, tone and structure, the best candidates were able to push into the higher marks, although as in Component 1, the best responses began by focusing on the content and not on feature-spotting. As indicated above, many saw that his descriptions of the 'tiny' window, the 'concrete slabs' or the 'tiny' mattresses all emphasised the harshness of the conditions and perhaps reflected Binelli’s own view of the regime, despite what appeared to be a rather detached tone dealing with much factual information. Others explored the way that structurally the article began with the historical perspective that 'the worst of the worst' prisoners had always been punished especially harshly and that Florence was merely a continuation of that tradition. Having given details of the conditions faced by prisoners, Binelli then moved on to how the regime was viewed by those outside and then inside the system itself. It was perhaps telling that Binelli chose to quote the director of the American Civil Liberties Union and many candidates noted his view that the conditions were 'extraordinarily harsh' and were 'shattering' for some inmates. Some candidates then went on to explore the way the article concluded with the views of the warden, Robert Hood, who described the prison as a 'clean version of hell', and a place 'not designed for humanity', and some saw this as another way in which Binelli made clear to his readers that Florence was like no other prison. Those prepared to explore the way Binelli structured the article sometimes commented that the final paragraph offers a view from Hood that perhaps the conditions seen in Florence are more appropriate to a bygone era and that those in charge of prisons might reflect that, in the 20 years that Florence has existed, 'the world has changed'. In using this to conclude the article, some candidates commented that there seemed to be the clear implication that there may be better solutions available than the 'harsh conditions' faced by those incarcerated in Florence.
