With the opening question giving candidates the opportunity to have some broad understanding of the content of the article, this next question asked candidates to explore how the writer tried to show that Mark Poulton loved his work as a Punch and Judy man. Previous reports have repeated the message that in tackling any `craft of the writer` question, the most effective and efficient approach is to work methodically through the text, selecting appropriate evidence and then commenting, where appropriate, on the impact of the details and the way these have been presented by the writer. Working in this way, good candidates were able to accumulate a wide range of details and information and present a clear and detailed response. Readers were introduced to Mark Poulton, one of just three licensed Punch and Judy performers in the UK, and it becomes quickly apparent that the role is “the only one he’s ever wanted.” Some candidates commented on the way the reporter allowed Poulton to tell his own story, and highlighted details about his early fascination, even obsession, with Punch and Judy shows from a very early age, selecting one or two telling details to add weight to their comments. They noted, for example his determination to succeed, using details such as obtaining his first summer season at just 16 and then “taking his show all over the country.” Whilst there are points in the article where Arnott, the reporter, invites Poulton to tell his own story, good candidates were also aware that Arnott himself heaps praise on to Poulton with details that confirm his commitment and dedication to his work. He gives the example of Poulton carving his own wooden puppets and designing and making the costumes to view him as “a master of his craft” and further on in the same paragraph describes him as “a man in love with his work.”

In giving Poulton the opportunity to tell his own story, readers are told that he believes his work is now part of the town’s history and tradition, and many candidates commented on the implied sense of pride this gives him. He goes on to talk about the `big crowds` he attracts and the fact that many visit Weymouth simply to see the Punch and Judy show.

Arnott describes the way Poulton tells him this by saying, “he tells me proudly.” Many candidates seized upon the word `proudly` (variously described by candidates as an adjective, adverb, verb and a noun!) but too often it was simply `spotted` without any reference to the context in which it had been used. For some candidates, the hunt for a telling quotation or a particular feature sometimes seemed more important than reflecting on the impact of what was being said or the context of the textual detail. In some cases, the response became a series of quotations with a catch-all tag along the lines of “…this shows he loves his work”, but lacking any real exploration of the quotation or detail mentioned. At times, this became more problematic when candidates unwisely chose to use ellipsis, and in doing so, lost clarity. One example from a candidate trying to use some detail from paragraph 4 of the text was: “I love the thrill…an audience”, with the comment: “this shows he loved his work.” More assured candidates tried to give sufficient explanation and context to the details they selected, for example explaining that in trying to find “new routines” to attract audiences, Poulton constantly challenged and pushed himself to be the very best, was never complacent and was always looking for ways to improve.

Most candidates were able to select at least a few details that indicated Poulton loved his work, perhaps the most obvious being the way he put the work over any financial reward. Others wrote about the difficulties he had with unruly children that made him consider ending his shows but was then convinced to continue by the many “messages of support” he received. Some candidates continued to explore how he had tried to survive financially, giving details from the penultimate paragraph about how he sold souvenir key rings or used a crowdfunding page to raise money and commenting on his resilience and determination to continue his craft. In the final paragraph, readers are once again given Poulton’s own words as he explains that whatever the circumstances, he is “always happy to do the shows, come rain or shine.” Less-assured candidates often simply quoted this with little or no explanation, whilst more able ones were prepared to give a little explanation and a comment on the way this concluding comment captured neatly Poulton’s positive attitude and love for his work, with some saying it was a further example of him determined to overcome every difficulty or obstacle.

Successful candidates found plenty of material from the text to show how the writer had presented Poulton, and the best responses had a good range of relevant detail from across the whole text, with insightful comments, where appropriate, threaded through the answer, together with an awareness of how Arnott had presented the Punch and Judy man in such a positive light.
c700u20-jun22-13-q:
This question now asked candidates to read and respond to the second text from `London Labour and the London Poor`. As in previous examinations, there were three one-mark questions and like question 1.1 should have given candidates an overview of the text that would help them tackle the following question worth 10 marks. The first part of the question asked for one of the jobs undertaken by the partner of the Punch and Judy man. This was explained in the opening three sentences of the passage and almost all candidates were able to state that he played a drum to announce the start of a street performance. As he also collected the money after the performance, this was also a valid answer. A small number of candidates noted that the account mentions both men carry the show booth and this too was a valid answer. The passage explains in some detail about the money the Punch and Judy man received from performing and the second part of the question asked how much he was paid for performing at children’s parties.

This question required more care in reading, the information coming in the opening sentence of the fourth paragraph (“I used to attend very wealthy gentlemen’s houses for their children’s parties and get as much as two pounds for the performance.”), although later in the paragraph he explains how people now haggle with them for these performances and they get only “shillings and sixpences”. Either detail earned reward, although examiners noted that almost any amount of money mentioned in the text incorrectly found its way into this response. This and the incorrect responses to the final part of the question serve as useful reminders about the need for careful reading of both text and question. The final part of the question asked for one detail to show that not everyone paid to watch a performance. The answer to this came in the final paragraph, where readers are told that `soldiers never have any money` and also that most of the boys who watch the performances “ain’t got a halfpenny to bless themselves with”. Either of these details earned reward. Whilst most candidates gained good marks on this question, examiners noted that where candidates had not read the question carefully, it almost inevitably led to selecting wrong details that failed to answer the question. For those who had read carefully, it will have given them some understanding of the difficulties faced by the Punch and Judy man, and this should have prepared them for the 10-mark question that followed.
c700u20-jun22-14-q:
This question now asked candidates to consider the `London Labour and the London Poor` text in more detail. They were given a statement: “The account shows that making a living as a Punch and Judy man was hard and unrewarding work” and asked how far they agreed with this view. As with question 1.2, candidates who adopted a methodical approach, reading each paragraph of the account carefully in turn, selecting out relevant detail and commenting upon it had a more considered view of the statement, and were usually able to gain good marks as a result. A small minority of readers often limited their focus to one or two paragraphs or seemed to assume they had to try equally to find points of agreement and disagreement, which often led them into incorrect conclusions and selection of detail that failed to support their assertions.

One of the aspects candidates had to grapple with was that at various points in the account the man explained how the work had been financially rewarding in the past and contrasting this with much tougher times that he faced at the time of the account. Candidates who dealt successfully with this and concentrated mainly on what the Punch and Judy man had to say about his work at the time of the account generally avoided muddle and confusion. In any case, simply working methodically through the text should have made clear exactly how he felt about his work.

He begins by drawing a comparison between the money he made “in the early days” and at the time he gave his account. Many candidates saw that it was useful to give the specific details: he used to make “five pounds regular” but “a good day now seldom gets beyond five shillings.” Most used this information to comment that this proved his work was `unrewarding`, at least in financial terms. Good candidates were able to explain that if they could only earn five shillings in a full day, what could be earned during a single street performance was a pittance: “we take on average only threepence.” Sometimes less successful candidates seemed unsure how to untangle this and simply stated they “earned only five shillings and averaged only threepence”, running the details together with limited clarity or understanding.

Some candidates made the case that `better money` could be made from private shows, although more-assured readers were able to make the point that even here, they were robbed by maids who took some of the money that was to be paid to them so that they could “buy fancy ribbons.”

Most candidates recognised that it was in the third paragraph where the Punch and Judy man made it very clear that the work was hard in a number of different ways. He begins by saying that although there was money to be earned on Mondays, by the end of the week, little or nothing could be made “because then the poor have spent all their money.” The details of the daily work come in the following four sentences of the paragraph. Here, less successful candidates often simply included a long quotation, sometimes two or three sentences long with little more than a concluding comment suggesting, “this shows it was hard”. Better candidates dealt with each of the specific details, explaining how this impacted on the man. For example, some commented that for the man to perform twenty shows in a day would be extremely physically draining, having to work from “early in the morning…till dark at night” suggests that the long hours are necessary to make a living and having to walk up to twenty miles a day every day, would have a negative effect on his health and having to carry the weight of the booth “which weighs a good half-hundredweight” would make the job a physically exhausting one day after day. Candidates found further evidence of this when the man calls the work “great exertion” and goes on to say, “my voice very often fails me.”

The man goes on to give further details about how the business has become more difficult, explaining that where he was well paid for putting on a show at children’s parties, that side of his work has reduced, and where he had attended ten parties “in the olden time” he now says, “I don’t go to two now.” This loss of work is made even worse for him because of the way people now “haggle us down” from pounds to “shillings and sixpences.”

The final paragraph continues in a similar vein, with the man saying that some people, such as soldiers, who watch the show don’t pay and even when gentlemen stop to watch and sends his footman with money, he will take some of it for himself. He finally turns his attention to the boys who come to watch the street show, describing them as “the greatest nuisances” because of the way they try to disrupt the show and also because they too never have any money to put in the collection.

Although some candidates did attempt to view the man’s work as rewarding, using references to “the olden time”, most found it much more rewarding to track through the details of his daily routine to find lots of support for the view that his work was both hard and certainly financially unrewarding. Using the whole text allowed candidates to select a wide range of relevant evidence and this usually resulted in a good response that gained high marks.
c700u20-jun22-15-q:
This question asked candidates to select relevant material from across the two texts, with a little brief explanation, about how the Punch and Judy men made their money. As has been indicated in previous examination reports, the best approach to this question is to deal with each text separately. If candidates happen to explain details that apply equally to both texts, they will be rewarded but too frequently examiners report reading responses where the candidate is suggesting details about both texts, when in fact they only apply to one of them. In tackling this question, it is important for candidates to indicate clearly which detail applies to which text. Some examiners reported responses where details were muddled across the texts and this lack of clarity and precision meant candidates struggled to gain good marks. One example of this was a candidate who began his response with, “The performers made their money by selling key rings and performing at children’s parties.” Where candidates focused on each text separately, it often led them to a good mark.

In the `Knockout Punch` text, when Mark Poulton is performing on the beach, he relies on the donations made from his audience, his assistant going round with a collecting box.

He hopes that the many performances he gives to the large seaside crowds would give him a steady income, and he further supplements his income by selling souvenir key rings. However, this is still often insufficient to bring in enough money for him to live on. As a consequence, he has set up a crowdfunding page on Facebook, appealing for donations and this has allowed him to continue his Punch and Judy show.

In the `London Labour and the London Poor`, the Punch and Judy man also relies on donations from the many street shows he performs each day, but like Mark Poulton, he also looks for other ways to supplement his income. He will perform his show in `private houses` where he is able to pacify noisy children with the show, and he also talks about putting on his show for children’s parties at the houses of wealthy gentlemen, where despite parents who “haggle us down”, will still make much more money than he would from a street performance.

The instruction in the question asked candidates to `explain briefly` some of the relevant details, but some examiners reported candidates using a grid with a note of a detail but with no attempt to explain, for example, why Mark Poulton used Facebook or why the Victorian Punch and Judy man attended children’s parties. For candidates to gain good marks in the question, it is important that they follow the instructions and unless there is a specific instruction to organise their responses in a grid or other format, this should be avoided.
c700u20-jun22-16-q:
This final question invited candidates to make comparisons of the two texts, focusing on the two bullet points. These asked for comparisons of the impressions the Punch and Judy men give of the children who have watched their performances and how such impressions had been created.

In the `Knockout Punch` text, although Mark Poulton said he encouraged participation from children and saying that he wanted them join in and “to shout and yell”, there was a more disturbing impression of some children who behaved badly and lacked respect for him. He gave one example of their disruptive behaviour, saying that whilst he was performing, some would throw stones at the show booth. He went on to say that some children tried to even stop the show continuing by banging on the show booth whilst he was performing. When he told them off, he “got a load of verbal abuse.” Poulton uses the word `deliberately` when describing the children’s determined attempts to stop the show and the impact of this unruly behaviour on him is shown when he talks about how the incidents “destroyed my faith in humanity” and were so bad that it nearly caused him to end the beach performances.

The impression of the children in `London Labour and the London Poor` were in some respects similar but in other instances, rather different. When talking about the performances in the private houses, the Punch and Judy man says the children are pacified by the show and it is “something to quiet ‘em a bit.” However, out on the streets the problems are similar to those encountered by Mark Poulton. The impression of the Victorian children is that they too are unruly and will try to stop the performances with their poor behaviour. A further impression is that they never have any money and so are unwelcome spectators at the street shows. He describes them as “the greatest nuisances we have to contend with” and gives examples of their annoying and disruptive behaviour, saying they throw their caps into the show booth and try to poke their fingers through the cloth to try to make holes to peep through. The account ends with the man’s exasperated cry of “Bother ‘em” summing up the frustration he feels about them.

As has happened in previous examinations, some candidates failed to keep their focus on the bullet points: the impressions of the children in the two texts, and drifted into more general details of the work and lives of the Punch and Judy men. Others wrote only very brief responses, perhaps because of problems with time management, or they viewed the children in rather different ways from those presented in the texts. However, many made good use of the textual details to support the views given of the children in the two texts and their accumulation of detail and sensible comments allowed many to gain good marks on this question.
c700u20-jun22-21-q:
As indicated in the `General Comments`, candidates were given advance information that the writing tasks would be a formal letter and a magazine article. The letter took the form of a response to part of a letter that had appeared in a newspaper suggesting that zoos were no longer important. The letter included some points that candidates could choose to use in support of their own viewpoint and almost all did. It has been said in previous reports that letters in newspapers dealing with an opinion on an issue invariably argue their case, rather than offer a more balanced view with no real concluding viewpoint. Most candidates did the same, and the relatively few who tried to simply weigh up the different arguments without offering a personal or concluding viewpoint, struggled to some extent to give their letters real impact. The invitation to `give your views` on any controversial topic is almost certain best done by advancing a clear case, one way or the other. This was what the vast majority of candidates did, and examiners were treated to a range of arguments on both sides of the topic, many passionately held, with lots of supporting examples, statistics and persuasive techniques that suggested the advance information had helped in pre-examination preparation.

Most candidates were able to show some awareness of the layout of a formal letter, although many seemed to assume the `Editor` or whoever was receiving the letter, had put forward the original proposition that zoos were no longer useful and their letter was a personal response to him/her rather than the general readership of the newspaper. For less successful candidates this sometimes manifested itself in rhetorical questions along the lines of “How would you like to spend every day in a glass case?” that occasionally became something of a personal attack, rather than a series of well-considered points supporting a viewpoint.

That said, there were many impressive and persuasive responses on either side of the argument. Where letters worked well, there was a clear shape and structure to the work. Candidates used a brief introductory paragraph to make clear why they were writing and to give their opinion of the original letter. They then constructed a series of arguments, giving a paragraph to each one, in which they developed the point made in the opening `topic sentence` by giving further information, examples and other persuasive points before moving on to the next argument in support of their viewpoint. The most successful sustained and developed the point raised in their introductory sentence with three or four (and sometimes more) sentences that built their case ever more convincingly, before linking this to the next point in their letter; in some cases, candidates pursued their viewpoint with four or even five supporting arguments. Examiners saw some sophisticated and assured responses in which persuasive arguments were supported by wide-ranging information and details that sometimes touched on wider ecological issues that had national and international implications.

Most of the letters concluded with a brief overview of the arguments, and almost all tried to adopt a polite and measured tone.

Many examiners noted that a minority of candidates often made valid points in support of their views but were less successful in developing their arguments more fully; in some cases examiners saw some quite brief responses that nevertheless contained sensible and persuasive points that, had they been more fully developed, would have had greater impact.

Overall, this seemed to be a task to which candidates responded positively and had things to say. Examiners were treated to many excellent responses and it was disappointing when some candidates could only respond briefly or struggled to explain their views clearly.
c700u20-jun22-22-q:
The second task was to write an article for a travel magazine with the title, `Where I live.` This was intended to focus on the candidate’s home area and include what they liked about it but also what was less desirable. Candidates were free to decide what constituted their `home area` and examiners saw responses that ranged from an article on a single house or street, to articles on a village, town or city, whilst others declared their `home area` to be an entire country.

The task gave candidates the opportunity to be as wide-ranging as they chose to be, with the hope that responses would include a mixture of general information, specific details and some personal opinion. The best pieces balanced these different aspects well and gave examiners some clear insights into their home area and what was good, and not so good, about it. As the readership was intended to be travel magazine readers, it was useful to identify what village or city was the focus of the piece, although in many cases this information was not forthcoming or only revealed at the end of the article. Good responses tended to give a general introduction to the home area, perhaps with a sentence or two about its location, history, amenities and quite often, the excellence of the local football or rugby team. These responses then tended to deal with a number of specific aspects of the area. Many, for example, gave details of the shopping facilities (or lack of them), with more assured writers able to focus on particular shops that offered good discounts or the very latest in fashion. Some candidates tended to write in more general terms, perhaps suggesting rather vaguely that there were restaurants, cafes or pubs that catered for every possible taste, whereas better responses gave the name and location of a particular place to visit with recommendations about a particular dish, when it was the best time to visit and so on.

In a similar way, whilst many candidates wanted to tell their readers about shops, civic amenities such as parks, notable buildings and local leisure facilities, less-assured writers tended to offer information at a very general level, whilst better responses offered more details, gave more information and included personal perspectives on the things they wrote about. Although it might have been thought easier to write about a place that was busy and lively or thronged with tourists, there were many charming pieces about tiny villages tucked away in the countryside where candidates wrote about the sense of community, the village events, local walks and so on in a way that captured a sense of the place very well. Some wrote about particular celebrations that were held in their area and where they gave some specific details of the events and the time of year this happened, it gave useful information to any would-be reader.

Most candidates tried to balance what was good about the home area with one or two aspects that needed improving, and litter and road congestion featured frequently, whilst others wrote of the dangers of being in less safe areas late at night. As this was the final task in the exam, some responses suffered from time-management issues and examiners reported that some were quite brief and lacked development.

However, there was much to enjoy as examiners were taken on a tour of all corners of the country, and sometimes beyond, and the very best pieces were a delight in the way that they captured a real sense of the particular place but also clearly reflected the views, opinions and involvement of the writer in the places they called `home`.

As in the Component 1 report, writing was often impacted by poor control and technical accuracy, with too many responses placed in a higher band for its content and organisation than the band for vocabulary, spelling, sentence structure and punctuation. Some of the weaknesses and errors were basic, with many examiners reporting, for example, in the letter that many candidates repeatedly wrote `zoo’s` when an apostrophe was not appropriate and candidates frequently mis-spelling words such as `endangered` and `enclosures`, even though they were in the question and, in the article, frequently omitting capital letters for names of places.

Summary of key points

In the reading section:

• Candidates should ensure they are clear about the focus of each question and in questions 1.2 and 1.4 try to base their answer on the whole text (unless directed to a specific part or parts of the text), so that it includes as full a range of relevant textual details as possible and these are supported by clear comments and analysis where appropriate. • Reading responses that are clear and precise gain the greatest reward, so textual details need to be given explanation and context where appropriate. Where quotations are used in responses, they must be accurate and clear and where ellipsis is used, the quoted piece should always make complete sense. • Question 1.5 is best tackled by dealing with the details from each text before considering those details that appear in both texts. Where the question asks for a brief explanation of the detail, responses should always be in full sentences. Making notes in a grid format to answer this question is not helpful and does not fulfil the requirement to `briefly explain`. • Responses to question 1.6 should always focus on what is asked for in the bullet points. More general points of comparison gain no reward. • Candidates should ensure that the reading section is completed in the first hour of the examination, so that sufficient time is available to tackle and fully complete the two writing tasks.

In the writing section:

• Responses that are planned are generally the most successful, so two or three minutes spent planning the content and structure for a response is time well spent. …
c700u20-jun23-11-q: This first question focused on the newspaper article, ‘We save people. It’s just our job’, with the familiar three one-mark questions that invited candidates to select specific details from across the text. The questions were straightforward ‘search and find’ but meant that candidates had to read the complete article before tackling the more demanding second question. The first part of the question simply asked for the date of the rescue that Aileen Jones was involved in and this information, 24th August 2004, was given in the second paragraph. Most candidates had no difficulty with this question, although some had incorrectly homed in on ‘January 2005’, mentioned in the opening paragraph, and others simply gave the year of the rescue rather than the date, and gained no reward. The other parts of this question were equally straightforward: ‘Give the name of the boat that got into trouble’ and then ‘How long did the rescue last ?’ Candidates who read both the question and the text carefully had no difficulty in gaining all three marks, but some incorrectly called the boat the ‘Gower Pride skipper’ whilst others just appeared to have guessed the time for the rescue. For most candidates, this opening question gave them a clear sense of the events in the article and prepared them for the second question but some read with insufficient care.
c700u20-jun23-12-q:
Having already read the article for the opening question, there should have been little surprise that this second question asked candidates to explore how the writer showed that the rescue was both dangerous and dramatic. As in previous examinations, tackling this type of ‘craft of the writer’ question was best tackled by working methodically through the text, selecting appropriate details and commenting where appropriate how these reflected the drama and danger of the situation.

In the opening paragraph, careful readers noted that the area was ‘one of the most dangerous stretches of coastline in the world’, which clearly set the scene for the dramatic events that followed. Readers were also told in the second paragraph that the weather and sea conditions were especially bad because of the ‘force eight winds and 10-foot waves’. Although the article then gave some background information about Aileen Jones and her motivation for being a member of the lifeboat crew, candidates had to hold their nerve in the selection of appropriate textual details until they arrived at information that was linked to the actual rescue. This began in the fifth paragraph when readers were reminded about the ‘unseasonably stormy’ weather that day, and the urgency with which Jones responded to her alarm pager: she ‘dropped everything’ and rushed to the lifeboat station to lead the rescue. The article then gave details of how the events unfolded, and candidates were able to write about the difficulties the fishing boat had got into and the fact that one of the crew had sustained an injury, which would have made a rescue attempt more difficult. Most candidates were at least able to comment on one or two of the dramatic details of the rescue attempt itself, during which the lifeboat was ‘frequently thrown airborne by the waves’ and struggled to get close enough to the fishing boat to effect a rescue. Many noted that Jones talked about the boat being like ‘a seesaw’, ‘being tossed vertically in the water’ and there were details of the unsuccessful attempt to secure a towline. When the lifeboat did eventually get close to the fishing boat, candidates highlighted the drama of the situation as one of the crew ‘managed to clamber across’ and ‘scramble on board’ to secure the towline. With the rescue taking three and a half hours, it was clearly dangerous as well as dramatic and resulted in Jones being awarded a medal for bravery. Good candidates selected a range of appropriate textual details from across the text, explaining and commenting on them, accumulating the details and shaping them into good, coherent

13 responses. There were many who gained good marks for this question and there was certainly no shortage of textual details to explore. Less successful candidates too frequently snatched at fragments of text that lacked clarity and really needed greater explanation or context to merit reward. Others simply tried to copy down lots of quotations with little or no comment or explanation and this approach limited them to lower marks.
c700u20-jun23-13-q: This question asked candidates to read and respond to the second text, from the New York Tribune newspaper in 1869. As with the opening 1.1 question, this comprised three one-mark questions that should have given candidates some overview of the text and prepared them for the next question worth 10 marks. The first part of the question asked how many people Ida Lewis saved in her first rescue. Although this was a simple ‘search and find’ question and the answer was in the opening paragraph, there were some candidates who failed to read the question sufficiently carefully and focused on her subsequent rescue of the two soldiers. Most however, noted that she had saved ‘four lads’. The second part of the question asked ‘how long the soldiers were in the water before the boy was swept away?’ and most candidates had no difficulty in selecting the appropriate information – half an hour. The final part of the question asked for one piece of evidence showing the soldiers were in a poor condition after the rescue. Some candidates failed to read the question carefully enough and selected details before they were rescued; this provided another example of the need to read both question and text with care.
c700u20-jun23-14-q:
This question asked candidates to consider the New York Tribune newspaper article in greater detail. They were given a statement: “The newspaper article paints a vivid picture of the difficult conditions faced by Ida and her brother on the day they rescued the soldiers” and asked to what extent they agreed with the statement. Those candidates who concentrated on the ‘difficult conditions’ of the rescue were able to select a wide range of textual details that supported the statement, each paragraph in the passage offering some appropriate detail. For example, in the very first sentence readers were told that it was ‘a stormy, cold March afternoon’ on the day the events took place, followed in the second paragraph by more precise details that many candidates commented upon: the ‘rain fell…in blinding torrents.’ Good candidates also commented on ‘a gale drove the waves across the harbour...’ in the second paragraph and were able to comment on the writer’s explanation about how difficult the conditions made for a rescue for even ‘the most experienced boatmen’.

Careful tracking and keeping the statement uppermost provided good candidates with lots of opportunities to gain reward, although less-assured readers tended to drift from the focus of the question in their responses, sometimes focusing on details not linked to the ‘difficult conditions’. Sometimes candidates were able to probe and comment sensibly on the writer’s use of language: the ‘fury’ of the storm, the ‘ferocious storm’, ‘the foaming water’, ‘fierce salt waves’ and so on. It was important to separate the ‘difficult conditions’ from other aspects of the newspaper account and weaker, less-assured readers sometimes found this difficult. When candidates moved through the passage as it described the soldiers’ boat capsizing, the details of this provided further proof of the strength of the storm and here candidates were able to comment on the ‘huge waves’ and the way these were ‘dashing against the upturned boat’ as evidence of the dreadful conditions. When exploring the details in the final paragraphs the importance of careful tracking was clear. Some candidates were able to comment on the ‘perilous situation’ for the soldiers but also the ‘heavy’ sea and the ‘fearful gale’ that greeted Ida and her brother as they set out on their rescue mission. Many were able to comment again about the difficulty facing the ‘management of the boat’ even for Ida, who was ‘an experienced oarswoman’.

14 Good candidates gained high marks on this question through their unwavering focus on the ‘difficult conditions’ and their selection and comment on many of the textual details mentioned above. Weaker candidates found it more difficult to sustain the focus on the key point of the statement given and too frequently drifted into other aspects of the newspaper account.
c700u20-jun23-15-q:
As usual, this penultimate question asked candidates to select relevant material from across the two texts, with a little brief explanation about the immediate reactions of Aileen Jones and Ida Lewis upon hearing that the fishermen and the soldiers were in danger. As indicated in previous reports, the best approach was to deal with each text separately. Those who tried to say what ‘both’ women did sometimes struggled. For example, some suggested that “both women dropped everything”, when in fact readers were not told what Ida was doing at the point when she was told of the situation out at sea.

Readers were told that Aileen Jones ‘dropped everything’ that she was doing when her alarm pager sounded and she ‘rushed to the lifeboat station’. She also realised that she would have the responsibility of taking the lifeboat out if she arrived first. In a similar way to Aileen Jones, Ida Lewis ‘rushed outside’ to the rescue, on the way grabbing a coil of rope before jumping into her boat and calling to her brother to assist her.

In this question most candidates were at least able to select a detail from each of the texts and many comfortably gained full marks. As with some of the other questions, some weaker candidates lost the focus of the question and gave details of the rescue itself, which gained no reward and probably meant they had less time to tackle the final question. As in previous examinations, this was a question that needed precision of detail and candidates could gain full marks with just a sentence or two providing they accurately captured the precise details.
c700u20-jun23-16-q:
This final question asked candidates to compare the impressions the writers created of Aileen Jones and Ida Lewis and how the writers had created those impressions. Although in some previous examinations this question has proved to be rather more demanding than others, on this occasion, perhaps because the two women shared some similar qualities, candidates on the whole found this question rather more accessible and the mean mark for all candidates was higher than in previous series.

As in the previous question, the most effective way of approaching the question was to deal with each of the women separately, even where the impressions of them were similar. The first impression readers were given of Aileen Jones was probably that she was brave. The details of the rescue provided strong evidence of this, and good candidates were able to link appropriate evidence of her bravery to that impression of her. Some offered the precise details about how she battled in the dangerous conditions to bring the two fishermen to safety and gave further evidence of her bravery from the recognition she received in gaining an award from the RNLI. Some quoted the words of the RNLI spokesman, while others pointed to the way she was viewed as ‘a local hero’ or the first woman to be given a medal for bravery since 1888. She was also seen as selfless, putting the safety of others before her own and being prepared to ‘drop everything’, including preparing food for her children, in order to get to the lifeboat as quickly as possible. Other impressions of Aileen Jones that candidates recognised in the account were her leadership skills linked to her skilful handling of the lifeboat that showed her determination to ensure a successful rescue. Other candidates were aware of her modesty and the way she eschewed the description of ‘local hero’, the best responses exploring her ‘ordinary’ nature which then seemed at odds with the bravery and selflessness demonstrated in the account

15 of the rescue. Sometimes weaker candidates snatched at any possible quality Jones might have, with some making a case that she was a ‘kind’ person or that she was ‘likeable’. In some cases, whilst candidates were able to correctly identify the impression given of her, the link to appropriate evidence was sometimes limited or even tenuous, and sometimes incorrect.

Many of the impressions gained of Aileen Jones could also be applied to Ida Lewis. She too was shown in the newspaper report to be exceptionally brave, the rescue of the two soldiers being described as ‘a deed of great heroism’ with the report also linking this rescue with one she carried out when she was younger. As with the focus on Aileen Jones, good candidates were able to select some well-chosen textual details that made it clear how this impression was gained from the article. Many candidates were also able to make the point that a further impression of Lewis was her selflessness, particularly seen in the way she rushed to the aid of the two soldiers with ‘little thought of her own safety’ and without even stopping for appropriate footwear or head covering. There were also candidates who pointed to her skills as ‘an experienced oarswoman’, with good candidates noting the way her skills in this area made it possible for the rescue to be effective in such difficult circumstances. As with the text about Aileen Jones, it was often the quality of the link between the impression of the woman and the careful selection of textual evidence that marked out the best responses.
c700u20-jun23-21-q:
The first of the two writing tasks was to write a school/college magazine article: The Best Way to Spend a Saturday. There were many lively and engaging responses from candidates eager to advise about the benefits of ‘a long lie in’, a hearty and substantial cooked breakfast that could only be a feature of a non-school day, the pleasure of playing online games without a time limit or the distraction of homework overshadowing the game or even the opportunity to get homework or revision completed so as to allow Sunday to be a stress-free day.

Most candidates understood that they were writing for their peers and whilst some were keen to give advice about filling Saturdays with a range of activities, there were many who took the view that this was a day where ‘doing nothing’ had just as many merits. Good candidates kept their intended readers firmly in mind and wrote at sufficient length (300-400 words) to ensure that they covered some range of suggestions and dealt with each in sufficient detail. For example, some wrote about spending the morning in a leisurely fashion, but with details that meant readers gained some insight into exactly how that time was spent, whether it be an account of watching morning TV in bed, cooking that hearty breakfast to the amusement of a watching parent and so on, whilst others advised that Saturdays meant not a minute was to be wasted, with trips to the local sports club, leisure centre or going to the local park for a meeting up with friends. Many of these good responses gave suggestions about how to spend morning, afternoon and evening in the best ways possible, giving their response shape and structure, and whilst suggestions often focused on filling the day with activities, whether with friends or family, or they offered an alternative view and were advocating that time should simply be spent relaxing with a book or spending time with the family, what marked out them out as good responses was the willingness to develop the suggestions: which books or films at the cinema had given the greatest pleasure, exactly how the day with the family would be spent or the finer details of the fortnightly visit to the football ground. Weaker responses were often quite brief and this meant that whilst some had tried to include a range of suggestions, details were often very limited and amounted to little more than a list in some cases.
c700u20-jun23-22-q:
The second writing task was to respond to a letter in a newspaper that had suggested young people should do a period of voluntary work when they had left school. As was indicated in last year’s report, most letters to newspapers tend to offer a clear personal viewpoint, sometimes forcefully, rather than offering a balanced view explaining why some would take a positive view of a situation and others a negative view. On this particular topic, most candidates sustained a viewpoint, and there was broadly equal support for and against the suggestion of voluntary work for school leavers.

Those who opposed such a scheme often offered a range of arguments, some saying it was an infringement of human rights, some saying school students deserved their free time after a gruelling five years at secondary school coupled with the stress and hard work leading to examinations, whilst others pointed out that in this particular suggestion, voluntary actually meant mandatory, and would surely conflict with students who had already secured work, had planned holidays or had college courses to prepare for. Others opposed to the scheme wondered how all school leavers could possibly be accommodated, with many businesses unwilling to accept those who did not want to be there anyway. What would be done, some asked, if the young people simply refused to go; would there be punishment meted out to those not turning up for this updated version of ‘national service’?

There were equally strong arguments put forward by those who felt this would be the making of a rather lazy, ‘want-it-on-a-plate’ generation, who would discover the world of work meant effort, discipline and giving back to the community. Others wrote about the benefit such a scheme would have on charities and local community groups, and how young people themselves would benefit, as the scheme might offer opportunities for them to experience the sort of work they might eventually want to be engaged in. Some who saw the benefit of such a scheme occasionally adopted the persona of a harassed mother of two or three 16-year-olds, feeling that such a scheme offered something useful to fill the long summer holidays. Overall, most candidates were able to offer a response, although weaker candidates’ responses were often brief, sometimes confused the intended audience and assumed the newspaper Editor to be the architect of the proposal or sadly, had incomplete responses because of time-management difficulties. In contrast, examiners saw many well-argued responses, set out correctly as a formal letter, where candidates made effective use of examples, anecdotes and ‘research’ evidence to support each of their arguments. These responses had well-organised paragraphs in which an argument was advanced and supported, and whilst putting forward their case forcefully, maintained an appropriate register and tone.

As has been mentioned in previous reports, the quality and accuracy of writing remains an issue for many candidates, with many gaining marks in one band for the content and organisation of the material, only to be marked in a lower band for VSSPS. Too many candidates failed to spell basic vocabulary accurately, even with words on the exam paper, such as ‘voluntary’ frequently mis-spelled. In many cases, such basic errors will have impacted on the overall mark for candidates’ written responses.

Characteristics of Successful Responses

• Methodical tracking of the text in 10-mark questions, selecting appropriate textual detail and commenting where appropriate. • Maintaining a clear focus on the statement and using appropriate evidence to support opinions in the evaluation question.

• Addressing both bullet points in the comparison question and dealing with what is specifically asked for in the bullet points, rather than other, general points of comparison. • In Q15 and Q16, making it clear which text is being referred to. • In writing, careful consideration of intended audience and writing at sufficient length to develop ideas, opinions, or information effectively. • Adopting a tone appropriate to the intended audience and task • Evidence of proof-reading to correct technical errors.

Areas for improvement

• Too many candidates still don’t read the questions properly and lose the focus of the question. Candidates should read the text related to questions 1.1 and 1.2 closely and carefully. They should then check exactly the focus of each question before they begin their response. They should then repeat this process for the second text and questions 1.3 and 1.4. • Questions focused on a specific text (1.2 and 1.4) are best tackled by tracking through methodically. The best responses always include a good range of detail from across the texts. • “Feature spotting” as a method of tackling these 10-mark questions rarely results in good marks and is to be discouraged. • The question asking for details drawn from both texts (1.5) was best tackled by dealing with the details from each specific text and being precise with this detail. • Candidates need to develop detail and ideas more effectively in the writing tasks to achieve higher bands. • Candidates should take the opportunity to plan their responses before they begin writing. • Lack of technical accuracy remains an issue. Basic punctuation such as full stops, commas and question marks are still missing from some candidates’ writing responses.

c700u20-jun24-12-q:
The second question focused firmly on Sally Minty-Gravett and how the writer showed her love for sea and Channel swimming. As has been indicated in previous reports, when dealing with AO2 `craft of the writer` questions, the most successful candidates worked methodically through the text, selecting appropriate textual details and commenting and/or explaining how they illustrated her love for sea and Channel swimming. There was a wealth of detail and information for candidates to probe and explore and the best responses showed good coverage across the whole text, with insightful comments on details or quotations. Weaker responses sometimes only focused on one or two paragraphs of the article, or stabbed at fragments of text without explanation or context; in some cases, these responses were little more than a collection of quotations, with no attempt to explain or contextualise the information.

The article began by telling readers that Sally Minty-Gravett has the sea “in her heart and soul” having swum the Channel on eight occasions, and giving details of her most recent success, which set a new world record for the number of successful crossings. The article continued by giving Minty-Gravett the opportunity to explain in her own words her love of the sea, and how she had come to the point where she attempted her first Channel swim at the age of 18.

Many candidates were able to select quotations from these early paragraphs which made clear her love of the sea. Some explored the impact of the language she used: her “passion” for swimming or discussed how the lack of swimming pools in Jersey had made the sea the only option for learning to swim. Some candidates explained that even swimming in the sea in winter had never been a problem for Minty-Gravett; indeed, she said that for her, being in the water in cold temperatures was “exhilarating” and “invigorating”. Less successful responses tended to simply `spot` words such as these, while successful responses gave a clear exploration and context for Minty-Gravett’s choice of language. Readers were told how the swimmer had learnt to swim in the sea by the age of 4, had become a competitive swimmer by 10, and by 14 was involved in longer swims, including being part of a Channel relay team, before eventually successfully completing a solo Channel swim when she was 18. Some candidates recognised and then explored the way the article had used Minty-Gravett’s own words to emphasise her feelings for her sport: “I absolutely fell in love with being in the sea” or “Being in the water is where I’m happiest”. Some candidates were also able to discuss how the article was structured in such a way that paragraphs frequently concluded with her emphatic comments that made clear her love for sea and Channel swimming, while others explained how the writer had interspersed details about her achievements alongside Minty-Gravett’s own words. As the article drew to an end, with information about her `retirement swim`, many candidates noted how the final paragraph emphasised her love and enjoyment of Channel swimming by reporting that she had said if she found she missed doing such swims, she could “always dive right back in” and do another one.

Whilst there was a wealth of detail that candidates could use in their responses, it was the quality of the exploration of quotations or details from across the whole article that marked out the best responses. Many gained good marks for this question with comments that were thoughtful and often insightful. It was certainly possible to gain some marks by the selection of a few relevant quotations but to move into the higher mark bands required good coverage across the whole text, combined with a willingness to explain, explore or contextualise the details or quotations.
c700u20-jun24-13-q: This question asked candidates to read and respond to the second text, the account of Captain Matthew Webb’s successful Channel swim in 1875. As usual, the question was in three parts, intended to ensure candidates had some overview of the text, were able to select some simple details, but also the question should have prepared them for the more demanding question that followed. The first part of the question simply asked what Webb was compared to by the writer as he began his swim. Candidates only needed to read the first paragraph to obtain the answer to this, where readers were told “he very much resembled some large seal or huge fish”. The second part of the question asked how long the swimmer had thought it would take him to complete the swim, the answer, fourteen hours, being indicated in the third paragraph. Finally, candidates were asked what could be heard as Webb came close to completing his swim, this information being contained in the final paragraph. Candidates gained reward for either the cheering from the crowd on the sands, or that some people “struck up `Rule Britannia`. As with question 1.1, candidates who read both the text and the question carefully gained good marks, but it was sometimes the case that an answer had little or no link to the question, an indication of a lack of care in the reading of the question.
c700u20-jun24-14-q:
This question asked candidates to consider the account of the 1875 swim in greater detail. They were given a statement: “We are never sure that Captain Webb’s attempt to swim the English Channel will be successful, until the very end of Arthur Payne’s account” and asked to what extent they agreed with it.

Candidates had to consider what readers were told about Webb and how the swim across the Channel developed. As with question 1.2, working methodically through the text, selecting and commenting on appropriate details allowed candidates to accumulate reward. There were relevant details in each of the four paragraphs that candidates could use to shape their responses, beginning with the details readers were told at the start of Webb’s attempt. He set off, his shoulders “shooting through the water” and resembling “some large seal or huge fish”, which suggested he had every chance of success, especially as he was “swimming strongly with a stroke of twenty-two to the minute”. This strong, confident start appeared to continue, as readers were told he was “evidently determined to do or die” until he cried out that he had been stung by a jellyfish. This darkened the mood of those in the support boat and for the first time there was doubt about his ability to complete the swim. However, this was a false alarm and he continued on his way.

In the third paragraph, readers were told Webb was showing “evident symptoms of fatigue” and had become anxious about the prospect of the tide turning, carrying him away from the French coast. Here, good candidates explained the issue well, linking his anxiety to the turning tide, whilst less successful responses merely `spotted` words such as `fatigue` and `anxious` without the context. Some candidates noted that Webb’s swimming rate had slowed, while others commented about the time he had been in the water, at this point already four hours longer than he had expected the whole attempt to have taken. As the tide turned “he began to lose all hope” and those in the support boat felt “that he had no chance”. In the final paragraph, good responses tracked the details of Webb’s final hours in the water with a careful selection of textual detail. Some commented that the account showed he was “fearfully exhausted”, whilst others saw that although this was indeed the case, he “still toiled on bravely”, giving some optimism for a successful attempt. More details followed, and candidates who tracked the account carefully were able to accumulate the details that had left any reader uncertain of the outcome until “Finally, Webb touched ground”. Responses that tracked the uncertainty of the outcome through the four paragraphs were able to gain good marks with a combination of detail and comment, whilst less successful responses tried to make the text fit a fixed viewpoint or selected just a few relevant details.
c700u20-jun24-15-q:
As usual, this four-mark question asked candidates to select relevant material from across the two texts with a brief explanation of the weather conditions faced by Webb and Minty-Gravett on their Channel swims. Dealing with each text separately was the obvious and sensible approach and those who looked at the weather conditions that Minty-Gravett faced saw that her first crossing was made “in thick fog” that meant she only realised that she had made the crossing when she was just three-feet from the sand. She had also faced inclement conditions in 2013 when she completed her swim “in a storm”, but for her `retirement swim` she said that she started out when there was “just a light breeze”. In the account of Webb’s attempt to swim the Channel in 1875, readers are told that when he set out his shoulders were “gleaming in the sunshine”.

He swam through the night and there was “early morning mist” as he approached the French coast and some hours later, in the final stages of the swim readers are told that “rain clouds had begun to form”. Most candidates were at least able to select a detail from each of the texts and many gained full marks. In some cases, responses drifted from the focus of the question but as in previous examinations, candidates could gain full marks with just a sentence or two on each text if they were able to capture succinctly the precise details
c700u20-jun24-16-q:
The final question asked candidates to consider what made Minty-Gravett and Webb successful Channel swimmers, and how the writers showed what made them successful. The article about Sally Minty-Gravett made it clear that she had been a sea swimmer from a very young age and took part in swimming competitions and longer swims before attempting to swim across the Channel at just 18. Her swimming career as “one of Jersey’s best known swimming coaches” and record of completing a swim in every decade had given her years of experience as a sea and Channel swimmer. Candidates who saw that coupled with her experience, she was also a very determined swimmer; some noted that even as a youngster she was “fiercely determined” as a competitor and “determined to be a winner”, exactly the qualities needed to be a successful swimmer in the sea for a very long time; many noted that even on her first Channel swim, she had to have that determination needed to swim “in completely thick fog”. Other candidates noted that “she always had the self-belief” that she could complete such an arduous swim, using support from the article, where she explained that she didn’t find it difficult to summon up the physical and mental strength required for each of her Channel swims. Many candidates also went on to say that the over-riding reason Minty-Gravett was such a successful Channel swimmer was simply her enormous love of the sea and the fact that through the years she had continued to “swim all the time” and sea swimming “has always been a huge part of her life”. Throughout the article, her love of the sea was clear: she said, “I live for it” in the early paragraphs, and went on to tell readers that it was her “natural place to be” and “Being in the water is where I’m happiest”.

In Arthur Payne’s account, he wrote about the bravery of Webb and of him being “committed to being the first person to swim the English Channel”. This was supported by some of the details that indicated his single-minded determination: six hours into the swim Payne noted that Webb was swimming “with the same steady stroke”, and that he “rarely spoke, evidently determined to do or die”. In the early part of the account, it was made clear that Webb was a strong swimmer, even to the point that he was compared to a “large seal or huge fish”. The quality that most candidates were able to identify that made him successful was his resilience or endurance, his refusal to give up, even when exhausted or when circumstances seemed to make success appear less likely. Lots of candidates noted that he battled through what initially appeared to be a jellyfish sting, or struggled as the tide turned, making his progress more difficult. Many were able to document the details of his increasing fatigue and exhaustion as he neared the shore, using relevant details from the text to support this, up to and including the point where success was assured, and recognising the attempt to be “a triumph of his endurance”.

As in previous examinations, there were too many candidates whose time-management was such that they had allowed themselves too little time to tackle the question in sufficient detail.

Some candidates had interpreted the first bullet point as “How do we know they are successful Channel swimmers?” and struggled to make good progress, but for those who read both question and texts carefully, there were good, detailed responses where the qualities of each swimmer was supported by a range of relevant detail.
c700u20-jun24-21-q:
The first of the two writing tasks for candidates was to write what they would say in a talk to their class with the title: `Toys/games of my childhood`.

It was an opportunity for candidates to explore what was important to them when they played as young children and most candidates approached the task with engaging anecdotes of games played in primary school or at home, reminiscences of toys loved from a very young age and so on, whilst some wanted to discuss the importance of toys/games in shaping and developing their imaginative play and creativity. There were confident responses about the part Barbie had played in some candidates’ young lives, or the creative power of Lego, whilst others focused on playground games: `Bulldog` and its many variants featured in lots of responses – many candidates keen to explain why and how it had frequently been banned from their primary playgrounds, but the simple games of childhood `Hide and Seek` and `tag` also featured widely. Others wrote fondly of their time with Wii or their pleasure when they had been engaged in computer/online games such as Minecraft, Roblox and Fortnite. Board games also featured in responses, with accounts of marathon Monopoly games, Snakes and Ladders and Frustration clearly having a special place in some candidates’ lives. Many responses were lively, assured and sustained, mixing information about the toys or games with personal anecdotes. Successful responses often contained detailed and personal accounts of two or three particular favourites, sometimes with information about how games were played but always with an awareness of their intended audience. For many, the task seemed to awake feelings of nostalgia for their childhood games, and some wrote about how they felt fortunate to have lived at a time when they could enjoy games and toys without the intrusion of social media. That said, there were responses that were sometimes quite brief and struggling to move very far beyond a simple list of games and toys played with. These responses lacked detail and development and often lacked sense of their intended audience.
c700u20-jun24-22-q:
In the second writing task candidates were asked to write a lively article for their school/college magazine with the heading: The Ultimate Teenagers’ Guide to Keeping Fit and Healthy`. Most candidates seemed to approach the task with enthusiasm, with many keen to show their knowledge of healthy eating and the opportunity to offer advice to a generation of young people who, in the opinion of those writing, clearly needed some prodding into fitness. Readers of the articles were frequently reminded how unfit their generation was, with some shocking statistics being used to hammer home the message that becoming fit and making time for regular exercise was both necessary and fun. Most responses tried to deal with the task by exploring fitness, healthy eating and mental wellbeing and this frequently helped in the shaping of the article. Keeping fit was given the key focus in many responses, with advice that ranged from the benefits of a daily gentle ten-minute walk to those who felt fitness could only be achieved by visiting the local gym three of four times a week for a punishing regime that would then guarantee complete fitness for life.

Some candidates showed good knowledge of the fitness routines they espoused, explaining in considerable detail how particular exercises or gym equipment would enhance abs, quads, heart health or energy levels for anyone, beginner or potential Olympic participant. Other candidates explained that fitness was simply a matter of `moving more`, whether that be a regular walk round the park or substituting the bus for a walk to school, cycle rides with friends or a regular trip to the local swimming pool.

When it came to eating healthily, there was again no shortage of advice on offer, with many suggestions about how to achieve a balanced diet, the benefits of “eating your greens”, the menace of ultra-processed foods and how it was essential to swap sugary drinks for frequent glasses of water.

Almost all agreed that allowing oneself to consume a little chocolate or a few sweets could be allowed as long as it was seen as just an occasional treat.

Some candidates went into considerable detail to explain the importance of knowing about daily calorie intake or the health-giving properties of particular foods, whilst others offered suggestions such as how to cook healthy meals every day of the week. Linking fitness and health to mental wellbeing was a focus for many, with advice about how to achieve good sleeping patterns, reduce stress and how to reduce a reliance on social media.

Good responses adopted a reassuring `you-can-do-it` tone and examiners reported many engaging and informative responses. As ever, those who organised their work well, developed the points they felt were important and ranged over the topic well, were highly rewarded; less successful responses often managed to keep their intended audience in mind, but content was more limited and brief. As in previous examinations, and in too many cases this year, this task also fell victim to poor time management, resulting in incomplete responses.

Too many candidates gained marks in a higher band for content than for VSSPS, with simple spelling and punctuation errors again costing candidates valuable marks.

Characteristics of Successful Responses

• Careful tracking of the reading texts, and responses that linked closely to the focus of the question was the basis for gaining good marks, especially on 10-mark questions. • Good responses balanced detail and coverage, focusing on key words, phrases or details where appropriate but then moved on to other points, so that the response achieved good coverage of all parts of the text. • Responses to the 10-mark questions were sustained and thorough, and clearly explained and contextualised quotations and relevant textual details. • Writing responses had both range and development, kept their intended audience in mind and in both tasks balanced information and personal response/anecdote to good effect.

Areas for improvement

• In some cases, the reading of the question was insufficiently careful, leading to time being spent on answers that were not the focus of the question, and gaining little reward. • Where textual details and/or quotations were used to illustrate a point, the lack of explanation or context, where appropriate, was limiting and often failed to gain reward. • Responses that only focused on parts of the text, rather than using the whole text, resulted in missed opportunities for reward. This was particularly an issue for some candidates in questions 1.2 and 1.4. • In writing, too many responses were brief and lacked sufficient detail or development; many of these responses were well below the 300-400 words indicated in the exam paper.

This question asked candidates to read and respond to the second text, the four diary entries from Fridtjof Nansen’s 1895 expedition to the North Pole.
