c700u20-nov18-12-q:
Whilst the opening questions allowed candidates to get some sense of the content of the text, this second question invited them to consider how the writer had tried to show that the attempt by Wallenda to cross Niagara Falls on a tightrope was both astonishing and dramatic. Well-prepared candidates heeded the advice given in examiner reports over a number of years about the most effective way of dealing with this type of question: track the text methodically, focus the response mainly on content and language but where appropriate, recognise and comment on the way the structure and tone adds impact. The least effective method of tackling this question is for candidates to write a response in which ‘feature-spotting’ dominates; candidates who spend valuable time on a wild search for alliteration, personification, dashes, the mystical power of a comma or full stop to astonish or convey drama are rarely successful and they often miss the most relevant parts of the text.

8 In the Jacob Burnett article, the opening sentence captures neatly the drama of the occasion as he comments that Wallenda, on a tightrope high above Niagara Falls had a view that no other living human could have had, and he then goes on to describe the ‘churning waters’ and Wallenda being ‘enveloped in mist’ amid the noise of the ‘thundering falls’. This arresting opening is then developed to describe the circumstances Wallenda faced as he made his way, ‘One careful step at a time’ along the tightrope. If this feat alone is astonishing to report on, that Wallenda had to ‘battle winds and near-blinding spray’ gives the account added drama.

Good candidates combined relevant selection of detail with appropriate comment on how the details captured the drama of the occasion and the sense of seeing history being made. These better responses moved methodically through the text, ensuring good coverage of key details but recognising the impact of particular words and phrases. Where such details were given a context, they gained good reward and showed good understanding of how the account captured the occasion effectively. There were lots of details that rewarded candidates’ focus, such as the writer’s description of Wallenda as he ‘slowly, painstakingly, proceeded step-by-step’ across the falls, that re-paid attention to both detail and the language. Other candidates focused on and then added comments about specific details that were astonishing: that a crossing had not been attempted for more than a hundred years; that an expectant crowd of over 125,000 people gathered to watch the spectacle, some waiting for more than 12 hours; that Wallenda could dare to kneel down on the wire and then wave to the crowd. Others gave some focus to the manner of his crossing, exploring his decision to change his tactics and ignore, ‘the first rule of tightrope-walking’ because of the conditions, which again added to the drama of the occasion.

Some candidates explored the impact of the writer using phrases such as ‘historic performance’ or the way the account used the repetition of ‘history/historic’ in the text to emphasise the unique event being witnessed. Others looked at how the spectators reacted, from the eight-year-old jumping with excitement, to those adults who had arrived early and talked about the event as ‘fantastic’, describing Wallenda as being ‘brave and very clever’ and being there for this ‘once-in-a-lifetime event’, all helping to capture the admiration as well as astonishment of those onlookers.

Where candidates adopted this methodical approach there was always plenty to select and write about but still too many adopted the ‘feature-spotting’ route, desperately searching for the next ‘feature’, but with little to say that was really telling about the impact any of the ‘features’ made. One candidate even homed in on the dash in the words ‘near-blinding’ and suggested, “The dash between near-blinding creates impact on the readers because there’s a word missing, that’s why the dash is there, to slow the readers down”. I suggested as recently as the Summer 2018 report that in employing this approach, “careful exploration of the text is often a casualty”, and so it proved to be again. Other responses where candidates gained only modest marks were those that were brief and lacking in specific detail. The opening lines of the article were worth exploring for content, language and tone but it was also important for candidates to move through the text and get coverage of the whole article; those who limited themselves to an exploration of just two or three lines of the text struggled to move into the higher mark bands. Sometimes candidates saw words or phrases they recognised as being important but struggled to give them a context or comment and this limited the impact of the details selected. Because only about fifteen minutes can be committed to a 10 mark question, effective selection and comment is key to success and the best responses accumulated high marks by exploring lots of details, adding comments or analysis where appropriate, and by ensuring good coverage of the whole text. There was a lot to comment on and candidates who worked hard at including plenty of textual evidence were able to gain high marks.
c700u20-nov18-13-q:
The third question focused on the ‘Blondin’ text by George Banks. Like the first question, this was in three parts, each requiring some fairly straightforward selection of detail and/or simple inference. It should have presented few difficulties to careful readers.

The first part of the question simply required candidates to give a detail from the text that suggested Niagara Falls is a very impressive place. Most recognised that Banks’ opening paragraph contained a number of relevant details. Many noted that it was ‘a stupendous and awe-inspiring place’, whilst others focused on it being described as ‘one of the grandest objects of nature…’. Some wrote about its physical features, that it was ‘1100 feet across’ or that Banks described it being ‘at the dizzy height of 160 feet’. The importance of keeping a focus on what was being asked for was illustrated when some candidates responded to the question by writing about the people who came to visit or that Blondin found walking across the falls easy. The second part of the question, asking candidates for the number of spectators present at the event caused few problems, although some unfortunately wrote down the wrong figure. Some put the figure as 2500, whilst others, presumably remembering Burnett’s article, wrote 125,000. The final part of the question asked how long Blondin’s whole performance lasted, and whilst this, again, was just a matter of careful reading to select the correct detail from the final paragraph: ‘about an hour’, there were candidates who offered ‘twenty minutes’, a time mentioned in the penultimate paragraph and others who stabbed at any time but the correct one. Most candidates gained the three marks available without difficulty but there were others who lost a mark or even two because they took too little care to be precise.
c700u20-nov18-14-q:
This question now asked candidates to consider the Blondin text in greater detail. They were given a statement: “In this extract, George Banks presents Blondin in a very positive way” and asked how far they agreed with the statement. In considering the statement, candidates needed to select appropriate evidence to support their views and on the whole, most found there was compelling evidence to suggest Banks did present Blondin in a positive light. Some tried to suggest Banks was being negative, at times implying he was a show-off, but that was to ignore the way Banks reported the way the crowds reacted to him, or to take little note of the way he described what Blondin did as ‘miraculous antics’, although some did suggest that the word ‘antics’ was to suggest a rather foolhardy way of behaving. Most took the view that Banks admired Blondin and his account of the day captured pretty clearly the admiration he felt. For example, he begins by explaining the feat was ‘the first time that any human being had dared to cross the terrible Niagara’ and many took this to be a sign that he felt positive towards Blondin implying that he was brave to undertake such a challenge. He goes on to write about the crowd and the way they were ‘eager’ and ‘expectant’ whilst waiting for Blondin to appear. When he did appear, Banks writes about how the ‘air rang with shouts and encouragement of the heartiest kind.’ Whilst it is probably true that Banks’ account recognises Blondin’s bravery to consider such a dangerous undertaking, he also tells his readers about the skill Blondin possesses. He tells us that Blondin ‘stepped nimbly upon the rope’ and then proceeds to give details of the ‘miraculous antics’ he performs whilst on the rope. He writes of the way Blondin ‘seated himself complacently’ on the rope, then lay full length before performing a ‘back somersault’. Banks reports how he was ‘greeted with loud cheers’ by the audience. He continues by giving details of a further, amazing ‘antic’, in which he carried a ‘picture-taking apparatus’ on to the rope with him, then proceeded to dispense with his balance pole so that he could take a picture of the crowds on the shore. Banks captures these amazing feats, describing how ‘people held their breath’, astonished at what they were seeing, and telling readers that some in the audience actually fainted at what they were seeing. Banks makes clear Blondin’s showmanship and confidence upon the rope and tells his readers that ‘he was enthusiastically received on his arrival’ by the crowd, including those who were, ‘eagerly pressing forward to shake him by the hand.’

10 In tracking through the text, candidates had plenty of material to select and comment upon. Some tried to complicate the task by suggesting he was both positive and critical, and whilst the quality of the response was ultimately about how the evidence was used and commented upon, those who started from the view that he was positive and then went about finding the evidence, probably gave themselves an easier route to a higher mark. Weaker readers often suffered because the range of their exploration was limited and brief responses rarely had sufficient coverage of the whole text to merit high marks.
c700u20-nov18-15-q:
This question, requiring candidates to show the ability to select and synthesise materials from the two texts, asked how the spectators reacted to Blondin and Wallenda. Some candidates began their responses with a general overview of how both sets of spectators responded, some simply using the word ‘positive’ to describe them, whilst others went a little further, explaining that in both cases spectators were excited or amazed or full of admiration at what they were seeing. This approach offered an effective opening but it was then appropriate to look at each text in turn to give some specific details about spectators’ reactions.

Those who confined their response to ‘both’ sets of spectators could only be rewarded if they talked about the way they cheered the performers. Some candidates muddled up what one set of spectators did or said, or wrote about ‘both passages…’ and then went on to mention something which was only true of one of them. Better candidates separated out the details from each text, noting that in the Banks text, the spectators were particularly vocal, shouting encouragement and congratulating him at the end of his feat by shaking his hand and going up to him to talk to him.

In Burnett’s article, the writer made it clear that people reacted to Wallenda’s attempt to walk across the tightrope by arriving early, with all the equipment such as chairs and food that would be needed for a long day. Individuals reacted by calling him ‘very brave and very clever’, by barely being able to contain their excitement as they jumped up and down, or by reacting to the event by calling it, ‘history in the making’. The marks for this question covered every mark from 1 to 4, along with candidates who either mis-read the question, lost the focus of the question or muddled up details to such an extent that they gained no marks. In reality, close reading of the question and a little care across the two texts usually meant candidates could gain full marks fairly easily.
c700u20-nov18-16-q:
This final question in the reading section required candidates to use both texts, taking relevant details from each, comparing first, what each of the tightrope walkers did when they made their crossings of Niagara Falls, and then secondly, comparing how each of the writers tried to convey the dangers the men faced. The bullet points provided the clear areas of focus for the response, although some candidates struggled to keep a focus on the question and sometimes drifted into a response that had little to do with what was asked for. Where candidates had found difficulty in managing their time in the examination, this question often proved to be a casualty, with some very brief or incomplete responses. In some cases, candidates tackled only part of the question, which inevitably limited their mark. Others however, showed a clear understanding of what was required and produced detailed and focused responses that were often succinct and accumulated marks quickly and effectively.

11 Most good responses were able to note that Blondin began by stepping ‘nimbly’ on to the tightrope and having walked towards the centre of the rope, sat down on it and looked around at the scene. He then began the ‘miraculous antics’ as Banks described them, first ‘lying at full length’ along the rope and then turning ‘a back somersault’. He later made another tightrope walk, on this occasion carrying a camera with him and taking a picture of those watching him on the shore. In Wallenda’s crossing of Niagara Falls, candidates often noted that his journey was less flamboyant: he made his way more slowly and deliberately along the rope, Burnett telling us that he made his way, ‘slowly, painstakingly, step by step.’ However, he too had something of the showman in him, as he gave an interview to a television company, whilst in the middle of his walk. At one point, he knelt down on the wire and waved to the crowd. As he completed his walk, he ran the last few steps and punched the air in celebration.

Most candidates were able to select some appropriate details but weaker candidates often limited their responses to just a detail or two, whereas strong responses made a more thorough job of selecting and using a wider range of detail. When it came to looking at how the writers conveyed the dangers of crossing Niagara Falls, good candidates were able to focus on both the details in the text and the way in which the writers used language to emphasise the dangers the men faced. Banks wrote about the tightrope being at the ‘dizzy height of 160 feet’, emphasising the crossing was to be made on a ‘fragile’ rope, and describing Blondin’s attempt as the first time anyone ‘had dared to cross the terrible Niagara’. Following this, he explained that if Blondin were to miss his footing, he would be sure ‘to meet with certain death’. Most candidates were able to gain some reward for this final detail, but too few explored the whole of the opening paragraph sufficiently thoroughly. Some candidates were able to make something of the way the spectators reacted to Blondin’s dice with death, particularly when people ‘held their breath’ and several became so overcome that they fainted. In contrast, Burnett describes how the weather increased Wallenda’s vulnerability, as he ‘battled winds’ during the crossing, and goes on to write about the ‘near-blinding spray’ and the ‘rising mist’ that made conditions even more dangerous. Many selected details such as the ‘churning waters’ or the ‘raging waters’ as evidence of the dangerous nature of the river, should Wallenda be unfortunate enough to fall, while others noted how he changed his approach, ‘ignoring the first rule of tightrope- walking’, which suggested he employed a more dangerous tactic. These were details that offered good opportunities for accumulating marks, but many examiners reported candidates often covered too little ground to gain high marks, and in some cases, struggled to comment on more than a detail or two. As in other areas of the reading section, the best responses were often those where it was clear that a methodical approach had been taken, with sufficient focus given to each part of the question.
c700u20-nov18-21-q: For this task, candidates were asked to write what they would say when asked to give a talk to people in their class about their ambitions and what they hoped to achieve in the next 10 years. Many examiners reported that candidates engaged very positively with the opportunity to look ahead, set out their goals for their future or, in some responses, reflect on what had led them to think about their plans in the first place. Responses ranged from those who had set themselves along a very clear path, knowing exactly what they wanted to do and how they would mark their achievements, to others who told their audience how their plans had already been affected by previous school experiences; many regretted not working hard enough in the previous year and failing to gain the grades that would have ensured a particular course could have been followed. Some explored the whole notion of ambition in wider-ranging, rather more philosophical responses, and whilst some were determined to eschew materialism and follow a path of helping others or achieving justice for those wronged, there were still plenty who saw themselves in big detached houses with their silver Mercedes cars parked on the drive, having built their own businesses with world-wide clients. The responses were varied and engaging, often heart-warming in their honesty and sometimes showing a maturity of thought and an awareness of the challenges that faced them. There was no set formula for what marked out the best responses, but it is fair to say that these tended to combine a sense of their intended audience along with shape and direction in the content. Often these candidates were able to weave in telling details, offer anecdotes or include relevant background details that helped clarify points or explanations. Less successful responses were often too brief and lacking in detail. In some cases they drifted into a rather bald list-like approach where sentences often began with ‘Also..’ or ‘Then…’ but lacked the detail or reflection seen in more confident responses. That said, there was much to enjoy in the responses to this task and it seemed to be one where candidates genuinely wanted to tell examiners about themselves and about their hopes, expectations and sometimes their anxieties about the next phase in their lives.
c700u20-nov18-22-q:
The second task was to write a letter to a magazine in response to what had been written in an article about the influence that celebrities and sports stars have on young people, particularly when they behave badly.

As this was a formal letter, some awareness of format was helpful, although some candidates ignored this entirely. The most effective approach for candidates was to first decide whether they wanted to agree or disagree with the views expressed in the article. A few confessed to being undecided and tried to shape a response that began by agreeing that celebrities had a negative influence but then switched their view and decided that in fact many had shown themselves to be good role models; it was an approach that made it hard to establish a clear overall viewpoint and although there were some exceptions, in most cases this was not the most useful approach.

A more effective approach was where candidates decided to offer a clear viewpoint and then construct a series of arguments in support of their stated view. Whether they agreed or disagreed with the article, it was the quality of the arguments and the way their response was shaped that determined the mark gained for content and organisation. The exam paper included the invitation to spend a little time planning and where this was taken advantage of, it meant that perhaps three or four clear arguments could be marshalled, which in turn then allowed candidates to organise and shape their content in advance of beginning to write their letter.

13 Good responses frequently offered a brief opening explanation about the issue in question and why it had been felt necessary to write to the magazine. As they moved into the body of the letter, these more assured responses used each paragraph to argue a specific point, adding examples and detail to support their assertions. For example, those who felt celebrities and sport stars were being maligned and were actually a force for good often began by explaining that such people had frequently had to overcome personal hardships or difficult family backgrounds, and knowing about such circumstances gave a message to young people about resilience and mental toughness. The best responses then gave an example or two of individuals about whom this could be said. Often these paragraphs included both detail and development of the argument in a neat, coherent way. They then linked their argument to another specific point that became the focus of the following paragraph, perhaps, for example, writing about the skills or talent that celebrities or sports stars were able to demonstrate and the hard work that was involved in becoming such a well-known figure. In some cases, they would then move on in a further paragraph to give details of the positive things such celebrities and stars had done, citing specific examples of charity work, or generous donations they had made.

Those who had agreed with the sentiments expressed in the article often built their arguments around celebrities whose behaviour was outrageous or who were involved with drugs or heavy alcohol use. Again, in assured responses, candidates often supported their case with specific examples: here, rappers often came in for particular criticism because it was felt that their lyrics were unpleasant or incited violence or hatred. Others argued that sports stars and celebrities were frequently too materialistic or wasted money that could have been put to better use. In some cases, candidates argued strongly that it was the fault of the magazine itself for printing negative stories about celebrities, and examiners also saw examples where the letters were written from the perspective of an outraged parent who was seeing his children copying the selfish and anti-social behaviour being reported in the magazine.

There seemed to be no shortage of views about the topic and many argued their case with some feeling and passion. Where examiners saw weaker responses, it was often a lack of development of the arguments that limited the piece. Some responses were particularly brief and were self-penalising and there were some that were clearly unfinished at the end of the examination. However, many responded with a clear line of argument and showed a good awareness of their intended audience. As with the first writing task, examiners often found the content to be well-focused on the task and often arguments were presented quite powerfully.

As in the June 2018 examinations, many candidates sitting this examination were rewarded in a higher band for communication and organisation than they were for technical accuracy. Basic errors in spelling, punctuation, grammar and sentence construction all contributed to lower marks in VSSSP and for some candidates, this will have contributed to the difference between them gaining the grade they wanted and the grade they actually achieved.

14 ENGLISH LANGUAGE

GCSE

November 2018
c700u20-nov19-11-q:
This first question followed a pattern seen in previous examinations of three one- mark questions that asked candidates to identify particular details from one of the texts, in this case the newspaper article about Harry West and the Kingsland Road market.

These were straightforward ‘search and find’ questions, but it was important to read the question carefully. For most candidates the questions afforded the opportunity to become familiar with the text which explained why Harry West continued to trade in the market.

The first part of the question simply asked candidates to give a detail from the text that suggested the market had been very busy in the past. This was explained in the first paragraph of the article, with two very specific details. Readers were told that at one time there were 150 stalls in the market every Saturday and that “there were so many people it was impossible to move.” In the second paragraph there is a reference to ‘this once-buzzing street’ so any of these details gained reward. Some candidates failed to select the correct detail, offering details such as how long Harry West had been trading in the market or giving details about what could be purchased in the market, but most candidates were rewarded. The importance of reading the question carefully was perhaps more apparent in the final two one-mark questions; the second question asked when trading had begun in the market, and for this candidates had to read further into the text, although this should not have been problematic as the fourth paragraph provided the answer in the opening sentence: ‘The market began in the mid-19th century…’, although some responses lacked the necessary precision, simply stating the 19th century. For most candidates there was no difficulty in locating the correct detail but some did not read the question carefully enough and incorrectly used the date mentioned in the first paragraph – 1970s. If some candidates got this part of the question wrong because they did not read the text carefully, others were guilty of not reading accurately the third part of the question. This asked for a detail about what Harry West’s grandson sold in the market. For careful readers, this presented little problem as readers are told that his grandson sells ‘what the youngsters want’ and his table stall displayed ‘rows of smartphone accessories and computer games.’ Unfortunately, some candidates mis- read the question and instead told examiners all about the household items that West sold, and as a result gained no reward. The questions required a little careful reading to gain full marks so it was disappointing that too many made simple errors and lost a mark or two.
c700u20-nov19-12-q:
Having had some opportunity to become familiar with the newspaper article in answering question 1.1, this question now asked candidates to explore how the writer tried to show that Harry West was ‘determined to continue as a street seller.’ It has been pointed out in many previous examiner reports that the best way to tackle this type of question is to work methodically through the text, selecting appropriate evidence and detail and, where appropriate, commenting or exploring the impact of the detail along with the way in which the evidence or detail has been presented by the writer. In this particular article the writer gives the reader some background information about West and the market he works on, and alongside the writer’s own comments, we are also given first-hand comments from West himself. The article begins by telling readers how long West has been a trader in the market: ‘For 40 years, Harry West has been selling second-hand goods from his east London market stall’, a detail that many candidates recognised as evidence that he was long-

established and therefore unlikely to want to cease trading. We are then told about the difficulties the market found itself in when the council stopped issuing trading licences but given the first clear indication of West’s determination to continue, when the writer tells us that the council ‘did not bank on the staying power of 72-year-old West.’ Many candidates who tracked the text carefully saw these details given by the writer as evidence of West’s determination. In some cases, candidates wanted to write unnecessarily lengthy explanations about ‘staying power’ and some focused on his age rather than his staying power but better candidates simply collected the evidence, made a brief comment and moved on. Most candidates were able to note that the writer went on to say that West was ‘fiercely determined to continue’ in the following paragraph, some pointing out the impact of the adverb whilst others focused on the way in which this reinforced what the writer had already said about the trader. The skill of selecting the appropriate detail and then deciding how much to write about it was key to gaining a good mark in this type of question. Through the article were many references to West’s determination to continue trading and accumulating a good number of these usually resulted in very creditable marks. In too many cases examiners saw candidates write at unnecessary length about just two or three textual details, rather than try to select a good range of details and comments from across the whole text. In some cases, candidates just explored the first few paragraphs and as a result, failed to gain higher band marks.

The writer builds up a picture of the way West operates in the market that suggests his skill and acumen in establishing a positive relationship with prospective buyers makes him successful. Despite the threat of market closure: he ‘cheerfully greets’ customers and has built up a ‘steady stream of regulars’, he jokes and chats, ‘puts the world to rights’ with them and is ‘on first-name terms with many.’

More able candidates often noted that where the writer gave information about West and the way he operated in the market, there was often a concluding comment in some of the paragraphs that confirmed West’s determination to continue trading. This had already been noted by some in their comments about West’s ‘staying power’ in the second paragraph and this was seen again at the end of the fifth paragraph when readers are told, ‘For West, buying and selling has always been part of his life and he has no plans to stop.’ These comments make clear West’s determination and good candidates were able to make appropriate selections from the text. It is also made clear that West feels he is there to stay by training his grandson, who sells ‘what the youngsters want.’ Again, the writer sums this up by saying that West sees this as giving ‘the business a new lease of life’, implying that his stall will continue to be there. Some candidates were also able to gain reward when they explored the idea of the stall having a new lease of life and then going on to note that having his grandson involved was “a way of continuing the family tradition.”

Candidates who continued to track the text found plenty to select and comment on from what the writer told readers about West, but it became clear to some candidates that allowing West to offer his own views was an equally powerful way to demonstrate how determined West was to stay in business. The writer uses West to tell readers how he views market trading when he quotes West saying, ‘The people who fail are the people who don’t change with the times.’ This gives clear evidence of West’s determination to do whatever it takes to continue trading, and this is further supported when we are told that he will adapt to change and if necessary, will sell articles more suited to the area’s increasingly wealthy clientele. Some candidates also noted that West had offered to meet members of the local council to discuss how he can continue to trade, seeing this as another way in which his determination is apparent. The writer sums this up at the end of the penultimate paragraph, telling

readers, ‘He is not giving up without a fight.’ The article concludes with a quote from West that effectively confirms his determination: “they have to get rid of me first.”

Despite the point made in the summer examiner report about the unhelpful approach to this type of question, in which ‘feature spotting’ sometimes dominates responses, there were still candidates who used feature spotting as their starting point and looked for statistics or alliteration or dashes to try and explain West’s determination to continue trading. However, there were some very good responses that selected details well, noted and commented on the way the writer made West’s determination very clear and had good coverage across the whole text.
c700u20-nov19-13-q: This third question now turned candidates’ attention to the second text, ‘Petticoat Lane Market.’ The pattern of questions, with short one-mark questions preceding a more demanding question on each text is now well-established and gave candidates the opportunity to gain an overview of the text, with three questions. As with question 1.1, it was important to read the question carefully and those who failed to do this usually struggled to gain full marks; this happened on occasions even on the first of the questions, which should have presented no difficulties at all. The first question asked candidates to name one item of clothing the writer was invited to buy. Most candidates had no difficulty in selecting ‘a hat’ or ‘a nice coat’ from the text, but examiners were given answers that ranged from a couch, a sea-chest and an eight- day clock to cheap cakes and a hand-saw. The second part of the question caused fewer errors, candidates being asked to explain how the street traders reacted when the writer stopped in front of a stall. Many were able to say how he was immediately invited to buy an item, others noted the way the sellers stared at the prospective buyer, while others wrote about the way ‘a dozen eyes are upon us’ or the sellers became ‘like vultures looking for prey.’ Some candidates noted that the sellers would yell or shout their wares, and there was also an example of one seller pulling the writer back in an effort to sell him a coat. Reward was gained for any of these details. The final part of the question asked for the evidence that the public houses were busy and most were able to select appropriate detail from the penultimate paragraph to gain a mark, most quoting that these places were ‘generally crammed to excess.’
c700u20-nov19-14-q:
This next question now asked candidates to consider the ‘Petticoat Lane Market’ text in greater detail. The question was posed in a way that has been used in previous papers on this specification: candidates were presented with a statement which they had to evaluate, using evidence from the text to support their assertions. They were asked to consider how far they agreed with the statement that ‘…the writer paints a vivid picture of the sights and sounds of Petticoat Lane Market.’

As with the second question, the most profitable approach was to track methodically through the text, selecting relevant detail and commenting upon it. Some candidates were uncertain of the meaning of ‘vivid picture’, suggesting that it meant ‘positive picture’, but where they were able to select and evaluate relevant detail, they were still able to gain reward.

The writer begins the passage with a short, emphatic sentence that gives little room for an interpretation that readers are in a pleasant place: ‘Petticoat Lane is long, narrow and filthy.’ The passage goes on to give a little more detail, telling readers about the poor sanitary conditions in the small houses on the lane, the inadequate drainage and ‘in summertime the foul waste water remains in stagnant pools’, a picture that leaves little to the imagination. Just in the brief opening paragraph, candidates had lots of material to explore and comment on, and most did so quite well. Having seen this bleak portrayal of the place, they often then noted the contrast with the Sunday morning activity on the lane as the market came to life. Those candidates with an eye for detail saw the way the writer captured the noise of the

place in the phrase, ‘what a din!’ or the way the lane is described as ‘seething with life’ and its suggestion of hectic, even chaotic human activity, especially as visitors have to ‘push your way through the crowd’ to see the ‘keen bargaining’ taking place all along the lane. Even in these opening lines there were details to evaluate and comment on and many wanted to dwell on specific words that captured a sense of what was going on. It is perhaps worth saying that some candidates only dealt with these opening lines of the passage, failing to explore the rest of the text, and whilst there was some reward for sensible comments and selection, it was nevertheless, self-penalising to focus on just a small section of the whole text.

The writer moved on to capture something of the flavour of the market by giving some of the cries of the street sellers, and some candidates commented on the rather desperate attempt of the hat seller to entice a prospective customer. As the writer moved deeper into the market, we are told that stopping at a stall immediately has a ‘dozen eyes upon us’, with many commenting on the appropriateness of the simile, ‘like vultures looking for prey.’ Whilst some attempted to explain the simile in more detail than was necessary, almost all candidates were able to say this captured the pushy, rather aggressive nature of the street sellers. Some candidates attempted to describe all that could be seen and bought in the market, sometimes with over- long quotations, while others picked out one or two telling details to suggest most of what was on sale was of poor quality, despite the urgings of the sellers. Some commented on the way the writer tried to show how busy the place was, noting details such as having to, ‘squeeze our way through’ and the image of nearly being ‘crunched like snails’ particularly appealed to many candidates.

Those who were prepared to cover the full text were able to comment on the picture of the public houses: filthy, ‘crammed to excess’ and full of men drinking in smoke- filled rooms where stolen goods would often appear. This rather sinister picture provided another contrast to the bustle going on in the lane outside, but readers were then taken back to where a visitor would be accosted to buy a coat or where it was possible to see a seller ‘sitting amid a pile of old iron, boots and shoes’ shouting his wares, apparently unaware that most was discarded junk.

Where candidates tracked the text, it was difficult to avoid finding some relevant detail that helped to capture a sense of the noise and activity, and those who did so frequently gained high reward for the range of detail and quality of comment. Weaker responses were often brief or showed limited coverage and in some cases stabbed at a few textual details with little sense of how they contributed to the overall picture presented by the writer, but as ever, examiners came across some perceptive responses that showed an appreciation of how the writer made the lane come to life.
c700u20-nov19-15-q:
This question, asking for the ability to select and synthesise materials from the two texts, invited candidates to explain what is learnt about Petticoat Lane and the area around Kingsland Road. To make the focus of the question absolutely clear, candidates were told not to spend time writing about the markets themselves; this instruction was given in emboldened type and should have helped candidates to focus on the correct details. However, as with some of the responses to questions 1.1 and 1.3, it became apparent that too many candidates failed to read the question with sufficient care and wrote responses that did not contain appropriate detail.

For those who were clear about what was required, there was no shortage of material to use in an answer. In looking at the Petticoat Lane text, many said that it was clearly a poor area to live in, often giving details such as the small houses with unsanitary conditions. The lane itself was narrow and filthy, but always busy on Sundays. Some candidates focused on the unhealthy or dangerous conditions in the lane, whilst others explained that the busy, filthy public houses were places of

criminal activity. In moving from this text to the ‘Kingsland Road’ text, candidates noted the contrast: this was a much wealthier area, where those with money had moved in. The area now had luxury flats and million-pound properties and as a result there were now ‘high-end’ restaurants and trendy shops, appealing to people with money.

It was possible to gain full marks with just a few sentences that included relevant details and it was certainly not necessary to write at great length or comment on the writers’ choice of language. Although pointed out in previous reports as an approach that was rarely the most effective, some candidates still attempted to write about what ‘both texts’ contained, but for little reward; there were also candidates who wrote at length about just one of the texts, which significantly limited the mark that could be awarded. It was disappointing to see responses from candidates who wrote about how the markets were different or what was sold in these markets, although occasionally examiners found one or two relevant details in a response that mostly focused on the wrong details. However, many of those who read the question carefully and understood what was required were able to select and explain some of the relevant details from each of the texts, shape their answers into a few sentences and gain good marks.
c700u20-nov19-16-q:
This question, asking candidates to compare across the two texts, is often viewed as presenting the greatest challenge in the reading section, although the two bullet points gave a clear indication of what was required. In the last examiner report for this component (June 2019), I wrote in the ‘Summary of key points’ that for this final reading question, “it is imperative that candidates deal with what is specifically asked for in the bullet points, rather than other, general points of comparison.” It is advice that is worth repeating, as a number of examiners reported candidate responses that failed to focus on the bullet points and as a result gained little reward.

This question focused on the street sellers in the two texts, the first bullet point asking candidates to compare the ways in which the Kingsland Road market trader, Harry West, and the Petticoat Lane street sellers tried to sell their goods. The second bullet point asked how each of the writers showed what these street sellers were like.

In addressing the first bullet point, good candidates tracked the details to see that Harry West helped his potential customers to feel comfortable as they browsed his stall. Readers are told that he ‘cheerfully greets’ visitors to his stall, many of whom are described as his ‘regulars’ who have been ‘coming to his stall for decades.’ We were told that he knows them well and ‘is on first-name terms with many’ and we were given examples of him sharing a joke with one man who is buying some chairs or ‘putting the world to rights’ with another. It revealed an avuncular, confident trader who knew the business he was in, but he was also aware that he needed to ‘change with the times’ to stay successful; readers were told he was willing to expand the range of goods he sells, aided by his grandson who sold ‘what the youngsters want’ in the form of smartphone accessories and computer games. He was aware of the area’s increasing wealth and recognised that in order to cater for a new clientele he might have to ‘sell goods like antiques.’ In contrast, Petticoat Lane street sellers were shown to sell their goods in an altogether different way. They shouted their wares to the passers-by, and were not afraid to exaggerate the quality of what were, in reality, cheap and often shoddy goods. Where there was any hint of interest in an item, the sellers focused on the prospective buyer with ‘hard-sell’ techniques. Readers were given examples of the way one seller ‘yells into our ears the praises of an eight-day clock’, or of the way another seller pulled back the writer to try to sell a coat with some persuasive patter: ‘that’ll fit you nicely...Fit you in a minute, sir.’ Here the sellers spread their goods out on stalls tightly packed together all along the lane, whilst others sat on the street among piles of old junk, shouting ‘of the excellence of

a hand-saw and jack-plane.’ Good candidates selected relevant details from each of the texts, clearly seeing the difference between the way West and the Petticoat Lane sellers invited a sale.

In dealing with the second bullet point in the question, candidates often made the obvious comparison that whereas the writer of the Kingsland Road market article presents Harry as friendly, approachable and even as a reliable trader who had built up a regular client base, in Petticoat Lane, the street sellers are presented as pushy, aggressive and desperate for any sale they can get. In the article, the writer frequently offered his own view about West’s character and dedication to the job he does and he used West’s own words that captured his determination to survive. To show what the Petticoat Lane street sellers were like, the writer compared them to ‘vultures looking for prey,’ and used the actual shouts and cries as they tried to effect a sale. In contrast to Harry West, we were told that one seller, ‘yells into our ears’ and another ‘insists’ they looked at his goods. Further on in the passage, another seller was described as having ‘an oily voice’ as he pulled the writer back. The writer’s choice of verbs and adjectives all confirmed the insistence, and even desperation, of these sellers to make money.

It was possible to tackle the question by dealing with each text separately and then making comparisons, or by dealing with each of the bullet points in turn. Either approach was perfectly acceptable and good candidates found little difficulty in explaining how the sellers operated, using a wide range of textual details. It became a straightforward task to then sum up what West and the Petticoat Lane sellers were like, if only because of the stark contrast between them that the details revealed. Many selected the striking ‘vultures’ simile in the Victorian text as evidence of the predatory nature of the sellers and it was easy to contrast this with the cheerful greetings and good-natured chatting and joking that was a feature of West’s relationship with his customers.

Where candidates failed to read the question carefully or to focus fully on the bullet points, it was impossible to gain good marks. Some wrote at length about anything except that which was asked for or desperately sought any points of comparison: one sold records while the other sold song-sheets. Some candidates argued at length that whereas Petticoat Lane sellers sold poor quality goods, Harry West sold high quality goods that wealthy people wanted. Just a little time spent reading the question would undoubtedly have resulted in a better outcome. It was also the case that some struggled to manage their time effectively and this resulted in brief, limited responses and in some cases, just focused on one text, which significantly limited the mark they could gain. That said, there were candidates who were able to gain good marks in this question, showing skills of appropriate selection and understanding about how the writers showed what these street sellers were like.
c700u20-nov19-21-q:
In the first of the two writing tasks candidates were asked to write what they would say to their class when giving a talk on, ‘The person I’d most like to spend a day with.’ They were invited to consider people who were famous such as a sportsperson or musician, someone from the past or someone not necessarily famous but one who was admired. It was a task that gave candidates the opportunity to write from personal experience or use information they knew about the person who was the subject of their talk. Because the audience was clearly specified, candidates also had to consider how to establish their engagement with the class. It was a task with which candidates seemed to genuinely engage and predictably the subjects of these ‘talks’ ranged very widely. Musicians, particularly members of rock bands and rap stars, were popular subjects and sports stars, especially footballers, also proved

to be a focus for many, whilst others chose figures from the online world, giving examiners insights into the lives of YouTube personalities and ‘influencers’ with huge followers. Figures from the worlds of politics, science and literature, both current and from the past, also appeared regularly and examiners were treated to responses on people as diverse as Albert Einstein, Donald Trump, Ghandi, Steve Jobs and Elon Musk. Whilst many chose subjects who they admired but were not personally known to them, others chose to write about special friends who had supported them and there were many who wrote about close family members. Whilst some wrote affectionately about the love and support they continued to receive from ‘Mum’, ‘Dad’ or a sibling, others wrote warmly, and often poignantly, about members of their family who had passed on. Many of these responses recalled special times in earlier childhood, with often charming anecdotes of simple, shared pleasures.

Whilst examiners reported very high levels of engagement from virtually all candidates, weaker responses were often short and as a direct consequence, these responses lacked detail, range or development. In some weaker responses, it became clear that the candidate knew little about the person they had chosen as their subject and the ‘talk’ consisted largely of a series of questions they felt they would want to ask, where they would go for dinner and the advice they would ask about in order to emulate their subject’s success. Better responses combined some useful biographical details, along with the qualities or skills possessed by the person and some exploration of why the writer would find a day in their company enjoyable or inspiring. Often these more assured responses focused on a specific quality or key point in their subject’s life that they expanded upon, and explained why this had made a particular impression on them, which often gave the response a greater impact. Many of the responses about close friends or family had a powerful, reflective honesty about them and were often moving. Across the many varied and different subjects of this response, examiners found much to enjoy.
c700u20-nov19-22-q:
This second task was for candidates to respond to an invitation in a teenage magazine to give their views on the subject of tattoos: ‘just harmless fun and fashion or something to regret in later life?’ The task offered the opportunity to express a clear viewpoint or to explore both the positive and negative views about the subject. In order to write a successful piece, the task required some planning and organisation of the material. Good responses that gave a clear viewpoint often had three or four clear arguments to make and these were organised into paragraphs that began with a topic sentence setting out why a particular view about tattoos was valid. The argument was then expanded, often including examples. For example, one of the points frequently made by those who felt tattoos would be regretted in later life was that tattoos were often unplanned. Having outlined the folly in this, some went on to give examples of friends or relatives who had been tattooed whilst on holiday or they had been drunk at the time; some of the examples given of tattoos done under these conditions were amusing and alarming in equal measure. Where arguments were developed along with telling examples they were often presented with some passion and conviction. Those who were positive about tattoos were equally passionate, arguing for example, that they were often a way of celebrating loved ones in the family or important dates. They then went on to give examples of how this might apply in their own family, why a particular tattoo might have been chosen and how it helped strengthen the bonds of family.

It was a subject that candidates warmed to and whilst some brief responses struggled to have impact, there were many that made a strong case for or against tattoos. Those against pointed out the permanence of it, the health dangers of having ink injected into the skin, the expense and pain of a tattoo removal, the way in which a tattoo might change over the course of a lifetime and the way that employers might

have a negative view of a prospective employee who sported a tattoo at interview. Candidates who were positive about having tattoos saw them as art, and the opportunity to have a design or pattern unique to the wearer, they argued about the importance of an individual’s right to choose how to treat their own body or that they could be a reminder of loved ones. Many who supported the wearing of a tattoo argued that removal was possible and could even be used as a way of covering an unsightly scar. Although the topic allowed for some passionate support or dislike of tattoos, others tried to offer a more balanced view, and whilst these perhaps lacked the passion of those firmly for or against tattoos, their more measured responses were often just as effective.

In some cases, candidates had not managed their time efficiently and for this final part of the examination found they had too little time to construct good, developed responses. A few candidates mis-read the task details and wrote about a topic of their own choice, and although they gained some credit for the organisation of their material, it made it difficult for them to achieve a good outcome. The best responses on the topic were well-planned and well-argued because they offered and developed a number of points and gave examples that supported the points they made. They were also aware of their intended audience and often made a direct address to their peers at points in their article.

Whilst both of these writing tasks showed high levels of engagement that rewarded candidates with creditable marks for communication and organisation, there were many who struggled with basic accuracy. Simple spellings were often incorrect – many found it impossible to spell ‘tattoos’, even though this was in the task instructions – and incorrect punctuation and sentence construction often meant candidates were in a lower band for this aspect of their responses.

Summary of key points

In the reading section:

• Candidates need to read each question carefully. There were too many instances where questions were mis-read and as a consequence, candidates gained few marks.

• In questions 1.2 and 1.4 it is important to have a range of textual details that support comments or analysis. It is more effective to write briefly about a good range of points from the text than to write at great length about just a few details. Good responses to these questions invariably show good coverage of the texts.

• The advice given in the summer examiner report about tackling 1.5 and 1.6 is equally relevant again: The question asking for details drawn from both texts (1.5) is always best tackled by dealing with the details from each specific text before considering any details that appear in both texts. In the final question (1.6) it is imperative that candidates deal with what is specifically asked for in the bullet points, rather than other, general points of comparison. As a final point on these two questions, there were still too many candidates who failed to read the questions with sufficient care and as a result, they gained few marks.

In the writing section:

• Candidates should take the opportunity to plan their responses before they begin writing. They should consider content and their intended audience and write at sufficient length to develop ideas, opinions or information effectively.

• Many candidates need to pay more attention to technical accuracy, especially basic spellings, sentence construction and punctuation.

This first question followed the pattern of three one-mark questions that asked candidates to identify particular details from one of the texts, in this case the newspaper article, ‘Trekking with the Gorillas of Rwanda’. It gave the opportunity to gain an initial familiarity with the text but although these were straightforward ‘search and find’ questions, it was important to read both the text and the question carefully.

The first part of the question simply asked candidates to note the numbers of gorillas said to be in the Rwanda National Park. Most candidates found no difficulty in locating the number, 480, from the fourth paragraph but some failed to read the question with sufficient care and wrote down ‘900’, which was the number remaining

8 across the world, rather than those in the national park. In some ways, this was a simple error but illustrated very well the importance of careful reading, not just of the text but of the question too. The second part of the question asked candidates how much time visitors were allowed to spend with the gorillas and there were very few who failed to get the correct answer of one hour. In order to find the correct answer to the final part of the question, to name another animal found in the national park, candidates had to read the entire text, as it was only in the penultimate paragraph that antelope and buffalo were mentioned as being snared in traps in the park. Although many were able to select the correct detail, others struggled to find the relevant detail and responses included ‘bamboo’ or the gorilla named in the article, while others failed to offer an answer.
c700u20-nov20-12-q:
Having had some opportunity to read the article in the search and find answers to question 1.1, candidates were asked how the writer had tried to make the trip to see the gorillas sound like a very tiring but memorable experience. As with previous questions of this type, the best way for candidates to tackle this type of question was to work methodically through the text, selecting appropriate evidence and detail and, where appropriate, commenting or exploring the impact of the detail along with the way in which the evidence or detail has been presented by the writer. It was sensible to take the two key words in the question, ‘tiring’ and ‘memorable’ as separate areas to explore, although working methodically through the text meant that evidence of the arduous nature of the trek to get to see the gorillas was sometimes juxtaposed with a detail that suggested being close to the animals provided a wonderfully memorable experience for the tourists.

The writer begins by suggesting to readers that there would be few occasions where it is possible to be so close “to wild beasts capable of mauling you”, thus setting the scene for a rare and unforgettable experience. However, the writer makes it clear in the second sentence of the article that the trek to get to the gorillas is physically difficult and involves navigating tough terrain: “One second you are exhausted, struggling through thickets of bamboo….pulling yourself up a steep slope, step by painful step.” Many candidates found this a useful sentence to begin their exploration as it provided proof of the difficulties the trekkers faced. Some went further, selecting and commenting on individual words such as ‘exhausted’, ‘struggling’ and ‘painful’ to emphasise the tough conditions. Some candidates chose to organise their answer by first exploring all the details of the tiring nature of the visit before they turned their attention to considering what the writer found memorable. Whilst this might have appeared as a sensible way of organising a response, it meant the text had to be ‘combed’ separately for each aspect of the visit and this sometimes resulted in responses that said little about how memorable the visit had been, as candidates realised the need to manage their time and move on to the subsequent questions.

Those who chose to follow the more methodical tracking of the text found that having explored the second sentence of the text, they could immediately consider how the difficulties of the journey were rewarded by the way in which they suddenly happened upon the gorillas: “The next (second), you turned a corner and gasp” to see just 30 feet away a female gorilla “lovingly cradling” her infant. Many commented on the way this would have had a lasting impression on the tourists, with some noting how this sight mirrored that of human behaviour. The writer went on to say how the tourists instantly reached for their cameras to record what some candidates said would be ‘once in a lifetime experience’. Some felt the most important thing was to show they had identified a simile and went no further but those who kept the question in mind and commented on how memorable a sight this would have been made better progress. The writer went on to give a flavour of the gentle behaviour of the young gorillas and the mother’s response and some candidates found this more useful evidence that contributed to the trekkers’ memorable experience.

9 The writer offered some details about the efforts to protect and increase the gorilla population in the national park and how this is done alongside managing visits to see them. Although simply selecting some of these details on their own brought little reward, more assured readers saw that the relative exclusivity of the visits would be another way they would be seen as particularly memorable.

Those candidates who chose to write all about how tiring the trip was before considering how memorable it might have been, had to read to the sixth paragraph before discovering further evidence of the tough journey. An “early 6am start” and “three hours of intense hiking” made it clear that the tourists would work hard for their reward of the sight of gorillas in the wild. The information about the make-up of the group of which the writer was part engaged some candidates but more careful readers made more progress with their focus and subsequent comment on the evidence that “even the fittest of us were huffing and puffing twenty minutes in” or that “everyone stumbled down a hill on their backside at some point.”

When the writer provided a number of specific details of the gorillas’ antics, good candidates were able to select and comment on those they felt would live in the tourists’ minds for a long time. Candidates who were able to explore both aspects of the question almost invariably gained higher marks than those who focused exclusively on just ‘tiring’ or ‘memorable’ and those who approached the question from the perspective of building a response around ‘feature spotting’ struggled to make a great deal of focus. The best responses kept a clear focus on the question, tackled the text methodically, selecting and commenting where appropriate on a good range of evidence; these responses often also had good coverage of the whole text.
c700u20-nov20-13-q: This third question now turned candidates’ attention to the second text, the extract from ‘Travels in West Africa’ by Mary Kingsley. Three one-mark questions asked for specific details and provided careful readers with an opportunity to gain three marks as they gained familiarity with the text, in readiness for the more demanding question that followed. However, as with question 1.1, candidates had to read the question and the text with sufficient care to locate the correct information. The first question asked candidates to note how far away Mary Kingsley was from the gorillas. Kingsley tells her readers she got to where the gorillas were, “some thirty yards off” and most candidates correctly had this as their answer but others gave fifty yards, this being the distance Kingsley and her guide had crawled forward to arrive thirty yards from them. It was an example of a straightforward question that simply needed a little careful reading to gain a mark, so it was disappointing that examiners saw too many incorrect answers. The second part of the question, asking for the name of another animal Kingsley had come across in Africa seemed to pose no great difficulties and almost all candidates correctly identified elephant, leopard or python, this information being found in the third paragraph of the extract. The third part of the question asked candidates to identify what had disturbed the gorillas as Kingsley and her guide, Joseph, watched them, and again most were able to note that Joseph had given ‘an explosive sneeze’ that had startled the gorillas, sending most scuttling back into the forest. Although this was an opportunity to gain three marks relatively easily, the lack of careful reading meant too many failed to do this, and examiners also noted that a small number had answered on the wrong text.
c700u20-nov20-14-q:
This next question asked candidates to consider Kingsley’s text in greater detail and to consider how far they agreed with the statement: “Mary Kingsley’s account captures her mixed feelings about the gorillas she sees on this trip.” Opinion was free and whether candidates agreed or disagreed with the statement, what counted here was the exploration of her account and the way in which the candidate viewed her experiences. As with the second question, the most profitable approach was to track methodically through the text, selecting relevant detail and commenting upon it. The best responses were often those that showed good coverage of the whole extract, using details from each of the four paragraphs.

Kingsley begins her account by saying that as they tried to get as close to the gorillas as they dared, they approached “with great caution” which to some candidates suggested that she felt anxious and wary of them. This feeling of anxiety may have increased when she saw the savagery with which they were attacking the pineapple and bananas, candidates often selected details such as “tearing to pieces’ the fruit, “noisily attacking” and “destroying more than they ate” and felt it showed her negative attitude towards them, seeing them as violent and aggressive creatures.

This view of the gorillas seems to be confirmed in the second paragraph, where she writes about the “shrill, whinnying, chattering noise” made by the animals and the way they “moved awkwardly…in a most inelegant style.” By tracking the text in a methodical way, good candidates were able to use details like these to support a view about the feelings and attitudes Kingsley had about the animals she viewed. In the same paragraph, Kingsley tells the readers that she was “fearful of an attack” indicating her view of the gorillas as potentially dangerous but interestingly, prevents her guide from taking action to defend her, lowering his gun “to prevent him from firing.” Those who had used some of the previous textual evidence to decide she held entirely negative views of the gorillas now saw there was perhaps a case to modify their evaluation of her, at least in part. Many candidates gave these opening paragraphs only limited scrutiny, perhaps because it appeared from the third paragraph that she only saw the gorilla as “the most horrible wild animal”, and in this paragraph she certainly expanded this view, even to the point that they were compared unfavourably with leopards, pythons and elephants. Many were able to select and comment on her condemnation of the gorilla with phrases such as “horrible disgust” and the gorillas’ “hideousness of appearance.”

Unfortunately, a significant number failed to then explore the final paragraph where it is clear she sees an entirely different aspect of the gorillas’ behaviour. She tells her readers that she watched the animals “with great interest” and when the huge male gorilla was frightened by Joseph’s “high-pitched screeches” and made off into the forest, she confesses to being captivated and entranced by the speed and graceful nature of his departure, calling it a “superbly perfect hand-trapeze performance.”

Where candidates tracked the text carefully, it was possible to make some comment on her ‘mixed feelings’ in each paragraph of the extract. That some chose only to focus on part of it limited their opportunity to explore the range of feelings and attitudes she appeared to have about the gorillas. However, some more careful readers were able to gain good marks with thoughtful evaluation supported by textual evidence.
c700u20-nov20-15-q:
This question, asking for the ability to select and synthesise materials from the two texts, invited candidates to briefly explain how the guides helped to keep the writers safe when they came across the gorillas. In previous reports I have suggested that the most useful way of approaching this question has been to deal with each text separately, rather than try to insist that both texts had similarly appropriate details, especially when this was not the case. However, in these two texts there were points of similarity and whilst it was perfectly sensible to tackle each text separately, many gained good marks by indicating those similar details. In both texts it was stated that the guides carried guns for protection. Some candidates went on to give additional detail such as in the text ‘Trekking with the Gorillas in Rwanda’ where the writer explained that no guides had ever had to use a gun to protect a tourist. In the Kingsley passage, it was made clear that the guide was prevented from using the gun he carried. It was not necessary to give any additional detail and many candidates gained reward for simply recording that both guides carried guns. In the ‘Trekking’ text, candidates were able to identify other measures that the guides used to ensure safety: the tourists were told that as a basic rule they must stay at least 22 feet away from the gorillas. They were also told they must stay calm if a gorilla were to move towards them and if necessary “just move calmly out of the way. In the ‘Travels in West Africa’ extract, Mary Kingsley’s guide ensured they kept out of sight as they ‘wormed their way forward ‘towards the gorillas, her guide then keeping her at a distance of 30 yards from the gorillas. When there appeared to be a threat to the writer, her guide warded off the attentions of the old male gorilla by making lots of noise, clapping his hands and making “a set of high-pitched screeches” that sent the gorilla swiftly back into the forest.

As in previous examinations it was possible for candidates to gain full marks on this question with a careful concentration on two or three relevant details from each text. Many were able to gain good marks, although some responses lacked the necessary precision, sometimes muddling up the details between the texts or only including one detail from a text. Where candidates failed to gain good marks some candidates only wrote about one of the texts or their responses lacked the specific details needed to gain reward. Good responses were clear and succinct, pointing out where guides took the same steps to keep safe those in their care and then selecting other appropriate details from each text without adding unnecessary detail. The very best were able to shape their responses into just a few sentences and gain full marks.
c700u20-nov20-16-q:
For candidates to achieve good marks on this question, which asked candidates to compare across the two texts, it was essential that they read the whole question carefully and shaped their responses so that they focused on the two bullet points. It was a point made in previous examiner reports but once again examiners saw responses that made general points of comparison but failed to focus on what was asked for in the bullet points.

This question focused first on the impressions the writers give of the gorillas they see and then invited candidates to explore how those impressions had been created. In the ‘Trekking with the Gorillas of Rwanda’, the writer offers an impression of the gorillas as unthreatening, even friendly animals, who almost seem to put on a show to entrance the tourists. Readers are given the impression that the female gorilla has all the attributes of a loving human mother, while the young ones are playful with each other and the mother. The tourists are also given the impression that the gorillas sometimes like to give a display, showing off by beating their chest, but also when the guides use oral prompts, they are animals that can be communicated with through language. The writer tells readers that the impression they have of the dominant male is like a king “surveying his domain” yet at the same time grooming one of his youngsters in the manner of a doting father. Good candidates were able to

12 focus on the descriptions used to create these positive and sympathetic impressions of the animals, the little cameos of their behaviour being explored and commented on to good effect. They were also able to consider the language used to describe their behaviour and antics, often considering words and phrases such as ‘tumble’ and ‘scampered’ with their associations of childish behaviour.

These impressions contrasted significantly with those created in Kingsley’s text, where the gorillas were viewed as wild and dangerous animals that could only be approached with extreme caution. The impression Kingsley’ gives of the gorillas is one of unpleasantly noisy creatures that aggressively ‘attack’ ‘tearing’ their food to pieces. These animals walk awkwardly and ‘inelegantly’ and her impression is often negative. She calls the gorillas ‘horrible’, suggesting they are more repugnant than other dangerous animals. For all that, she watches them “with great interest” and even prevents her guide from shooting one when she was “fearful of an attack.” There were points in the extract where candidates felt her impressions were not entirely negative and in the final paragraph, her impression of these ‘awkward’ and ‘inelegant’ animals is replaced by something close to being in awe and wonder as she creates the impression of swift, graceful creatures disappearing into the forest in a display she describes as a “superbly perfect hand-trapeze performance.” These impressions are largely created by the descriptions she gives of the gorillas’ behaviour and good candidates used the text well, selecting and commenting on specific adverbs, adjectives and verbs to illustrate how her impressions changed depending on what the gorillas were doing.

For candidates who kept their focus on the impressions given of the gorillas, there was plenty of material to select and comment on, and careful readers who organised their responses well gained high marks. However, examiners also saw responses where the focus became the impressions of the writers’ experiences or their attitudes towards the gorillas. Sometimes these were quite detailed responses but because they failed to focus on the question, there was little to reward. In some cases, examiners saw only very brief or limited responses and it was clear too, that issues of poor time management meant some candidates failed to attempt the question.
