In the first of the two writing tasks candidates were asked to write a lively guide to surviving the teenage years for a school or college magazine. It gave candidates the scope to range as widely as they wanted around the topic and the invitation to be ‘lively’ offered the opportunity to be informal, humorous or even a little controversial in approach. The nature of the task invited a mixture of advice and information, and to be successful required an awareness of the intended audience, most of whom would know only too well the trials and tribulations of being a teenager. The best responses managed to do this without ‘talking down’ to their readers and were often written in an easy, engaging style that suggested they themselves had managed to navigate their way through these difficult years and were happy to share their experiences as well as their advice. On occasions, little personal anecdotes gave the guidance they offered greater weight, particularly where the writer showed they had benefited as a result of what happened to them or what they had done.

It is perhaps true to say that the majority of the responses were earnest rather than lively, with quite a number taking a narrow, but nonetheless entirely acceptable approach to give advice exclusively about the preparation for school or college examinations. Others focused on managing school life more generally, with advice about how to manage all the distractions of the opposite sex, awkward teachers and homework regimes. Those who chose to offer guidance on an altogether wider perspective sometimes touched on topics such as the importance of friendships, keeping healthy, having good family relationships and maintaining mental wellbeing. The best of these displayed a wisdom far beyond the candidates’ years, with advice that would gladden the ears and hearts of their teachers and their parents.

Whilst not necessarily being the only way to organise material in the guide, some candidates used sub-headings to make clear what they regarded as the key elements in successfully surviving the teenage years. This did have the advantage of helping writers to expand and develop each of their suggestions, whereas weaker responses sometimes failed to develop some perfectly sensible ideas and advice, leaving their work brief and lacking in detail. As in previous examinations, there was an expectation that responses would be a minimum of 300 words in length and those that were significantly briefer usually struggled to gain good marks because the overall content was limited and lacked detail.
c700u20-nov20-22-q:
This second task was for candidates to write what they would say when giving a talk to their class about a hobby or special interest they had to try to get others in the class involved in. Most candidates had little difficulty in writing about some interest they had, and although sports such as football, rugby and swimming were frequent and popular choices, examiners were usually treated to a wide range of topics that included voluntary work, gaming, interests in music, computing, films, drama groups, cookery, reading and cadet groups.

Good responses were sufficiently detailed to give information about the hobby or interest but also how the writer had become interested in it. In some cases, anecdotes gave engaging insights into the benefits the writers had gained from their involvement and there was useful and practical advice offered about how members of the class might find out more or where to begin their own involvement. The best pieces showed good awareness of the intended audience, offered a range of interesting information and advice and the material was balanced, well organised and structured. Rather less successful responses sometimes struggled to balance the information about the hobby/special interest with guidance or encouragement to also become involved; on occasions the second aspect of the talk seemed to be little more than a concluding comment along the lines of, “I hope you are now interested

14 too.” In addition to lacking this balance in structuring of the piece, weaker responses were often rather brief, lacked very much sense of the intended audience or offered only very generalised information about their topic.

As the final task in the examination, some candidates struggled to complete their work, and sadly, some mis-managed their time so badly that they never gave themselves time to attempt it.

In terms of the communication and organisation of the writing responses, examiners found much to enjoy and engage them but there remains a concern about basic technical accuracy. Examiners reported that many of the writing pieces were awarded marks for communication and organisation that were sometimes one or even two bands above the band for vocabulary, sentence structure, spelling and punctuation. These concerns have been a feature of previous reports but continue to weaken the overall impact of candidates’ written work.

Summary of key points

In the reading section:

• Candidates need to read each question carefully. There were too many instances where questions were mis-read and as a consequence, candidates gained few marks. This was particularly the case in question 1.6.

• In questions worth 10 marks, coverage of the whole text is important as this gives candidates a range of relevant details they can use to support comments and evaluation.

• Methodical tracking of the texts is the most effective way of selecting the details to use in an answer. Where candidates focus their responses mainly on ‘feature spotting’ it rarely allows them to gain very good marks.

In the writing section:

• Responses need organisation and structure to be effective; the use of paragraphs (or sub-headings where appropriate) help the organisation of material; similarly, the use of an opening topic sentence in each paragraph can usefully lead into greater exploration and detail of that particular topic.

• Candidates should write responses of sufficient length, allowing them to explore and develop the subject matter in sufficient detail. Brief responses invariably lack depth and development.

• Many candidates need to pay more attention to technical accuracy, especially basic spellings, sentence construction and punctuation.

c700u20-nov21-11-q:
This first question focused on the Tim Peake passage, with three one-mark questions that required candidates to select details from across the text. As in previous examinations, these questions were straightforward location of explicit information questions but candidates needed to read both the text and the questions carefully. The first part of the question asked candidates to note the job that Peake had to do during his spacewalk.

Most candidates were able to correctly identify that he had to repair a faulty solar panel, thus ensuring that the space station was restored to full power. Some candidates failed to read the question carefully enough, responding to the question with answers such as `astronaut` or `to fly into space`. These incorrect responses serve to illustrate the importance of reading the question just as carefully as the texts. The second part of the text asked candidates why Mission Control ended the spacewalk and to locate this information it was necessary to read the seventh paragraph in the text, where Peake explained that his partner, Len Kopra, had a faulty spacesuit, resulting in water entering his space helmet. Mission Control told both astronauts to return to the space station. Again, most candidates gained reward for this question, but there were still candidates who failed to identify the correct detail, losing the opportunity for what should have been straightforward reward. This was also true for the final part of the question, where candidates were asked who Tim Peake received a message of support from. The penultimate paragraph made it clear that among many messages that had flooded in, Sir Paul McCartney had sent a special message to Peake, and whilst most found this an easy detail to locate, there were candidates who failed to gain a mark.
c700u20-nov21-12-q:
Tackling the first question meant reading the whole text and this should have prepared candidates for the 10-mark question: How does Tim Peake try to make his account of the spacewalk vivid and interesting for his readers? As I have reported in previous exam series, the most effective way for candidates to tackle this type of question is to work methodically through the text, selecting appropriate evidence and detail and, where appropriate, commenting and considering the way in which the evidence or detail has been presented by the writer. Peake’s account could be considered `vivid and interesting` in a number of ways, and whilst moving through the text methodically, perceptive readers were able to see, for example, that one of the ways the text made an impression on its readers was the way he wrote about it being a unique experience, one that he called “unreal”. He gave examples of the incredible speed at which they orbited the Earth while outside the space station and the rapid change of night into day. He wrote about his spacewalk being his “most vivid memory” and reflected that few in history had been given the privilege of seeing “the widescreen beauty of Earth” that he had been given. His account could be regarded as vivid, even dramatic, as from the very beginning of the passage, Peake made it clear that everything during a spacewalk was completed in “perilous conditions”. He went on to give examples of the dangers faced, from being hit “by a hurtling micro- meteorite” to losing his grip and finding himself “floating away into space” or miscalculating his time outside the space station and being exposed to temperatures that would suddenly fluctuate from 200 degrees Celsius to minus 200 degrees. Many candidates saw the dangers that he faced and were able to write about how they added to the impact of the passage, with good readers commenting purposefully on them.

Peake writes powerfully about the emotional impact of being in space and good readers were able to comment on his tone of “awe and reverence” as he surveyed Earth from afar. Many candidates saw that when he wrote that seeing day change into night was “like having a front-row seat in nature’s own widescreen cinema” it had a huge effect on him. While some were only able to note that it was an example of a simile, others went further to explore the image and comment on Peake’s awe and wonder at what he saw unfolding.

There were many points through the passage where Peake writes about the feelings he experienced during his spacewalk and good candidates selected and explored both individual words he chose, such as “marvelling” at the view of Earth or the specific details he writes about such as seeing Earth slip “gracefully into shadow” and feeling “completely detached – utterly removed from Earth” or the image of him “being a tiny spectator in an immeasurably vast universe”. Some candidates were able to successfully explore the way he wrote about feeling “awe and reverence” and the “humbling” impact it had on him.

Although the emotional impact of his experience is a powerful element in the passage, his account of the repair work undertaken during his spacewalk, and the emergency that arose during it, also provided candidates with opportunities to consider aspects that were `vivid and interesting`. Some candidates wrote about how his initial anxieties were replaced by his determination to complete the task he was assigned, while others considered how Peake used the comparison of what would have been a simple repair task on Earth to it having a potentially fatal outcome whilst in the “vacuum of space”. The fact that in completing the repair “timing was critical” encouraged some candidates to comment on the ever-present danger Peake faced, while others gave details of the faulty spacesuit and how this emerging danger curtailed the spacewalk. Finally, for candidates looking to consider an overview of how Peake had made his whole experience both vivid and interesting, the final paragraph gave them the opportunity to comment on Peake’s reflections and his sense of achievement in being the first Briton to walk in space.

The best responses to the question showed the ability to select and comment on appropriate textual details and showed good coverage of the whole text. They were able to explore Peake’s text from different standpoints, whilst less effective responses focused on just the danger of the mission, for example. Some candidates tried to tackle the question as a `feature-spotting` exercise but quickly found themselves resorting to unhelpful searches for similes or short sentences or asserting that it was an interesting account because of the alliteration in `Ask an Astronaut`.
c700u20-nov21-13-q:
This third question now turned candidates’ attention to the second text, an article written by an American, Robert Wood, in response to being invited to watch and photograph Otto Lilienthal’s attempt to make a flight in his `flying machine`. Like question 1.1, these three one-mark questions asked for specific details and provided careful readers with an opportunity to gain three marks as they gained familiarity with the text, in readiness for the more demanding question that followed. The first part of the question asked candidates how long Lilienthal had been experimenting with flying machines. The answer could be found in the first paragraph and unsurprisingly most candidates had no difficulty locating the information that Lilienthal had spent eight years experimenting and working on designs for a machine that would take to the air. However, there were candidates who simply mis-read the question and examiners saw responses that gave information about the cloth that covered the wings of the flying machine, the fact that there was not a single loose cord on the machine, or that Robert Wood was witnessing the start of the flying age. The second question also just required a little careful reading of the question. This asked how high Lilienthal went in his flying machine; those who read the third paragraph carefully had no difficulty in obtaining the answer: about fifty feet. The final part of the question asked candidates for the evidence that Lilienthal was pleased with his flight. The answer lay in the fourth paragraph where Wood describes the way Lilienthal cleverly brings his `flying machine` back to the ground, describing him as being “quite breathless from excitement”.

More candidates struggled with this part of the question than the first two parts, with some simply saying he was pleased or incorrectly focusing on Wood’s reaction to the flight, rather than Lilienthal’s. Although most candidates found this an opportunity to gain all three marks, once again, the lack of careful reading, either of the questions or the text, meant that some gained only limited reward.
c700u20-nov21-14-q:
This next question asked candidates to consider Wood’s text in greater detail and to consider how far they agreed with the statement: “Robert Wood admires Otto Lilienthal’s skill in building and flying his `flying machine`”. It would be difficult to suggest Wood was not impressed by Lilienthal and this was an opportunity for perceptive, careful readers to track through the text, selecting relevant detail and commenting upon it, whether it be about Wood’s admiration for Lilienthal’s skills as designer, builder and engineer of the `flying machine` or his admiration of the skills and daring Lilienthal shows as a pilot of a machine that Wood described as being “at the very start of the flying age”.

Wood begins his account by telling readers about the flying machine and even in this opening paragraph, he makes it clear that the machine is an impressive sight. He writes that it had been constructed “so perfectly” that no fault could be found in the supporting cords for the wings or in the tautness of the cloth for the wings. As early as the second sentence he writes that he “felt privileged” to be witnessing what he saw as “the very start of the flying age” and went on to describe Lilienthal as “an engineer of great ability”. Good candidates gave themselves an effective start to their response if they probed this opening paragraph to suggest that Wood’s view of Lilienthal’s skill as a builder of the flying machine is already clear, even before he sees him flying it.

Each of the five paragraphs contains material that candidates could select and comment on and good candidates worked methodically through the text. In the second paragraph, Wood comments on the way Lilienthal worked hard to get the machine in a position for take-off, noting the protections he had taken from the cold or in the case of an emergency landing. The following two paragraphs detail the actual flight and here some candidates commented on the way Wood describes him standing “like an athlete” in preparation for the starting pistol, some suggesting that the simile captured Wood’s view of Lilienthal as being perfectly prepared for this historic flight. He goes on to explain that the take off was timed to perfection and Lilienthal flew the machine “at a terrific pace, at a height of about fifty feet”. He continues that the machine flew so fast he struggled to photograph the event.

For candidates keen to comment on Lilienthal’s skill in flying the machine, the penultimate paragraph offered details to select and Wood’s account makes clear how the machine was “expertly brought…under his control” after a gust of wind threatened disaster, and then as the flight neared its conclusion, how Lilienthal “cleverly allowed the wind to strike under the wings” so that it could drop lightly to the ground. Candidates were rewarded where they were prepared to probe Wood’s use of adverbs or the specific details to illustrate Wood’s admiration of the skills Lilienthal exhibited towards the end of the flight.

The final paragraph also offered more evidence of Wood’s admiration of Lilienthal, writing about his skills as both designer and pilot of his flying machine. Some weaker readers struggled to make an effective selection of text, offering just a few words that lacked sufficient context to make a point clearly, but others selected more skilfully, combining comment with a telling phrase, perhaps focusing on “how perfectly

designed his invention was” or the flight “produced an impression that can never be forgotten” to convey his admiration.

Weaker responses were often brief and frequently only focused on a limited section of the text, but as indicated above, the best answers used the text extensively, had coverage of all five paragraphs and explored Wood’s response to Lilienthal as both builder and pilot.
c700u20-nov21-15-q:
This question, asking for the ability to select and synthesise materials from the two texts, invited candidates to identify what Tim Peake and Otto Lilienthal wore for the spacewalk and the flight in the flying machine. This simply required candidates to select the appropriate details for each of the men and although most who attempted the question were able to gain a creditable mark, at this point in the examination almost 10% of the candidates failed to tackle the question.

In the `Ask an Astronaut` text, Tim Peake made reference to his preparation for the spacewalk, telling his readers in the second paragraph that he remembered “pulling on my pressurised space gloves” in readiness for stepping out of the space station. A little later in the text he recalls that as he and Len Kopra waited by the solar panel he was told by Mission Control to “raise the visors on our space helmets” as they moved into darkness. Finally, he goes on to explain the problem that Len Kopra had with his faulty spacesuit, when water began to enter his helmet and the pair were ordered back to the space station.

In Robert Wood’s article, he gives information about how Lilienthal was dressed for his flight, explaining that he was dressed “in a thick flannel shirt for protection against the cold” and he also wore “baggy trousers” with thickly padded knees, that Wood explains would provide some protection in the case of an emergency landing.

There was no requirement to explain the details of their clothing, although some candidates did so in considerable detail. As has been the case in previous examinations, it was possible to gain full marks by selecting two details from each text or by focusing rather more on one text; providing at least one detail was selected from the Robert Wood text, details from the Tim Peake text could gain a further three marks. Although most candidates who tackled the question gained good or full marks, some candidates contented themselves with a single detail from each of the texts and there were others who either mis-read the question, gave only details from one of the texts or failed to give adequate details – for example, examiners saw a number of examples where Lilienthal was “dressed in a flannel”.
c700u20-nov21-16-q:
Although this final reading question was focused, as ever, on comparison of the two texts, it was essential that they read the whole question carefully and in particular responded specifically to the focus of the two bullet points. There were still candidates who chose to ignore the bullet points and instead shape their answer to a more general comparison of the texts and these rarely gained reward. It has been a point made in almost every post-exam report that reading the question and following the instructions is the only way to achieve success in this question.

The question invited candidates to compare the difficulties and dangers faced by Tim Peake and Otto Lilienthal and then to consider how the writers showed these difficulties and dangers in their respective texts.

In the Tim Peake text, there were a number of dangers that he faced, most of which would have resulted in his demise. In the opening paragraph he writes about the possibility of being “hit by a hurtling micro-meteorite” when outside the space station and then if something were to go wrong during the spacewalk “you could find yourself floating away into space”. He also wrote at length about the way temperatures outside the space station fluctuated from one extreme to another in a matter of minutes and made it clear that any fault with the spacesuit worn for work outside the space station, as happened to his companion, could quickly become life-threatening. Peake uses adjectives such as “perilous” and “critical” when describing the work he had to undertake as a means of emphasising to readers the potential dangers of his spacewalk.

He also uses comparison to emphasise how a perfectly simple job on Earth carried a much greater risk in space and gave specific details of the rapid and extreme temperature change as the space station moved from night into day.

In Robert Wood’s text, although the dangers and difficulties may have seemed less immediately life-threatening than the situation Tim Peake described, they were no less real. One of the obvious difficulties Wood wrote about was the awkwardness Lilienthal had of controlling the machine as he waited for the perfect time to catch the wind and take off. He wrote about how the weight of the machine and the huge wings made it difficult to hold, especially when there was any gust of wind. He explained why Lilienthal wore a thick flannel shirt and the importance of having thickly-padded knees on his baggy trousers, protection in the event of an emergency landing. The flight itself carried significant dangers for the pilot, as Wood described the machine flying “at a terrific pace, at a height of about fifty feet”. When it was caught by a sudden and dangerous gust of wind, he described how it was only brought under control because of Lilienthal’s expertise as a pilot. Wood makes clear the difficulties that Lilienthal faced as he watches “anxiously” before Lilienthal is airborne and goes on to describe the machine rocking and tipping “with every puff of air” or how it “swerved dangerously” in mid-air. To convey the speed and inherent danger of the flight, he describes the machine as flying “at race horse speed”.

Where candidates focused on the bullet points it was possible to accumulate appropriate textual details fairly easily across the two texts and there were some good responses. Unfortunately, too many candidates failed to attempt this final reading question or wrote only brief or generalised comparisons.
c700u20-nov21-21-q:
In the first of the two writing tasks candidates were asked to write a lively article for a school or college magazine with the title: Things I can’t live without. Candidates were free to range widely over a number of topics or could focus their attention on just one or two indispensable necessities. In some cases, candidates wrote their responses as more of a talk than an article and examiners occasionally saw a response that drifted from the focus of the task, but for those who attempted the work, most were able to explain why they simply could not function without a mobile phone, for example. More assured candidates were able to explain the reasons why this was an essential item and how it kept them in touch with life as we know it. Some candidates approached the task earnestly, writing about family life, friends or the importance of education and schools. Others waxed lyrical about their beloved X-box or online games, and hobbies and sports were also considered indispensable. Perhaps predictably, many also said it was impossible to live in the modern world without Netflix.

Examiners saw some lively and engaging pieces, although there were many less successful responses where candidates struggled to manage their time successfully and wrote only brief and limited responses. Where candidates wrote significantly briefer responses than the indicated 300-400 words, the work almost inevitably lacked range and development, and although most pieces captured a sense of writing for a specific intended audience, the limitations of the content were obvious.
c700u20-nov21-22-q:
This second task was for candidates to write what they would say when giving a talk to their class about how people in their everyday lives can help protect the environment and save the planet.

Like the first writing task, there was a significant percentage of the entry that failed to tackle the task, and for many who did, it became a struggle to complete the work. Examiners saw brief and limited responses, with too many unfinished pieces. The task itself was particularly topical, because of the COP26 conference which was taking place at the time of the examination and enjoying much national press coverage. Candidates wrote about a variety of topics related to the question, ranging from information and advice about recycling and dealing with litter to reducing meat intake, changing to electric vehicles, taking more care of the oceans and reducing waste. Whilst some candidates focused their attention on what many described as simple changes everyone could make, others widened their focus to encompass the dangers posed by the melting polar ice caps or the Amazon de-forestation. Many presented facts and opinions with a compelling urgency and there was no shortage of passion as the talks implored or demanded those in the class should take action.

Where the writing tasks were complete, examiners saw engaging and often thought- provoking responses but there were many who failed to complete all of the reading and writing tasks, and some who seemed simply ill-prepared for the demands of a two-hour paper, either in terms of their time management or in the quality of their responses. Technical accuracy in writing has long been flagged up in reports as an ongoing concern but in this examination paper, there was little excuse for so many candidates to incorrectly spell words such as `environment` or `planet` which appeared in the writing task details. Although a message in the previous examiner’s report, issues of incorrect or missing punctuation, basic spelling errors and poor sentence control continue to weaken the impact of candidates’ written work.

Summary of key points

In the reading section:

• Candidates need to read each question carefully to ensure their answers have the appropriate focus. In question 1.6, responses must focus specifically on the two bullet points and not be seen as a question inviting a more general comparison of the two texts.

• Candidates should track the texts methodically to select appropriate details, commenting where appropriate. In questions that ask candidates to consider the craft of the writer, `feature spotting` is an ineffective approach.

• Questions 1.1, 1.3 and 1.5 are essentially those requiring specific details from the texts. Where candidates fail to gain full marks it is often because they have mis-read the question or supplied insufficient detail or information.

In the writing section:

• Candidates must manage their time in the examination to leave sufficient time to tackle both writing tasks. In this examination, markers reported that many responses were incomplete or so brief that there was little to reward. Responses that are significantly below the 300-400 words indicated in the exam paper are likely to struggle to have the range and development of content that mark out more successful responses.

• Lack of technical accuracy remains a significant issue and many writing responses were rewarded marks for VSSSP in a lower band than was gained for the communication and organisation of the work.

November 2021
c700u20-nov22-11-q:
This first question focused on the newspaper article by Alan Lee, with three one-mark questions that required candidates to select details from across the text. These questions were straightforward ‘search and find’ questions but candidates needed to read both the text and the questions carefully. The first part of the question asked candidates to note where the skeleton of Jumbo was kept and most candidates were able to correctly identify that it was kept in the American Museum of Natural History. Some candidates failed to give the specific detail, responding with details like ‘a museum’ or ‘America’ and this perhaps serves to emphasise the importance of precision in what should be simple location and selection of textual detail.

The second part of the question asked candidates why Jumbo had been sold to the Barnum Circus. This was made clear in the later part of the article, where Lee explained that Jumbo’s behaviour and ‘violent rages’ caused zoo officials to fear he would attack Scott or a zoo visitor. Because he had become ‘problematic’ and the zoo wanted to get rid of him, when the Barnum Circus offered to buy the elephant for £2000, they accepted the offer. Although this part of the question required a brief explanation, again most candidates were able to gain a mark. Some candidates mis- read the question, selecting incorrect details as a result or tried to respond with too little detail to make the reason clear.

The final part of the question asked candidates to give one piece of evidence that showed people did not want Jumbo to go to America. The penultimate paragraph made it clear that ‘there was an outcry’, with 100,000 children begging Queen Victoria to stop the sale and adults protesting at the zoo. Any of these details gained reward and most candidates were able to gain full marks for this part of the question.
c700u20-nov22-12-q:
Tackling the first question meant reading the whole text and this should have prepared candidates for the 10-mark question that followed: ‘How does the writer, Alan Lee, try to show that Jumbo was a much-loved `Victorian sensation’?’

As usual, the most effective way for candidates to tackle this type of ‘craft of the writer’ question was to work methodically through the text, selecting relevant textual evidence and detail and, where appropriate, commenting and considering the way in which the information or detail had been presented by the writer. Where this was done effectively, candidates accumulated a good many details, explored quotations, commented on how these showed Jumbo was a ‘much-loved Victorian sensation’ and gained good marks as a result.

From the very beginning it was made clear that the elephant had an enormous impact on Victorian visitors to the zoo. In the subtitle, Jumbo was described as an ‘animal celebrity’, indicating the popularity of the elephant and the opening sentences captured this very effectively, giving good candidates immediate opportunities to probe and comment on the details. Readers were told that ‘millions of visitors’ went to see Jumbo and that he was ‘a firm favourite of Queen Victoria’s children’. Some commented on the impact that royalty had on visitor numbers, while others explored and commented on the way the animal became the inspiration for the Disney film ‘Dumbo’. The opening paragraph gave candidates an immediate opportunity to link details to the question, with good candidates also able to comment on words and phrases such as ‘adoration’ and ‘firm favourite’ to show that Jumbo was much loved.

Paragraph two introduced the research into Jumbo that Sir David Attenborough had conducted for his BBC documentary. Here, the elephant was described as a ‘gentle giant’ and readers were told that the skeleton of the elephant had been preserved at the American Museum of Natural History in New York, which for some candidates suggested the impact the elephant had made during its life. Good candidates were alert to the way Lee described the impact the elephant had on zoo visitors, commenting on phrases such as ‘an instant hit’, the crowds being ‘awe-struck Victorians’ when they came to ‘marvel at his growing size’. Some also used details such as how rare the sight of an elephant was to the Victorian public or that they delighted in taking photographs and rides on the animal. The mention again about how Queen Victoria’s children ‘adored’ Jumbo was also an area explored by many candidates.

Although candidates had to be selective in their use of material from the newspaper article, when Lee explains that Jumbo was sold to the Barnum Circus in America, the reactions of the Victorian public made it clear that the elephant was much-loved. Lee explained that ‘there was an outcry’, and that 100,000 children wrote to the Queen to try to prevent the sale of Jumbo from happening and even adults protested at the zoo about the sale. When the animal arrived in America, his fame had spread, with ‘huge crowds’ awaiting him and ‘Jumbo-mania erupted’.

Across the text, there were lots of details that good candidates were able to select and comment on and these candidates often also probed the way Lee used language to make clear how Jumbo was viewed by the Victorian public. Good candidates showed they were able to make use of the whole text, whilst weaker candidates’ responses lacked whole-text coverage or struggled to comment effectively on the details they selected. Despite the advice offered in past reports, some candidates still tried to tackle the question as a ‘feature-spotting’ exercise but this approach proved to be largely unproductive.
c700u20-nov22-13-q:
This third question asked candidates to look at the second text, a passage from the autobiography of Matthew Scott, Jumbo’s keeper at London Zoo.

Like question 1.1, these three one-mark questions asked for specific details and provided careful readers with an opportunity to gain marks as they gained familiarity with the text, in readiness for the more demanding question that followed. The first part of the question simply asked candidates how much Jumbo weighed. The answer came in the first paragraph: ‘nearly eight tons’, and most candidates found the detail without difficulty, although some appeared to have referred back to the newspaper article, where it had stated Jumbo’s weight as being ‘more than seven tons’.

The second question, which asked how long had Jumbo been giving children rides in London Zoo, was also just a matter of locating the correct detail, which came in the second paragraph. In this paragraph Scott wrote about the elephant being a ‘busy, industrious creature’ and gave as an example of this that he had been ‘carrying around children almost daily for twenty years.’ Most candidates were able to gain reward on this question, although again, examiners occasionally reported responses that were clearly the result of a misreading of the question.

The final part of the question asked candidates to give an example from the text that showed Jumbo would usually do what Matthew Scott asked him. This was a more demanding question as candidates had to see that although the elephant would normally do as he was asked, the answer to the question was about the one time he failed to obey Scott. This came towards the end of the anecdote about Jumbo saving a small child who had fallen in front of him. Scott had not seen the infant and shouted to the elephant to ‘go along’; in response, readers are told that, ‘for once he did not obey the order.’ Many candidates gained reward but it was clear that not all had read the text with sufficient care and there were examples of quotations that showed a lack of understanding.

Although many candidates found this an opportunity to gain all three marks, once again, the lack of careful reading, either of the questions or the text, meant that some gained only limited reward.
c700u20-nov22-14-q:
This next question asked candidates to respond to the statement: ‘Matthew Scott writes about Jumbo in a way that shows feelings of pride and affection for the elephant,’ saying to what extent they agreed with that view. From the initial reading of the passage in order to tackle the questions in 1.3, it should have been clear that Scott felt enormous affection for the animal he looked after, and also wrote about him with great pride, praising the elephant for being the ‘fine-looking creature’ he had become and for the ‘busy, industrious’ life he led. The question gave candidates the opportunity to gain marks for careful tracking of the text and for selecting relevant details as they occurred, whether it was evidence of Scott’s affection for the animal or for his admiration of the elephant’s prowess.

The passage began with Scott telling readers about Jumbo when he was first delivered into his care. In the first sentence he called the elephant ‘the poor thing’ as he related how he was ‘full of disease’. He told readers how he had nursed the elephant back to full health ‘with all the care and affection of a mother’, which many candidates noted as a clear example of the bond he forged with the animal. As the elephant regained his health and strength, Scott showed his pride in Jumbo by praising what he had become, and candidates used textual details such as ‘fine- looking creature’, ‘most intelligent’, ‘most powerful living creature in creation’ to support the evaluation of the statement. He went on to talk about the shared experience he had with the elephant, saying it, ‘is a pleasure to me and is great reward.’ The paragraph concluded with Scott saying his days were happy as long as he was ‘permitted the company of dear old Jumbo’ and that he would not wish to be parted from what was now his companion. There was plenty of detail to explore in the opening paragraph and good, careful readers were able to accumulate lots of material that supported the view expressed in the statement.

When candidates began to explore the second paragraph, they saw that Scott now gave details of the life Jumbo had in the zoo. He began the paragraph by telling readers what a ‘busy, industrious creature’ he was, which was done with a mixture of pride but also showed the effect he felt he had on the elephant, having ‘brought him from his sick bed.’ He clearly admired the work Jumbo got through, showing his pride in the animal’s industrious nature: ‘he has no idle days for `loafing’ or otherwise wasting his time.’ and the tone was one of pride when he wrote about the elephant ‘carrying around children almost daily for twenty years.’ Readers were told that no animal did his work, ‘more affectionately or tenderly, and without accident’ as Jumbo. Scott then related the anecdote about an occasion when the elephant saved an infant who had fallen in front of him, while his mother was screaming that the child would be killed.

Scott said the animal ‘gently picked up the child by the waist with his trunk’ and returned it to the mother, using the word ‘tenderly’ to show how careful Jumbo had been. Good candidates were able to use the anecdote to demonstrate Scott’s pride in the animal but also comment on words such as ‘tenderly’ and ‘gently’ as evidence of the affection held for the elephant.

In the final paragraph, Scott gave more details of the calm nature of the animal, particularly when children were near and the passage concluded with Scott repeating what a ‘kind, affectionate creature’ the elephant was and that readers should follow the example set by Jumbo of always going to help anyone in trouble. This again gave candidates the opportunity to confirm the view that Scott showed both pride and affection for the elephant.

Each of the paragraphs contained material that candidates could select and comment on, and good candidates worked methodically through the text to gain creditable marks. However, weaker responses were often too brief and frequently only focused on a limited section of the text and in some cases, just a few lines of the passage. In order to gain good marks, candidates must use the whole text and make reference to a range of details they can comment upon.
c700u20-nov22-15-q:
This question, asking for the ability to select and synthesise materials from the two texts, asked candidates to explain briefly what the two writers told readers about Jumbo’s food and drink. This required candidates to select the appropriate details from each text and where appropriate, to give a little explanation about what readers are told. As this question was worth just 4 marks, brief responses that gave the details and explanations with precision and clarity were all that was required. Some candidates wrote more than was necessary, others failed to be sufficiently precise and some tangled up the details from the texts, making it unclear which detail was linked to which text. However, many were able to gain full marks by simply being clear and precise.

In Scott’s autobiography, readers are told that Jumbo eats ‘hay, oats and bread’. For drink, Jumbo was given ‘chiefly water’ but Scott went on to say that for ‘a treat’ he would be given ‘a big dram of whisky’. Later in the passage, he wrote about the children feeding Jumbo cakes, and any of these details gained candidates reward. In Alan Lee’s article, he shed a little more light on the elephant’s diet, saying that he existed on ‘sticky buns and hay’. Earlier in the article, Lee had said that the elephant had ‘violent rages’ and that scientists had discovered the reason may have been bad toothache, the result of what Lee described as the elephant’s ‘monotonous diet.’ Lee went on to say that rather than Scott giving him whisky ‘as a treat’, this, together with beer, had been used to pacify the animal when he was in pain.

As in previous examinations, it was possible to gain full marks by selecting two details from each text or by focusing rather more on one text; providing at least one detail was selected from the Scott autobiography, details from Lee’s newspaper article could gain a further three marks (and vice versa). Although most candidates were able to gain good or full marks, some candidates gave only a single detail from each of the texts and there were others who wrote in very general terms without any specific details.
c700u20-nov22-16-q:
Although this final reading question focused on a comparison of the two texts, as ever, candidates were asked to specifically focus on the two bullet points for the focus of the comparison. Candidates who chose to ignore the bullet points rarely gained good marks.

The question invited candidates to compare what the two writers told readers about Jumbo’s life in London Zoo and then to consider how the writers got their views about Jumbo’s life in the zoo across to their readers. Many candidates were able to see that whilst Scott focused only on the positive details of the elephant’s life in the zoo, Lee gave a much more balanced view that suggested despite the animal’s huge popularity, the animal actually lived ‘a sad, often painful existence.’

In the newspaper article, Alan Lee made it clear that the elephant was a favourite at the zoo, attracting large crowds of adoring Victorians and giving rides to zoo visitors. Readers were also told that Matthew Scott, his keeper, forged a strong bond with the animal, nursing him back to health when he arrived at the zoo ‘disease-ridden.’ Lee told readers that the elephant suffered from bad toothache, the result of his poor diet of ‘sticky buns and hay’, and had joint problems and bone damage caused by the daily rides he gave visitors. The pain he suffered meant there was another, ‘darker side’ to Jumbo’s nature, unseen by visitors but his suffering resulted in ‘terrifyingly violent rages’ that were calmed only by the whisky and beer Scott gave him. It was a different picture from that painted by Scott in his autobiography. He described Jumbo’s life in the zoo, once he had been nursed back to health, as being ‘busy, industrious’, his days filled with carrying visitors on his back. Scott writes of the ‘treats’ he was given: he would give him whisky and children loved to give him cakes, and there was no suggestion that the elephant was ever a problem. Scott made a point of stating how Jumbo could be relied upon to behave safely and remain calm in all situations.

The writers made their views about Jumbo’s life in the zoo clear in rather different ways. Alan Lee gave specific names of those who admired the elephant to emphasise its popularity, and made use of key phrases and language, such as ‘awe- struck’ to show the impact the elephant made on zoo visitors. He also quoted Sir David Attenborough to add weight to the views about the animal’s life in the zoo, and reported the findings of researchers and scientists who studied the elephant’s skeleton. In contrast, Scott’s writing was more subjective and passionate about the elephant, describing his own feelings for the animal and praising Jumbo for his intelligence, willingness to work and his affectionate and tender nature. He made use of the anecdote to illustrate Jumbo’s nature and used direct address to the reader at the end of the passage, asking them to behave in the same kind, affectionate way, helping anyone in trouble.

Where candidates used the bullet points to shape their responses, they were able to accumulate appropriate textual details, comment on how the writers made their views clear and there were some good responses. However, some candidates struggled to organise their work or make it clear which details belonged to which writer, and some responses were very brief. It also became clear that too many candidates had struggled with time management and as a result, failed to attempt this final reading question altogether.
c700u20-nov22-21-q:
In the first of the two writing tasks candidates were asked to write what they would say to younger students about how best to prepare for and cope with the demands of GCSE exams. Almost all responses captured a sense of awareness of the intended audience and most contained a mixture of suggestions for success, reflections on the speaker’s own examination performance and reassuring comments for those who might still not achieve the grades they sought. Good responses had a clear shape and structure, using separate paragraphs to introduce a particular strategy for success, developing the detail of that strategy and linking it to the next part of the talk. Revision was viewed as essential, with lots of suggestions about how to construct a revision timetable, at what point it was advisable to begin the process, and where to go when there were difficulties. Teachers reading these responses would be heartened to know that candidates were unstinting in their praise for them, and the extra lengths teachers would always go to, for anyone needing help. After- school lessons and requests for extra homework were all thought to be useful and many thought flashcards were essential for success. Others talked enthusiastically about YouTube programmes, BBC Bitesize packages or gave examples of memory games that had helped them. Sometimes, candidates tended to list the successful strategies but gave too little specific detail about them and some responses focused more on the speaker’s view of his/her own exam performance than on how others might be successful. Lots of responses wrote of their regret that they had not taken advice from others seriously and failed their exams first time around, but many went on encouragingly to say that once they had seen the error of their ways and worked hard, they had gone on to pass all of their exams with flying colours. Much of the advice given also emphasised the need for a balanced approach, taking time out from revision and work to relax with friends.

Examiners saw some lively, sensible and engaging pieces but there were also responses that were significantly briefer responses than the indicated 300-400 words. These inevitably lacked range and development, and the limitations of the content were obvious.
c700u20-nov22-22-q:
This second task was to write a letter to a newspaper in response to a comment seen that had appeared in a letter in a previous edition. This offered the view, “It’s about time teenagers thought about their responsibilities and contributed more to their communities.” The inclusion of a formal letter had been indicated in the ‘advance information’ to centres, so it was disappointing that some candidates offered no attempt at letter conventions or layout. Some candidates objected strongly to the criticism, writing about the pressures teenagers were already under, with examples of a heavy school or college workload, regular homework, responsibilities for younger siblings and so on. Whilst there were many who took this route, others chose to agree with the view, often adopting the persona of an older adult, witnessing poor or anti-social behaviour from youngsters who showed little care for others. There were also candidates who offered a view that while it was right for teenagers to become more involved in community work, greater opportunities needed to be created for training and guidance so that young people could get involved in community work effectively. Others gave detailed accounts of the work they and others did for their own families or local community groups and gave examples of raising money for those in need. Many were passionate about the views they held and the best responses were well-organised and when a viewpoint was expressed, there was sufficient supporting detail and evidence to convince the reader. As with the first writing task, there were too many candidates who wrote brief responses; these simply had too little content to warrant a decent mark. There were also candidates who offered no attempt at the task.

As has been reported on in previous examinations, and in the current Component 1 report, limited technical accuracy remains a concern, with basic spelling errors and poor sentence control continuing to weaken the impact of the written work of too many candidates.

Summary of key points

In the reading section:

• Candidates should try to track the text methodically to select details relevant to the question, commenting where necessary. This allows candidates, particularly in questions 1.2 and 1.4, to accumulate a range of appropriate information that is linked to the question from across the whole text.

• In selecting and commenting on quotations from the text, it is important that candidates give enough contextual information or explanation where it is helpful to do so. In their desire to avoid long quotations, candidates sometimes offer only fragments of the text, which, without explanation, often lack clarity and fail to gain reward.

• Questions 1.1, 1.3 and 1.5 are essentially those mostly requiring specific details from the texts. In order to gain good or full marks on these questions, it is important for candidates to give sufficient detail so that the answers are both clear and precise.

In the writing section:

• Responses that are significantly below the 300-400 words indicated in the exam paper are likely to struggle to have the range and development of content that mark out more successful responses.

• Candidates should plan their writing so that it has shape, structure and development. For most tasks, a brief introduction, three to five paragraphs each dealing with a specific topic or area of the task, together with a brief concluding paragraph will usually work well.

• Lack of technical accuracy remains a significant issue and many writing responses were rewarded marks for VSSSP in a lower band than was gained for the communication and organisation of the work.
