c700u20-nov23-11-q:
The first question focused on the newspaper article, ‘The schoolboy who conquered the Matterhorn.’ As usual, there were three one-mark questions requiring candidates to select details from across the text. Although these were straightforward ‘search and find’ questions it was important that candidates read these carefully, as well as the text. The first part of the question illustrated the importance of this, as it became clear to examiners that too many candidates rushed to offer an answer, rather than checking exactly what was being asked for. The question asked which mountain range the Matterhorn is in, but answers sometimes simply gave the height of the mountain and even more frequently, where the mountain is situated. The final sentence in the opening paragraph gave the information: “It is in part of the Alps, a mountain range straddling the border between Switzerland and Italy.”

The second part of the question asked candidates why climbers would set off early in the morning to tackle the mountain, and whilst most candidates were able to find this information without difficulty, there were responses that showed a lack of care in the reading of the question. The article had explained the reason for an early start was to reach the summit before the sun melted the snow on the top section, as this made it prone to avalanches, and many candidates gained reward for this part of the question. Those who failed to gain reward often showed they had not read the question carefully, some giving the time climbers set off and others showing they had not read the text carefully enough, with responses that were not based on the passage.

The third part of the question asked what was the most dangerous part of the climb, according to the 11-year-old climber, James Molyneaux. In his account, he had explained that the descent was the most dangerous because of the level of concentration needed and how “the legs start to feel like jelly.” Most candidates were able to select the right detail, although again, some seemed to ignore the text and offer their own thoughts. The three parts of this opening question were no more demanding than those seen in other examination papers of recent years, yet disappointingly there seemed more candidates failing to gain full marks; in many cases, it appeared that not reading the question carefully enough was the reason.
c700u20-nov23-12-q:
To have answered all parts of the opening question meant candidates should have had some understanding of how and why climbing the Matterhorn at the age of 11 was a significant achievement, preparing them for the 10-mark question that followed: ‘How does the writer try to show that it was a remarkable achievement for Jules Molyneaux to climb the Matterhorn?’

As in previous examination series, the most effective way for candidates to tackle this type of ‘craft of the writer’ question was to select appropriate details from the text, commenting on how or why these illustrated the idea that the successful ascent was a ‘remarkable achievement’. From the very opening of the article, the writer had made it clear to readers that Jules Molyneaux was unlike most 11-year-old boys, comparing the way most youngsters would spend their time playing football or visiting the local park with Molyneaux’s dream of conquering one of the world’s most challenging mountains.

13 Readers were given a little detail of the way the 11-year-old dreamed of climbing the mountain after a school project and how he felt ‘magnetised to it’ by the shape of it. Readers were then told about how the dream gradually unfolded into the plans made by his father, Chris, to increase the youngster’s endurance and technical skills, so that as he became fitter, the dream began to be a possibility. Good candidates used the details in the opening paragraphs to build the picture of Jules gradually moving towards the realisation of his dream, at the same time noting that the writer had frequently used adjectives such as ‘toughest’, ‘dangerous’ and ‘challenging’ along with phrases such as ‘potentially deadly’ to ensure readers understood the scale and level difficulty that faced any climber, never mind an 11-year-old boy.

The article then gave details about Jules Molyneaux having to prove his capability to tackle the mountain, suggesting that “normally you have to be 16” to even apply for permission to attempt the climb. Having successfully proved himself, Jules joined his father and Swiss guides for the climb, the writer giving details of the event, along with the words of Jules and his father to show the level of challenge and their feelings at various points during the climb. Again, good candidates selected those details and/or words of the youngster to capture both the sense of it being a momentous occasion in the young boy’s life but also how he coped with the potential perils of the climb itself. Many included the way in which the youngster distracted himself from the pain of the climb by singing to himself, or noted the way Molyneaux himself talked about the level of concentration needed “every second” for the descent where some of the “ledges that are only a foot wide” in the knowledge that “if you lose concentration…you slip and fall.”

The final paragraph of the article dealt with the arrival back at the Matterhorn Museum, where the youngster was “congratulated as the youngest person to climb the mountain” and one mountaineer describing it as “an amazing achievement.” The article concluded with Jules himself reflecting on his success, and here he was shown to simply have been glad to have had the opportunity of tackling the mountain with his father, and “having as much fun as possible”.

Throughout the article, the writer made clear that what Jules achieved was ‘remarkable’, although some readers tended to focus on just one or two sections of the text, rather than the whole text, and offered only brief and limited responses. Some struggled to make effective selections, sometimes using just a fragment of a sentence and failing to contextualise it clearly. In some cases, candidates had adopted an approach that appeared to be based on simply writing down as many quotations as possible in the hope that this would provide a formula for a good mark. It frequently went along the lines of: “The writer says [insert irrelevant quotation] and this shows it was remarkable.” With little or no comment, contextualisation or explanation, this approach gained them few marks. In contrast, those who tracked the text methodically, made appropriate selections of detail and were prepared to explain clearly why or how those particular details showed Molyneaux’s achievement was remarkable, and were able to range across the whole text were able to gain good marks.
c700u20-nov23-13-q:
This third question asked candidates to look at the second text, an account of Isabella Bird’s attempt to climb Long’s Peak, the ‘American Matterhorn’.

Like question 1.1, these three one-mark questions asked for specific details and provided careful readers with an opportunity to gain marks as they gained familiarity with the text, in readiness for the more demanding question that followed.

14 The first part of the question asked how readers knew that ‘Long’s Peak is higher than the mountains around it?’ In the opening sentence, readers are told that the mountain “dwarfs all the surrounding mountains” and this was all that was required to gain the mark. Most candidates used this opportunity to gain a mark but there were candidates who chose to simply give the height of the mountain or some other detail that earned no reward. The second part of the question seemed to prove more straightforward: “where did the real business of the climb begin?” Most candidates sensibly located ‘the real business’ in the text and were able to note the outcrop of rock called the Notch. The final part of the question asked how long it had taken the climbers “to reach the top of the gorge?” Some candidates went to the final paragraph, mistakenly giving the time for the final part of the whole climb, rather than the time to get to the top of the gorge, which Bird reported as taking two hours. Whilst most candidates gained reward for the correct answer, this again showed too many candidates not taking enough care over the reading of the question.
c700u20-nov23-14-q: This next question asked candidates to respond to the statement: ‘Isabella Bird’s account convincingly shows the difficulties Long’s Peak presents to climbers,’ and explaining to what extent they agreed with that view. Whilst it was apparent that Isabella Bird found the mountain presented both a physical and emotional struggle for her, the question invited candidates to consider the challenges the mountain presented to any climber, so those who confined their responses solely to Bird’s struggles could make only rather limited progress. Whilst there was some reward for candidates exploring her physical struggle, the fears she had as she climbed and the length of time it took her to make the ascent, there was much more to include. Bird’s account made it clear that for any climber, the mountain offered a serious challenge and good candidates noted how she called a successful ascent “a real mountaineering feat” and that it “dwarfs other mountains.” There were a number of references to the challenge the mountain presented and words such as “towered’ suggested how intimidating the view would be of the climb facing those attempting to reach the top. There were details of the loose rocks that “tumbled down when touched”, the “deep gorge with inaccessible sides”, the “smooth ice appearing where it was least expected” and so on. Good candidates were able to select and comment on such details and accumulate reward as they worked through the text, using some of these specific details to explain how they would challenge even the most able of climbers. Bird wrote about the peak looking “nearly vertical for 400 feet” and about the “terrifying cliff “ from where a climber could fall 3000 feet to certain death, and as she neared the final part of the climb she wrote about facing boulders “of enormous size” or dealing with steep climbs that were “fearful.” It was also clear that the higher climbers went, the thinner the air became, but for those climbers able to reach the top, their efforts would have been thoroughly worthwhile, with the experience described by Bird as “wonderful”. There were lots of textual details for candidates to select and comment on but too many confined their response solely to Bird’s personal struggles, and with only limited references to the details included in the account that clearly illustrated the challenges of the mountain itself.
c700u20-nov23-15-q:
This question, asking for the ability to select and synthesise materials from the two texts, asked candidates to explain briefly what readers learn about Jules Molyneaux and Bird’s guide, Jim Nugent. As ever, selecting specific details with precision and clarity meant candidates could gain good marks without writing at great length. Too many candidates tried to write about what was learned about ‘both’ men, rather than dealing with them individually and this almost inevitably meant some loss of precision or only being able to offer a rather limited or generalised overview. Previous reports have suggested that it is always more sensible to deal with each text separately and this was especially the case with this question.

15 In the newspaper article, readers learned that Molyneaux’s father initially thought Jules “was joking” when he asked about climbing the Matterhorn. When he realised he was serious he planned “a rigorous schedule” to improve his climbing skills and his endurance. We also learn that in climbing alongside his son, he had a “total focus” on the task of getting to the top of the mountain and was relieved to get to the top safely. In Isabella Bird’s account, she painted a picture of Jim Nugent, who was a local guide, as a physically strong climber, able to drag her up parts of the climb. However, more than this, he helped Bird “with patience and skill” so that she was able to continue, and we are also told that he “was gentle and considerate” with her.

As in previous examinations, it was possible to gain full marks by selecting two details from each text or by focusing rather more on one text, providing at least one detail was selected from the second text. Some candidates misread the question and wrote about Jules and about Isabella and those who shaped their answers around both struggled to find points of similarity, although those who offered that “both were supportive” did gain marks. Those who explored each text separately usually gained better marks, with many able to gain full marks.
c700u20-nov23-16-q:
Although this final reading question focused on a comparison of the two texts, as ever, candidates were asked to do this by specifically focusing on the two bullet points as the basis for the comparison. Candidates who chose to ignore the bullet points rarely gained good marks.

In the first bullet point, candidates were invited to compare the thoughts and feelings of Jules Molyneaux and Isabella Bird while they were climbing the mountains. Importantly, and to signal clearly the focus of the question, the final detail in the bullet point was emboldened in the question paper. The second bullet point then asked candidates to explore how they got their thoughts and feelings across to their readers. Where candidates kept their focus on exactly what each of the climbers thought and felt as they climbed were able to accumulate creditable marks from the first bullet point, particularly if they shaped their responses around the words ‘felt’ and ‘thought’. As with 1.5 it was usually better for candidates to deal with each text separately, although both climbers felt tired and in pain during parts of their climb and both thought about the dangers of slipping and falling.

In the newspaper article, Molyneaux began discussing how he felt at the beginning of the climb, explaining that he felt exhausted and then in pain. However, he felt better when he could distract himself from the tiredness by singing ‘Lose Yourself’ as he climbed. When he did get to the top of the mountain, he clearly felt it was a wonderful experience when he says, “it really does feel like being on top of the world.” For the descent, he recalls that he had to “concentrate every second” and think about “where you are putting each foot and hand.” He admitted he felt “nervous at times” but knew he just had to keep focusing. In Isabella Bird’s account, she made her feelings and thoughts about the climb very clear. At times she felt it was “impossible to continue” and felt scared when she encountered loose rocks that “tumbled down when touched”, describing her feelings as those of “extreme terror.” She wrote about her feelings of “fatigue and pain” and that she certainly would have given up the climb, were it not for Jim Nugent’s constant support and determination for her to succeed.

16 She wrote about the “terrifying cliff” that she came upon and her thought that one slip would lead to certain death. She also wrote about how she felt “tortured with thirst” before getting to the top of the mountain where her pain and fatigue were overtaken by the feeling that it was “wonderful” to see spread before her the views of the mountains around her. Some candidates found it difficult to confine their focus to the thoughts and feelings of the climbers as they climbed and gave details about Jules’ preparation or why he wanted to climb the Matterhorn in the first place. Similarly, some wrote about Bird’s decision to climb Long’s Peak or that she had “no head for heights”, but exploring these details brought no reward. However, those who kept the focus on the thoughts and feelings of Jules and Isabella while they were climbing were able to gain good reward, even before the exploration of the second bullet point.

The writers got their thoughts and feelings across to readers in rather different ways. For example, Molyneaux made clear how he feels by using similes on occasions. He wrote about the narrowness of the ledges as he made his descent as feeling like he was “standing on a knife edge” or that his legs started “to feel like jelly” to capture his feelings of anxiety. He also used precise details about the focus and concentration needed during the descent, having to “concentrate every second” and check “one step after the other.” In Bird’s account she was self-deprecating, comparing herself to “a bale of goods” being hauled up by Nugent. She used exaggeration to emphasise her fear during the climb, saying her “feet were paralysed”, and adjectives like ‘towered’, ‘gigantic’ and ‘enormous’ to emphasise the size and scale of the mountain.

Where candidates were clear about responding to the bullet points to build and shape their responses, they could select from a range of textual details, and the best candidates were also able to comment on how the writers made their views clear. However, too many drifted from the focus of the bullet points and included details that brought limited reward. Some weaker responses lacked clarity about which text was being referred to and some responses were very brief. It also became clear that a significant minority of candidates struggled to manage their time and as a result, failed to tackle this final reading question altogether.
c700u20-nov23-21-q:
In the first of the two writing tasks candidates were asked to write an article for a teenage magazine with the title: ‘The importance of friends’. Most candidates tried to explore the topic from both a general and a personal perspective, and the most successful were able to blend the two elements neatly into their responses. Many began by discussing the role a friend might play in an individual’s life: the support and help given in times of difficulty; the joint activities to be enjoyed with friends; the positive influence of a friend and so on. Responses often also included discussions about those ‘friends’ who proved to be unreliable and frequently candidates also offered suggestions about how to deal with such situations.

Less successful responses to this task were often brief and frequently lacked structure, with few links between one point of view and another and sometimes ending rather abruptly. More successful responses tended to range more widely, with particular opinions given some development. As indicated above, the best responses often fused general opinions or points about the nature of friendship with personal reflections on the candidate’s own situation or anecdotes that illustrated the point of view raised about either a ‘true friend’ or in some instances a group of friends that had proved to be supportive and helpful.

17 It is worth the reminder about the expectation that responses should be 300-400 words; where responses were much briefer than this, it almost certainly impacted negatively on the range and development of the content and made it difficult to achieve marks in the upper bands for communication and organisation.
c700u20-nov23-22-q:
This second task was to write a letter to a newspaper in response to a comment that had appeared in a letter in a previous edition. This offered the view, “My local supermarket shelves seem to be increasingly filled with vegetarian and vegan products. Will we all be expected to stop eating meat in the near future? What about personal choice?” The task offered the opportunity to express a viewpoint in a formal register and develop that viewpoint with a series of reasons, explained and supported by convincing information, personal anecdotes, ‘expert’ evidence and so on.

There were 12 marks available for communication and organisation, so it was disappointing that some candidates took little or no opportunity to organise their work as a letter. Showing an understanding about how a formal letter should be presented involved some illustration of address layout (my address/their address/suitable salutation and sign off is acceptable) so it was unfortunate that some candidates ignored this entirely. It was perhaps no surprise that those candidates who took care over the layout of the letter were often those who were able to adopt an appropriate register most successfully and whose work also had the most convincing content.

As in other examination series, the most successful pattern for the letter was to offer a brief introduction establishing why the letter was written and giving the writer’s opinion on the subject, followed by three to five paragraphs each dealing with a specific reason for the overall viewpoint, and ending with a brief concluding paragraph and sign off.

There were plenty of reasons advanced by candidates, either in opposition to increasing vegan and vegetarian products at the expense of the range of meat available, or supporting the move to increase non-meat options on environmental, ethical or religious grounds. It was the quality of the arguments that earned reward and whilst some tried to adopt a more neutral stance, those who were able to advance a clear viewpoint, developing each of their arguments in detail, perhaps by good explanation or by using specific supporting examples or anecdotes, tended to write the more convincing letters. It was important, too, that candidates read the task carefully; the letter to be written was intended for readers of the newspaper and as a response to the original letter indicated in the task details. Although most candidates understood who was to be the recipient of the letter, some candidates believed it was the newspaper editor who had decreed that supermarkets should stock fewer meat products, whilst others wrote their letters to the manager of their local supermarket, sometimes losing the thread of their argument and drifting into overlong suggestions about the design of the supermarket and where products should be placed in the store.

This final task on the examination paper suffered if candidates had not managed their time effectively and examiners saw too many brief responses, where the content lacked range and development of the argument, and unfortunately there were also too many candidates who failed to tackle the task at all. As has been reported in previous examination series, there are still too many candidates whose basic accuracy with spelling, punctuation and sentence construction and control remains an issue and this frequently resulted in their work gaining marks in a lower band for VSSPS than for their communication and organisation.

18 Characteristics of successful responses

• In the reading section, successful responses showed methodical tracking through the texts, with candidates selecting appropriate textual details as they worked through each paragraph, explaining the significance of the detail or quotation. • In the most successful responses, there was always a clear focus on the question. For example, in question 1.6 successful answers used the words ‘thought/thinks’ and ‘felt/feeling’ a number of times in the response, which limited any ‘drift’ from the question. • Reading questions worth 10 marks were answered with a wide range of textual details that showed good coverage of the whole text, and with comments and explanations on them that showed insight and perception. • In the writing section, successful responses were always well-sustained, showed a clear understanding of the intended audience and had shape and structure, often with paragraphs that began with a clear topic sentence, four or five sentences that explored the focus or topic of that paragraph, with the best showing the ability to neatly link one paragraph to the next. • Successful letters (the 2.2 task) showed understanding of an appropriate register and organisation of a formal letter and were able to construct convincingly developed arguments in a variety of ways.

Areas for Improvement

• In the reading section, although candidates will be anxious to ‘put pen to paper’, of even greater importance is knowing exactly what the question is asking of them. For example, in question 1.5 some candidates gave details about Jules and Isabella, rather than Molyneaux’s father and Jim Nugent; as a result, and however much they wrote, they gained no marks. • Where candidates select and use textual details/quotations in questions 1.2, 1.4 and 1.6 they should comment, contextualise or explain why or how they reflect the focus of the question. • Reading questions worth 10 marks were sometimes responded to very briefly, with few details from the text, or details that showed only a limited section of the whole text had been used in the answer. • In the writing section, it was clear some candidates had failed to manage their time and gave themselves too much to tackle in too little time in Section B, so these written responses were often brief, limited in range or development and lacked structure. …
c700u20-nov24-11-q: The first question focused on the newspaper article, `England beat Germany 2-1 in Women’s Euro 2022 final.` As usual, there were three one-mark questions requiring candidates to select details from across the text. Although these were straightforward `search and find` questions it was important that candidates read these carefully, as well as the text. The first part of the question simply asked for the name of the player who scored England’s winning goal; this information - Chloe Kelly - came in the second paragraph of the report and almost all candidates were able to find this correctly. The second part of the question should have been equally straightforward, as it asked for the name of the German player who scored the equalising goal. The answer was contained in the fifth paragraph, Lina Magull, but there were too many responses that only gave the name of the team Magull played for, Bayern Munich, rather than her name. The dangers of inefficient copying from the text were obvious. The final part of the question, which asked candidates to explain the reaction of England’s head coach at the end of the game, required the whole of the text to be read, as the information that Sarina Weigman `began to dance with happiness`, was in the penultimate paragraph. Most located the detail without difficulty but some focused instead on the reaction of the England captain and quoted what she had said. For some, the loss of a mark or even two marks, because of a failure to read carefully would have proved costly.
c700u20-nov24-12-q:
With an initial reading of the text completed, candidates should have felt prepared to tackle the next question on this text. This required them to consider how the writer, Alan Garry, had tried to capture the drama and excitement of the Euro final. This will have been a familiar type of question to many candidates and, as in previous examination series, the most effective way for candidates to tackle this type of `craft of the writer` question was to work methodically through the article, selecting appropriate details from the text, commenting on how or why these illustrated the drama or the excitement of the situation. There was plenty of material to explore and comment on.

In the opening paragraph, readers were told about the `extraordinary scenes of celebration` and how the game was won in `heart-pounding style`, and many candidates used one or both of these details to comment upon as they began their response. Others noted the details Garry gave about the size of the crowd and the way he described it as `record-breaking`, the `capacity crowd` or the `sea of England shirts`. As good candidates worked their way through the text, they often initially focused attention on the descriptions of the crowd’s behaviour to show the excitement of the supporters. Many selected and commented on details from the third paragraph, where supporters were `blowing horns and waving flags` or `roared on every England attack` or `loudly booed every refereeing decision they didn’t like.` Details about the way the crowd reacted to the game were threaded through the text and this proved a rich seam for good candidates to explore.

The game itself provided much of the drama for Garry to report on, and again, good candidates who worked methodically, captured the details of the `desperate goalmouth scramble`, how each of the goals were scored during the 90 minutes and then the drama that took the `nerve-wrenching contest` into extra time, and a `nail- biting` affair for spectators. Garry then described the goal that secured the victory for England, `the scrappiest of winning goals` but one that sent the England supporters `into a frenzy`.

The article included descriptions and details as the game finished and these offered more opportunities for exploration, particularly the scenes in the stadium, the reactions of players and the head coach, and also the `raucous celebrations` reported on around the country; these included quotations from fans, illustrating the excitement of those not at the match but watching on big screens around the country.

The most effective responses were from candidates who separated `drama` and `excitement`, as this helped them to focus clearly on specific details, which were then clearly explained or contextualised. Weaker candidates were often able to select relevant details but sometimes struggled to comment effectively about how or why they showed the drama of the game or the excitement of the spectators. Good responses also had coverage of the whole text, whilst weaker responses sometimes confined their focus to just two or three of the ten paragraphs, inevitably limiting the impact of the response. The message, often repeated in examiner reports, that merely `feature spotting` on this type of question is unlikely to be rewarded highly, appears to have been largely heeded and there was a greater focus from all candidates on trying to comment on the text itself. In some cases, weaker candidates used incomplete `sentence fragments` from the text, where a more compete quotation would have served them better; these `fragments` were often presented without a clear context and made it more difficult to comment on or explain with any precision. Occasionally too, weaker candidates tried to use ellipsis, but this often led to a quotation being reduced to a word from the beginning and a word from the end of a sentence, that then meant little and often led to a loss of focus in the comment. As in previous examinations, a clear focus on the question, working methodically through the text and linking text and comment to the question rewarded good candidates, whilst weaker candidates’ responses were often brief, had limited coverage and/or struggled to comment effectively on selected textual details.
c700u20-nov24-13-q:
This third question asked candidates to look at the second text, an account of the first official women’s football match in March 1895.

Like question 1.1, these three one-mark questions asked for specific details from the text and provided careful readers with an opportunity to accumulate marks as they gained familiarity with the text, and in readiness for the more demanding question that followed. The first part of the question simply asked how many spectators were reported to be at this match. The information was contained in the first paragraph, where readers were told `ten thousand had gathered to see the opening match of the British Ladies Football Club`. Most candidates had no difficulty with this, although some lost the specific requirement for a number and instead told examiners about a `huge throng` or that there were `train-loads` of people going to the match. The importance of reading the question carefully can never be over-emphasised. The second part of the question asked for the final score in the game, and again most could select the correct detail, 7 goals to 1, although examiners saw `7 goals` or `North won` on some responses. The final part of the question asked what was different about the ball used for the game, a detail contained in the penultimate paragraph. Most correctly noted that it was a `smaller ball than usual`, but some lost focus on the question and selected incorrect details. Whilst most candidates gained reward for all three correct answers, unfortunately these `search and find` questions again showed too many candidates not taking enough care over the reading of the question.
c700u20-nov24-14-q:
This next question asked candidates to respond to the statement: `The writer gives an entirely negative view of the first women’s official football match and women playing football`, explaining to what extent they agreed. It was very clear to the majority of candidates that the reporter was indeed critical of the skills of the women involved in the game, suggested that people would only watch women’s matches `out of curiosity` and was of the opinion that `ladies’ football matches will not attract crowds`. However, good candidates were able to recognise that the `huge throng` of spectators had been initially interested enough to see women playing football and that it had attracted 10,000 people to watch. Some commented on these details, suggesting the writer may have been open-minded at this point, although most candidates focused on the game, then described as `a huge disappointment`. In the second paragraph, the writer had focused on the costumes of the women, telling readers `they certainly made a pretty picture` and how the players were `greeted with cheers and good-humoured laughter`. Responses to these details were open to interpretation, some expressing the view that the details showed clearly the writer was sexist, mocking and patronising, others taking a more positive view, and here examiners rewarded responses that showed thoughtful consideration of the details. There was, however, little doubt that what followed in the final three paragraphs was an almost entirely critical view of women’s football. The players were described as `not having the slightest qualification to take the field` and their play `dreadful`. Readers were told that spectators felt they had `wasted their time and money` and that they left the ground early.

The penultimate paragraph gave candidates lots of material that would support the statement, some commenting on the writer’s view that describing the match was simply not worth the effort, and calling football by women to be `totally out of the question.` Many candidates homed in on the four qualities said to be required of footballers and on the writer’s comment that `not one of these qualities was apparent` in the match. Candidates who had tracked the text carefully also commented on the writer’s description of the women who `wandered aimlessly` around the field and then `danced around the ball` when it came to them. When this happened, it seemed they could kick it no further than a few yards. Some candidates used this paragraph well to support their view of the statement, but some only picked out one detail, rather than building a strong case with a range of details about the contest.

In the final paragraph, the writer offered some view that suggested there might be some positive outcome for women playing football: it could be seen as a `new and healthful form of recreation` for them but concluded the report by suggesting that `as a public entertainment it is to be deplored.` This was a question that offered opportunities to candidates to accumulate a range of relevant details to support the statement, and it was possible to gain very good marks with a selection of detail taken from each of the five paragraphs. Some candidates tried to take a more balanced view, but the weight of evidence in the text made this difficult, and some less successful responses simply offered two or three quotations from the text with simple and/or limited comments. Very brief responses struggled to move into Band 3, mainly because of the limitations of range. That said, examiners saw some good and often insightful responses that gained very creditable marks.
c700u20-nov24-15-q: This question, asking for the ability to select and synthesise materials from the two texts, asked candidates to give the details of the football kits worn by the two teams in the two football games. As always with this type of question, selecting specific details with precision and clarity meant good candidates could gain good marks without writing at great length. In the Euro 2022 game, readers were told that England played in white shirts and white shorts, while Germany played in dark green shirts and shorts. In the 1895 game, the North team played in red blouses, black knickerbockers, red caps and brown leather boots, while the South team played in similar kit but with blouses of light and dark blue squares and blue caps. Where candidates adopted the decision to be clear and precise, they inevitably gained full marks, but too many failed to gain the four marks available, in some cases by only giving the kit of one of the teams in the match, giving only general, often vague details (`they played in shirts and shorts`) or not identifying specific teams – or in some cases, which game.
c700u20-nov24-16-q:
Although this final reading question focused on a comparison of the two texts, as in previous examinations, candidates were asked to do this by specifically focusing on the two bullet points as the basis for the comparison. Candidates who chose to ignore the bullet points rarely gained good marks.

In the first bullet point, candidates were asked to compare the impressions the writers created of the spectators who watched the games at Wembley and the Crouch End ground, and the second bullet point asked how the writers had created those impressions. It was the type of question candidates will have seen in previous examinations (summer 2023 for example), and where candidates kept their focus on `impressions`, it was possible to make good progress quickly. In the Euro 2022 article, for example, it was clear that one impression of the spectators in the stadium was that they were noisy, loudly giving their `raucous` support to the team. These spectators were also hugely supportive, passionate and excited for their team, Garry describing the way they showed their support for the team, whether by `blowing horns and waving flags`, booing the referee when they disagreed with decisions or roaring on every England attack. There were also points in the game where the supporters appeared nervous about the outcome, whether as a result of the `dramatic equaliser` by Germany or the game going into extra time, when `nail-biting intensified` for these spectators. Finally, the impression of these spectators at the end of the game was one of celebrating joyously at the result, as readers were told of the `extraordinary scenes of celebration` and of `jubilation in the stands.` These impressions served as a real contrast to the impressions of those attending the 1895 game, where at the outset, the most that could be said was that spectators were `curious` to see what the game would bring.

Perhaps it could be argued that another impression of the spectators was that their `good-humoured laughter` as the players took the field suggested they may have been initially supportive. However, it became quickly obvious that many spectators were disappointed by what they witnessed on the field and `felt they had wasted their time and money`, the writer telling readers that `people began leaving before the game was half-way through`.

Where candidates could link textual details with a specific impression of the spectators in each text, and then move on to explore a second or a third impression, they quickly gained reward, the best responses moving confidently between the two texts and using appropriate detail to illustrate and support these impressions. Weaker responses were often brief and limited and sometimes drifted from the focus of the bullet points into more general comparisons, such as the difference in the size of the crowds or the final scores in the two games, but gaining little reward. It also became clear that a significant minority of candidates struggled to manage their time and as a result, failed to tackle this final reading question altogether.
c700u20-nov24-21-q:
In the first of the two writing tasks candidates were asked to respond to an extract from a letter to a national newspaper in which a view had been expressed suggesting schools gave too much emphasis to exams, to the detriment of `other important things` pupils should be learning about. Voluntary work, learning to manage money and learning more practical skills were given as examples of what schools should be offering. All candidates had some views to offer on this topic, some explaining that exams were vital for good work or further education opportunities, whilst others took the view that life-skills, such as learning to manage money, were so important they merited a key place in the curriculum. Others felt examinations disadvantaged some students who had skills and knowledge not tested in an examination room. Many drew on their own personal experiences and it was clear that there was a genuine engagement with the topic.

Good responses managed to adopt a suitably formal tone and showed an awareness of the intended readership; these letters often showed some understanding of how to set out the addresses correctly and had a clear idea about how to structure their work. A clear explanation about why the letter had been written, the reaction to the original letter and something of the writer’s views on the topic was all that was needed for an effective opening paragraph. This was then followed by two to four paragraphs, dealing in more detail about a specific point the writer wanted to raise, but developed with examples, personal anecdotes, more information about the point raised and so on. The best responses showed the ability to introduce, develop and then sustain an argument convincingly; these responses were then often able to make a neat link between one paragraph to what then followed in the subsequent paragraph. A final paragraph, often no more than two or three sentences, that brought the letter to a neat, often convincing conclusion again marked out strong, assured responses. Less successful responses were often brief, some significantly shorter than the 300-400 words indicated in the exam paper, and as a result, these struggled to develop the points raised in any detail; often, brief and weaker responses offered only general concerns about a limited curriculum, sometimes only repeating what had been said in the original letter, but with little development.
c700u20-nov24-22-q:
This second task asked candidates to write a speech to try to persuade their fellow students to vote for them in the school/college elections for student president, saying why they would be a good choice and giving details of the issues they would seek to pursue with the headteacher, for the benefit of students and the school.

As with the first task, many candidates had plenty to say and the best responses balanced the need to persuade their peers why they were the ideal choice, with some clear suggestions for improvements that needed to be made. While some candidates had borrowed slogans from recent political rallies (`Make XX School Great Again`) and went to some length to extol the qualities only they possessed, others made it clear that previous student presidents had failed to bring about changes and that the other candidates in the forthcoming election were unconvincing. The `improvements` that needed a strong student president to bring about often seemed to involve toilets or the school dining room, with lots of details about what was wrong and how things could be improved. Other responses advocated even more radical changes: no school on Fridays, extended lunch breaks, free or greatly reduced lunch prices, reductions to homework, and reviews of detention policies were all among the subjects that the prospective school presidents warmed to and promised that they would bring about change. It would have been interesting to know how their headteachers would have responded to such changes.

Good responses captured a sense of the speaker’s passion and persuasiveness when they described their `fitness for office`. There were many claims that as the new student president they would ensure other students’ voices would be listened to and when they moved on to the improvements they wanted to make, they described the current concern and tried to explain how they would approach the issue with the headteacher and governors, giving details and in some cases facts and figures to support their case. These good responses were sustained, engaging and persuasive. Weaker responses were often too brief or lacked specific detail, and in some cases became little more than a list of complaints about the school, with few clear or developed suggestions for improvement. As this was the final task in the exam, unfortunately there were also too many candidates who failed to tackle the task at all. Across both of the writing tasks, basic accuracy remained an issue, with too many candidates being given marks in a lower band for VSSPS than for communication and organisation.

Characteristics of successful responses

• In the reading section, good responses showed care in the reading of the question, a willingness to track the whole text methodically and to select a good range of textual details upon which to comment. • In successful responses, comments were always linked to the key words in the question. For example, in question 1.2 good answers kept a clear focus on the `drama` and the `excitement` of the Euro final – and these key words were to be found in many of the sentences in the response. • Reading questions worth 10 marks had sustained responses that covered a number of points or details, and these were commented upon with some perception and in some cases, with insight. • Candidates used quotations to good effect and with precision, contextualising and/or giving clear explanation of their effect where appropriate. • In the writing section, responses were well-sustained, and were shaped and structured effectively (some examination scripts contained an outline content plan, showing thought and planning before the writing had been tackled). • Basic accuracy and control were features of good responses, with some attempt at using a more extended vocabulary.

Areas for Improvement • Careful reading of the questions is vital, and errors in the 1.1 and 1.3 `search and find` questions show that this is still an area where candidates can make improvements. • Candidates do not always use quotations effectively. Where this is the case, they are sometimes only `sentence fragments` that lack clarity or need more explanation. It is better for candidates to make use of a longer quotation, even a full sentence, rather than a fragment that makes limited sense on its own. • Very brief responses on 10-mark reading questions are almost inevitably limited in terms of coverage and unlikely to progress beyond Band 2. • Writing tasks are expected to be 300-400 words; where responses are much shorter, both the range and the development of the content are limited as a result. • Time management remains a key issue for too many candidates. Missing out a reading question and/or not tackling one of the writing tasks significantly limits the chances of real success in the examination.
